file: 2000/2000-05-07_presidential candiditae_funny haired one_social policies_exact opposite_tax plan_bad plan_make out_like intelligent men_she lied.gif
title: Voter Gets Lectured Before Date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which presidential candidate do you like?

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I strongly favor the one with the funny hair. I forgot his name.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: His social policies are the exact opposite of your views.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Well, I like his tax plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every credible economist thinks it's a bad plan.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a good thing we talked before you polluted the system with your vote.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want to make out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She claimed to like intelligent men but she lied.

setting: Outdoor hillside path on a walk
situation: Dilbert walks with a date and asks which presidential candidate she likes. She picks the one with funny hair, not knowing his name or his policies, and Dilbert condescendingly corrects her on his social and tax positions. After insulting her uninformed vote, he asks if she wants to make out, and she angrily refuses.
punchline: Dilbert insults his date's political ignorance and then is surprised that she won't kiss him, showing his smug arrogance is the real problem, not her intelligence.
summary: A man belittles his date's uninformed voting preferences with a lecture on policy and then wonders why romance fails.

file: 2000/2000-02-12_cynics annoymous_naive sense_trust_paid dues_beer_gambling cruis.gif
title: Cynics Anonymous Spends Dilbert's Dues

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Cynics Anonymous

transcript.speaker: Audience member
transcript.text: My company sent me here to regain my naive sense of trust.

transcript.speaker: Group leader
transcript.text: All in favor of using Dilbert's company-paid dues on beer, say aye.

transcript.speaker: Group leader
transcript.text: Make sure you sign up for our gambling cruise.

setting: A meeting room where a Cynics Anonymous support group is gathered
situation: At a Cynics Anonymous meeting, one attendee says his company sent him to regain his naive sense of trust. The group leader then calls a vote to spend Dilbert's company-paid dues on beer and promotes a gambling cruise as the attendees drink.
punchline: A group meant to cure cynicism immediately gives the newcomer reasons to distrust it by spending his dues on beer and pushing a gambling cruise, so his trust is destroyed on the spot.
summary: A support group for curing cynicism promptly proves itself untrustworthy by blowing a newcomer's dues on drinks and gambling.

file: 2000/2000-09-27_forty million dollars_needs approval_over budget_whose side.gif
title: Saving Millions, Costing Ten Thousand

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This needs your approval.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The company will save forty million dollars but you'll be ten thousand over budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And before you ask, no it won't work the other way around.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whose side are you on?

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a document needing approval and explains that it will save the company forty million dollars but push the Boss's own department ten thousand dollars over budget. He preemptively adds that the trade-off can't be reversed. The Boss, reading the paper, responds by asking whose side Dilbert is on.
punchline: The Boss cares only about his own department's budget and treats a forty-million-dollar company-wide saving as disloyalty to him personally.
summary: A manager reacts to a huge corporate savings proposal as a betrayal because it slightly dents his own department's numbers.

file: 2000/2000-08-19_brenda utthead_email addresses_first inutial_plus last name_whiner_butthead.gif
title: Email Address Name Pun Rejected

transcript.speaker: Brenda
transcript.text: I know our e-mail addresses are supposed to be our first initial plus our last name.

transcript.speaker: Brenda
transcript.text: But could you make an exception?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That Brenda Utthead is quite a whiner.

situation: A female employee named Brenda approaches the boss's desk and politely reminds him that email addresses are the first initial plus last name. She asks for an exception, and he flatly refuses. He then privately thinks she is a whiner, not realising that her name makes her email address an unfortunate one.
punchline: Brenda's last name is Utthead, so the standard first-initial-plus-surname email address would spell out an insult, and the boss callously refuses her reasonable request while calling her the whiner.
summary: A woman with an unfortunate surname asks her unsympathetic boss to bend the email naming rule and gets stonewalled.

file: 2000/2000-05-29_antimicrobial polymer_pick up lines_two women_stinky socks_turn off_a no no.gif
title: Dilbert's Disastrous Sock Pick-Up Line

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My socks use an antimicrobial polymer to bond chlorine atoms to cotton.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can wear these babies for days before they start to stink.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What was that other pick-up line we talked about?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It was "Hi."

setting: A social party with guests holding drinks, then Dilbert's home
situation: At a party, Dilbert tries to impress two women by bragging about his socks' antimicrobial polymer and how many days he can wear them without stinking. The women look unimpressed. Back at home, Dilbert asks Dogbert what the other pick-up line was, and Dogbert reminds him it was simply "Hi."
punchline: Dilbert chose an absurdly nerdy and off-putting boast about unwashed socks over the simple, obvious greeting his friend had suggested.
summary: A socially awkward engineer tries to charm women at a party with tech talk about his long-wearing socks, then learns the better opener was a simple greeting.

file: 2000/2000-03-05_new personlaity_non standard_approved corporate personalities_sycophants glad hander_sadist_prima donna_empty suit_whining misfit_spec sheet_dialoque.gif
title: Choose Your Approved Corporate Personality

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We've decided to give you a new personality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your current personality is non-standard.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You must choose one of the approved corporate personalities.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The choices are sycophant, glad-hander, sadist, quantoid, prima donna, empty suit or whining misfit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Empty suit sounds interesting.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Excellent choice. Here's the spec sheet.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How did it go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Same ol' same ol'. You got that right.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, then a hallway or cubicle area
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells Dilbert that his personality is non-standard and he must adopt one of the approved corporate personalities from a list of unflattering types. Dilbert chooses 'empty suit' and receives a spec sheet. Afterward, Wally asks how it went.
punchline: Dilbert's new 'empty suit' personality is indistinguishable from his usual self, so the mandated personality overhaul changes nothing, and Wally's greeting is answered with a stock, empty phrase.
summary: Human resources forces an employee to pick from a menu of dreadful stock personalities, and the one he selects turns out to describe how he already behaves.

file: 2000/2000-03-26_points at screen_oily finger_clean screen_hover finger_losing aura of infalliability.gif
title: Boss Obsesses Over Finger Oil

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, move that title...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...over here.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: AAAGH!!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Your finger oil is on my screen!!!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Now I have to spend ten minutes cleaning it...

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: ...because you don't understand how to hover your finger.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: See?! This isn't hard. You hover the finger! Don't touch!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope I'm not losing my aura of infallibility.

situation: The Boss leans over Tina's shoulder and points at her monitor to tell her where to move a title, accidentally touching the screen. Tina explodes in anger about his finger oil, scolds him that she must spend ten minutes cleaning it, and lectures him on how to hover a finger without touching. The Boss stands by meekly and worries about his image.
punchline: The Boss, normally domineering, is scolded like a child by a subordinate over a smudged screen, and his only concern is whether he's lost his aura of infallibility, which is obviously already gone.
summary: A meek boss gets chewed out by an employee for leaving a fingerprint on her monitor and frets about his authority.

file: 2000/2000-06-04_bikini pics_dismissal_technically_magnetic media_zeros and ones_auditors_40 gigs of pics.gif
title: Wally Pleads Innocent: Just Zeroes and Ones

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, our auditors found 40 gigabits of bikini pictures on your PC.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That is grounds for dismissal. How do you plead?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Innocent.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Technically, they didn't find any pictures.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What they found were zeroes and ones resting harmlessly on magnetic media.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was the auditors themselves who activated those harmless bits to form pictures on the screen!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I demand that those godless auditors be fired!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And if it's not too much trouble, I'd like my zeroes and ones back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was justice served?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a gray area.

setting: Catbert's courtroom-style H.R. tribunal, then an office hallway
situation: Catbert, as evil H.R. director, sits as judge and charges Wally with having 40 gigabits of bikini pictures on his PC. Wally pleads innocent on a technicality, arguing the auditors only found zeroes and ones on magnetic media and that the auditors themselves created the pictures. He demands the auditors be fired and his data returned, then tells Dilbert the outcome is a gray area.
punchline: Wally uses absurd pseudo-technical hair-splitting to claim stored image data isn't really pictures, and the 'gray area' remark hints the ruling was murky, with the bikini pictures possibly being the very thing that's gray.
summary: Accused of hoarding swimsuit photos, a lazy engineer defends himself by insisting his hard drive only holds harmless binary digits until someone else turns them into images.

file: 2000/2000-08-24_part time work_finish urgent projects_pay cut_come in on day off.gif
title: Part-Time Work, Full-Time Pay Cut

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Would it be okay if I worked part time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That depends.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you be willing to come in on your days off to finish urgent projects?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, basically you negotiated a fifty percent pay cut?

setting: The Boss's office, then a meeting room or lunch table
situation: A female employee asks the Boss if she can work part time. He agrees only if she will still come in on her days off to finish urgent projects. Afterward, Dilbert points out that she has effectively just taken a fifty percent pay cut for the same workload.
punchline: The part-time arrangement is a sham: she'll still work full time but now gets paid half, so she negotiated herself a pay cut.
summary: An employee's request for shorter hours is granted on terms that leave her working just as much for half the money.

file: 2000/2000-04-22_company saidst_fist of death_note from author_big bag_dumpster_disclaimer_nothing bad happened.gif
title: Alice Confronts Company Sadist, Disclaimer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Company Sadist

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay, Sadist, it's time to meet the fist of death.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Note from the author

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: If you are the sort of person who is influenced by comic strips, I assure you nothing bad or violent happens next. Alice and the Sadist discuss their differences and become lifelong friends.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What was in that big bag I helped you drag to the dumpster?

setting: Office cubicle area and break room
situation: Alice, fists clenched, threatens the Company Sadist with the 'fist of death'. A mock note from the author then reassures readers that nothing violent happens and the two become friends. In the final panel Alice sits with Dilbert and Wally at lunch while Dilbert asks what was in the big bag they dragged to the dumpster.
punchline: The author's disclaimer claims no violence occurred, but Dilbert's question about the heavy bag they disposed of implies Alice actually killed the Sadist and hid the body.
summary: A cartoonist's soothing assurance that a confrontation ended peacefully is undercut by a coworker's innocent question about a suspicious bag.

file: 2000/2000-03-19_dozen bugs_bugs in software_fix for 20k_defective porduct_evil euphria_no choice_making fortune_single source tsrategy.gif
title: Vendor Profits From Its Own Bugs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We found a dozen bugs in the software you sold us.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: We can fix these bugs for $20,000.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't charge us to fix your own defective product!

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Buwahaha!!

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Sorry... I was overcome by an evil euphoria.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess we have to pay. We have no choice!

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Excuse me.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Put more bugs in the software! I'm making a fortune out here!

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Phbllt!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm starting to question our single source strategy.

setting: Dilbert's office or a meeting room
situation: Dilbert confronts a software vendor about a dozen bugs in the product they sold his company. The vendor calmly offers to fix them for $20,000, laughs maniacally at the idea, and then admits Dilbert has no choice but to pay. Once on the phone, the vendor tells his developers to put more bugs in the software because he's making a fortune.
punchline: Because the company relies on a single vendor, the vendor profits from its own defective product and is even motivated to introduce more bugs, which Dilbert only realizes too late.
summary: A supplier happily bills a customer to repair flaws in its own faulty software and then orders its team to create more of them.

file: 2000/2000-03-07_dont pay enough_hire brilliant people_web team_stock options.gif
title: Web Team Seeks Unaware Savants

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: We don't pay enough to hire brilliant people for our web team.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I need webiot savants who don't know they should have better jobs.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'd expect stock options, of course.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Next!!

situation: Tina explains to the Boss that the company can't afford to pay brilliant people for its web team, so she wants talented people who don't realize their own worth. In an interview, a candidate who sensibly asks for stock options is immediately rejected.
punchline: A candidate who knows his market value and asks for stock options is dismissed instantly, showing the company only wants talent that is clueless enough to accept a bad deal.
summary: A manager hunting for cheap web talent dismisses the first applicant who shows any awareness of what his skills are worth.

file: 2000/2000-07-19_global communications_de orbiting satellites_swimming pools_deadly flame balls_speeding toward earth.gif
title: Satellites Aimed at Swimming Pools

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll be shutting down our global communications business and de-orbiting our satellites.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Wouldn't that create dozens of deadly flame balls speeding toward Earth?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why we're aiming for cities that have lots of swimming pools.

situation: The Boss presents a plan to shut down the company's global communications business and bring its satellites out of orbit. Dilbert raises his hand and asks whether that would send deadly flaming debris toward Earth. The Boss cheerfully answers that they are targeting cities with lots of swimming pools, as if that solves the danger.
punchline: The Boss treats swimming pools as an adequate safety measure against falling flaming satellites, showing how absurdly little thought management gives to catastrophic consequences.
summary: A manager explains that his cost-cutting satellite shutdown is safe because the burning wreckage will be steered toward pool-rich neighborhoods.

file: 2000/2000-01-25_expletive_fourth letter_myers briggs test_phb_nasty.gif
title: Boss Classified as PHB Personality

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I have the results of your Myers-Briggs personality test.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You've been classified as a "PHB."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There's a fourth letter, but that was for an expletive.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, stands at the Boss's desk holding the results of his Myers-Briggs personality test. He announces that the Boss has been classified as a "PHB," a three-letter code like the real test's four-letter types. Catbert then says a fourth letter exists but was replaced by an expletive.
punchline: Catbert insults the Boss by implying his personality type is the Pointy-Haired Boss and that the missing fourth letter stands for a swear word describing him.
summary: The HR cat delivers a personality test verdict to his boss that is really just a thinly veiled insult.

file: 2000/2000-08-31_network server_certifed_power of certifciation_embarrassing_c for certified_superman tech_class_forgets.gif
title: Certified Superhero Forgets His Training

transcript.speaker: Certified Man
transcript.text: Step away from that network server!

transcript.speaker: Certified Man
transcript.text: I'm certified!

transcript.speaker: Certified Man
transcript.text: I summon the vast power of certification!

transcript.speaker: Certified Man
transcript.text: Well, this is embarrassing; that's all I remember from the classes.

setting: Office cubicle with a computer at Dilbert's desk
situation: Dilbert is working at his computer when a man in a blue costume with a red cape and a "C" on his chest orders him away from the network server, claiming he is certified. He dramatically invokes the power of certification, then sheepishly admits that he cannot actually remember anything from his certification classes.
punchline: A person who relies on his certification as a source of authority turns out to have retained no actual knowledge, so the credential is all show and no substance.
summary: A caped coworker boasts of his credentials to push a colleague away from the server, only to confess he learned nothing in the courses that earned them.

file: 2000/2000-03-11_higher drag coefficient_interns head_quantify benefits_knowledge management.gif
title: Measuring Knowledge Management With Intern Heads

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've been asked to quantify the benefits of our knowledge management systems.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I measured our intern's head to see if it got bigger.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The higher drag coefficient means we lost a little in the sandwich-fetching department.

situation: Alice reports to The Boss on her assignment to quantify the benefits of the company's knowledge management systems. Her method is to measure the intern's head, shown on a slide, to see whether it grew from absorbed knowledge. She concludes the head's larger drag coefficient means the intern got slower at fetching sandwiches.
punchline: The only measurable effect of the expensive knowledge management system is a bigger-headed intern who is worse at fetching sandwiches, implying the system delivers no real value and may even make things worse.
summary: An employee presents a absurdly literal metric for judging a corporate knowledge system and reaches a useless, backhanded conclusion.

file: 2000/2000-04-18_self paced_online training_sharpen my saw_subject_don't know subject_confusing.gif
title: Self-Paced Training Course Mystery Subject

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been taking a self-paced online training course to "sharpen my saw."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the subject?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could you not know?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What part of "self-paced" is confusing you?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he has been taking a self-paced online training course to sharpen his saw. When Dilbert asks what the subject is, the Boss admits he doesn't know, and when Dilbert is astonished, the Boss responds as if Dilbert is the one being slow.
punchline: The Boss treats 'self-paced' as an explanation for why he hasn't learned anything, not even the topic, implying he has made no progress and that Dilbert is being unreasonable for questioning it.
summary: A manager boasts about an online course he has apparently never actually started, then blames his colleague's confusion on the course format.

file: 2000/2000-01-08_managing instanct_belly button lint_leave employee_unhygenic_weird_intimate_gone too far.gif
title: Boss Manages By Belly Button Lint

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got a good crop of lint in my belly button today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll leave it on Dilbert's keyboard.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder if there's such a thing as managing too much by instinct.

setting: Office, around Dilbert's cubicle and desk
situation: The Boss, in thought bubbles throughout, notes that he has collected a good amount of belly button lint. He decides on impulse to deposit it on Dilbert's keyboard, then walks away wondering whether he is relying too much on instinct in his management style.
punchline: The Boss treats an absurd, gross impulse as legitimate management instinct, and only mildly wonders whether he is overdoing it.
summary: A boss decides to dump his navel lint on an employee's keyboard and then muses about whether he leans too heavily on his gut.

file: 2000/2000-01-18_twenty year car lease_investment_hidden fees_burglar guard house_wag.gif
title: Paying Dogbert to Guard Against Fees

transcript.speaker: Man in red cap
transcript.text: This investment combines the best features of an annuity plus a twenty-year car lease.

transcript.speaker: Man in red cap
transcript.text: How can I tell if there are hidden fees?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can pay me 1% per year to advise you.

transcript.speaker: Man in red cap
transcript.text: Wouldn't that be like paying a burglar to guard my house?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Excuse me while I wag.

setting: Dogbert's financial advisory office, with a desk between Dogbert and a client
situation: A client in a red cap sits across a desk from Dogbert, who is pitching a dubious investment that combines an annuity with a twenty-year car lease. When the client asks how to spot hidden fees, Dogbert offers to advise him for a 1% annual fee. The client points out this is like hiring a burglar to guard his house, and Dogbert cheerfully wags his tail.
punchline: Dogbert, a financial advisor, is the very source of the hidden fees and conflicts of interest, and he gleefully accepts the burglar comparison as a compliment by wagging his tail.
summary: A skeptical customer worries about concealed charges in an odd financial product, only to be offered more fee-based advice from the same shady salesman.

file: 2000/2000-04-27_new engineering liason_claims of meaning.gif
title: Liaison Title Raises Romantic Hopes

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I understand you're the new engineering liaison.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Does that mean what I think it means?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: She claims it doesn't mean that.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ohhh.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, approaches a woman at her desk and says he heard she is the new engineering liaison, then asks whether the title means what he thinks it means. After she answers, he reports to Asok, who is clutching a bouquet of flowers, that she claims it doesn't mean that. Asok sadly realizes his romantic expectations are off base.
punchline: Wally and Asok interpret the word 'liaison' as a romantic or sexual arrangement, and the woman's denial leaves Asok holding flowers for nothing.
summary: Two coworkers misread a job title as a romantic invitation and get shot down, leaving a hopeful young engineer with an unwanted bouquet.

file: 2000/2000-04-28_demons possessed_view websites_unspeakable abominations_approve the purchase.gif
title: Demon-Possessed PC Upgrade Scam

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Demons have possessed my PC. They force me to view web sites of unspeakable abominations.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The only solution is for you to approve the purchase of a new PC for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How are the unspeakable abominations today?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Much faster!

setting: Office, in the boss's office and then at Wally's cubicle
situation: Wally tells the boss that demons have possessed his computer and force him to browse web sites of unspeakable abominations, and that the only fix is buying him a new PC. Later Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, asks how the abominations are today, and Wally, seated at his new computer, cheerfully says they are much faster.
punchline: Wally's demon story was just a ruse to get a new computer, and he reveals he is still viewing the same objectionable sites, only now at higher speed.
summary: A workplace slacker spins a supernatural tale to wangle a hardware upgrade, then admits the questionable browsing simply runs quicker now.

file: 2000/2000-05-31_call me_documenting everything_do anything.gif
title: Boss Documents Employee for Firing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm documenting everything you do so I can easily fire you someday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could call me if you do anything.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Leave it here and I'll fill it out for you.

situation: The Boss stands over Wally's desk with a notepad and announces he is documenting everything Wally does so he can fire him someday. He then asks Wally to call him whenever he actually does anything. Wally responds by offering to fill out the documentation form himself.
punchline: Wally, who does almost no work, turns the boss's plan to build a paper trail against him into another way to avoid effort by offering to write his own file.
summary: A manager plans to build a case for dismissal, but the lazy employee simply offers to do the paperwork himself.

file: 2000/2000-07-28_upgarding_sales support_unlock lexus_guy down hall_owns lexus.gif
title: Upgrade Locks Out Wrong Lexus

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished upgrading the sales support network.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Is that why I can't unlock my Lexus?!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't own a Lexus. You only look like a guy down the hall who owns one.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I hate that guy.

setting: Conference room or office meeting table
situation: Dilbert tells a salesman he has finished upgrading the sales support network. The salesman angrily asks if that is why his Lexus won't unlock. Dilbert explains that the car isn't his; he merely resembles a coworker down the hall who owns one.
punchline: The salesman has been trying to unlock someone else's Lexus because he looks like its owner, and he reacts by resenting the lookalike coworker rather than admitting his mistake.
summary: A man blames a network upgrade for his car not opening, only to learn he has been trying to get into a stranger's vehicle.

file: 2000/2000-08-10_billion dollar business plan_sec investigates_securities fraud_hancuffed_employees singing.gif
title: Business Plan Ends in Fraud Arrest

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you finished my billion dollar business plan yet?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Almost.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm up to the part where the S.E.C. investigates you for securities fraud.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't decide what the employees will be singing when you get handcuffed.

situation: The Boss asks Alice whether she has finished his billion dollar business plan. She replies that she is nearly done and is writing the section where the S.E.C. investigates him for securities fraud. She adds that she is still choosing a song for the employees to sing as he is arrested.
punchline: Alice's business plan predicts the Boss's own downfall for fraud, and she sarcastically treats his arrest as a celebration for the staff.
summary: A manager's demand for a grand business plan gets a deadpan reply forecasting his own criminal prosecution and a victory song for his staff.

file: 2000/2000-03-15_hired psychologust_handle stress_another engineer_freaking quack_outburst from alice.gif
title: Psychologist Hired, Alice Explodes, Pill Joke

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a psychologist to help you handle stress.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We need another engineer, not some freakin' quack!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is there a pill for that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I took it.

situation: The Boss tells his engineers at a meeting that he has hired a psychologist to help them handle stress. Alice furiously shouts that they need another engineer instead. The Boss asks if there is a pill to fix her anger, and Wally calmly says he already took it.
punchline: Wally's deadpan reply implies he is medicated into calm indifference, while the Boss responds to a staffing complaint by suggesting drugs instead of fixing the workload.
summary: Management offers a counselor rather than extra staff, and when an engineer erupts, the response is a joke about medication that a colleague claims to have already used.

file: 2000/2000-07-11_company a_dogbert consults_free sample_web strategy.gif
title: Dogbert's Free Sample Insults Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's a free sample of my work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So Company "A" was managed by idiots with no web strategy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What would you recommend for my company?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: First, change its name to "A".

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert standing on a filing cabinet
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, hands the Boss a report as a free sample of his work. The Boss reads that Company "A" was run by idiots with no web strategy, then asks what Dogbert would recommend for his own company. Dogbert advises him to rename it "A".
punchline: Dogbert implies the Boss's company is the idiotic one described in the sample report, since the anonymous Company "A" is clearly his own, and the Boss fails to notice.
summary: A consultant's anonymous case study turns out to describe his client, who obliviously asks for advice and gets the obvious answer.

file: 2000/2000-04-12_enlightenment_technology buddha_vanilla ice cream bowl_very wise_busy meditating.gif
title: The Technology Buddha's Secret Thoughts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take this to the Technology Buddha for enlightenment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (thought) He's busy meditating.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (thought) He must be very wise.

transcript.speaker: Technology Buddha
transcript.text: (thought) Huge bowl of vanilla ice cream.

setting: Office, the boss's desk and the Technology Buddha's office
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a paper and tells him to take it to the Technology Buddha for enlightenment. Dilbert finds the Buddha sitting calmly with his eyes closed and assumes he is meditating deeply, and therefore must be very wise. The Buddha's own thought bubble reveals he is simply daydreaming about a huge bowl of vanilla ice cream.
punchline: The calm, silent demeanor that makes someone look wise can hide a mind occupied by nothing more profound than dessert.
summary: A serene-looking company guru who seems deep in meditation is really just fantasizing about ice cream.

file: 2000/2000-05-11_marketing plan_annihilation_life on earth_serious competitor_tobacco_junk food_quarterly review.gif
title: Marketing Plan Targets All Life

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: My marketing plan calls for the annihilation of all life on Earth.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: Our only serious competitor is a company that sells tobacco and junk food.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: I'd like volunteers.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I need some accomplishments for my quarterly review.

situation: A marketing manager presents a plan to wipe out all life on Earth, justifying it by saying their only serious competitor sells tobacco and junk food. She asks for volunteers, and Asok raises his hand, hoping to earn an accomplishment for his quarterly review while Dilbert and a coworker look on.
punchline: Asok is so desperate for something to list on his performance review that he volunteers to help destroy all life on Earth.
summary: A marketing exec proposes planetary extermination to eliminate a rival, and an eager employee signs up because it would look good on his evaluation.

file: 2000/2000-03-20_more work_fewer people_future version_via time machine_porject_unmotivated.gif
title: Time Machine Solves Understaffing, Unless Demotivated

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As requested, I came up with a plan for doing more work with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A future version of me will arrive via time machine to help on the project...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...unless you say something now that makes me unmotivated.

setting: Office meeting room with a presentation easel
situation: Dilbert presents the Boss with the plan he requested for doing more work with fewer people. His plan relies on a future version of himself arriving by time machine to help with the project. He then warns the Boss that the plan fails if the Boss says something that demotivates him.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's demotivating management habits into a time-travel paradox: if the Boss discourages him, his future self will never be sent back, so the impossible plan collapses.
summary: Handed an impossible staffing demand, an engineer proposes help from his future self, a plan that only works if his manager keeps quiet.

file: 2000/2000-06-14_collaboration_defective_intranet_dogbert consults.gif
title: Dogbert Blames Employees, Recommends Cat Scans

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one uses the intranet collaboration software you sold us.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your employees are defective. I recommend cat scans.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This one is defective too.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Next in line!

situation: The Boss complains to consultant Dogbert that nobody uses the intranet collaboration software Dogbert sold the company. Dogbert claims the employees themselves are defective and recommends cat scans. Catbert, perched on a filing cabinet, 'scans' a worried employee and declares him defective too, and Dogbert calls for the next one.
punchline: Instead of admitting his software is unwanted or poorly designed, the consultant blames the employees and sells another absurd service, a cat scan, that will always find fault with them.
summary: A consultant deflects complaints about his unused software by declaring the staff faulty and sending them for pointless feline 'scans'.

file: 2000/2000-03-09_one page report_two page executive summary_spend the day_snapping underwear_elastic band.gif
title: Padding Report Versus Snapping Underwear

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you turn your one-page report into a two-page executive summary?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was planning to spend the day snapping myself with the elastic band on my underwear.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But your idea is good, too.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to expand his one-page report into a two-page executive summary, which is a pointless and backwards request. Dilbert deadpans that his alternative plan for the day was to snap himself with his underwear elastic, then politely concedes that the boss's idea is acceptable too.
punchline: Dilbert equates the boss's make-work request with the mindless self-inflicted silliness of snapping his underwear, implying both are equally worthless uses of a day.
summary: Dilbert answers a request to pad out a short report by comparing it to idly flicking his underwear waistband, then graciously calls the boss's task equally acceptable.

file: 2000/2000-02-26_bob flabeau_lifetime gullibility awar_biograohy_false memeories_herbal therapist_solid gold.gif
title: Lifetime Gullibility Award for Bob

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Lifetime Gullibility Award goes to Bob Flabeau.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I would read Bob's biography but it's comprised entirely of false memories planted by his herbal therapist.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It looks like a stick but it's solid gold.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Wow!

situation: Dogbert, standing at a podium, presents the Lifetime Gullibility Award to Bob Flabeau. He mocks Bob's life story as nothing but false memories implanted by an herbal therapist. Then Dogbert hands Bob a plain stick and claims it is solid gold, and Bob is amazed.
punchline: Bob proves he deserves the gullibility award by instantly believing that an ordinary stick is solid gold, right after hearing how easily he is fooled.
summary: A talking dog honors a man for being easily fooled and then promptly demonstrates it by tricking him with a worthless stick.

file: 2000/2000-05-22_advertsisemnst_fame_new ceo_recommend exploit_hi tech industry.gif
title: Consultant Suggests Exploiting Female CEO's Fame

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your new CEO is the most powerful woman in the hi-tech industry.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend exploiting her fame in your advertisements.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why do I have to be the one to suggest it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: CEOs love this sort of thing.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that the company's new CEO is the most powerful woman in hi-tech and advises using her fame in advertisements. The Boss then holds up a bra on a hanger and asks why he has to be the one to suggest it, implying the advertising would be sexualized. Dogbert reassures him that CEOs love this sort of thing.
punchline: The Boss twists the advice into a sleazy, sexist ad concept featuring lingerie, and Dogbert sarcastically assures him that a powerful female CEO would enjoy being objectified.
summary: A consultant's suggestion to leverage a female executive's celebrity turns into a tasteless lingerie-based marketing idea that the oblivious manager is reluctant to propose himself.

file: 2000/2000-09-05_judging people_meet new guy_training him_giant amoeba.gif
title: Boss Hires a Giant Amoeba

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet the new guy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You hired a giant amoeba?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't go around judging people by their looks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you mind...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Training him?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Keeping him moist?

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's workspace
situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a new hire that is literally a giant amoeba. When Dilbert comments on it, the Boss lectures him about not judging people by appearance, then asks him to train the newcomer. Dilbert assumes the request is about keeping the amoeba moist.
punchline: Dilbert is asked to train the new hire, but he assumes the real job is simply keeping the amoeba moist, a dig at how unsuited the hire is for the work.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for prejudice about a new coworker who is clearly a blob of protoplasm, then hands him the job of looking after it.

file: 2000/2000-01-11_air circulation_catbert_relevance_documents_email_shuffling paper_creates circulation.gif
title: Shuffling Documents Circulates Air

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Mister Catbert, could you help me see the relevance of my work to the well-being of society?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your shuffling of unimportant documents helps the air circulate.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: All of my documents are e-mail.

setting: Office, in Catbert's workspace and then at the employee's computer desk
situation: An employee asks Catbert, the evil HR director, to explain how his job benefits society. Catbert replies that the shuffling of his unimportant papers helps circulate the air. The employee sits at his computer and realizes that all his documents are e-mail, so he shuffles no paper at all.
punchline: Even the flimsy justification that paper shuffling circulates air fails, because the employee's work is entirely electronic, leaving him with no demonstrable value at all.
summary: Seeking proof his job matters, a worker is told his paper shuffling stirs the air, only to realize he handles nothing but e-mail.

file: 2000/2000-03-28_cd rom business ard_browsed personal oage_conversation.gif
title: Dating With CD-ROM Business Cards

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I reviewed your CD-ROM business card last night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I browsed your personal web page.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should do some conversation.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I already had one in my head.

setting: A restaurant table on a date
situation: Dilbert sits across from a woman at a restaurant and awkwardly talks about having studied her CD-ROM business card and personal web page. He then suggests they try some actual conversation, and she replies that she already had the conversation in her head.
punchline: Dilbert is so socially awkward and tech-obsessed that he treats a date like a data review, and his date dryly implies she has already imagined a better conversation than the one she is actually getting.
summary: A man on a dinner date can only talk about her digital business card and web page until she deadpans that she has already had the chat inside her own mind.

file: 2000/2000-02-25_worthless awards_famous people_celebrities_award ceremony_become pretigious_dogcart gullibility awards_honor_nominated.gif
title: Dogbert's Worthless Gullibility Award Scheme

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm planning to give worthless awards to famous people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If enough celebrities come to the award ceremony, it will become prestigious.

transcript.speaker: Celebrity
transcript.text: I've never heard of the Dogbert Gullibility Award, but it's an honor to be nominated.

setting: Dilbert's living room couch, then a man in a red convertible on a phone call
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch with a remote while Dogbert explains his plan to hand out meaningless awards to famous people, reasoning that enough celebrity attendees will make the ceremony seem prestigious. In the last panel, a man driving a red convertible takes a phone call and gushingly says he is honored to be nominated for the award, even though he has never heard of it.
punchline: The celebrity's eager acceptance of an award literally named for gullibility proves Dogbert's scheme works, since he is demonstrating exactly the gullibility the award is named for.
summary: Dogbert reveals a plan to manufacture prestige from a bogus honor, and a flattered driver immediately falls for it.

file: 2000/2000-05-12_untrained eye_no work_raging sea_knowledge managemnet_strategic thinking_gurgling sound.gif
title: Raging Sea of Management Knowledge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To the untrained eye it might look as if I do no work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But inside here is a raging sea of knowledge management and strategic thinking.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you hear that gurgling sound?

situation: The Boss sits at his desk talking to an employee, admitting that he appears to do no work. He taps his head and claims it holds a raging sea of knowledge management and strategic thinking, then asks if the listener heard a gurgling sound.
punchline: The Boss's supposed deep thinking is really just a gurgle, probably an empty head or a rumbling stomach, which implies he truly does no work and has no real ideas.
summary: A manager insists his idle appearance hides a torrent of brilliant strategy, but the only evidence he can offer is a mysterious gurgling noise.

file: 2000/2000-04-07_help remind you_what would dogbert do_bumper sticker_wwdd_sticker_ratbert_ask yourself.gif
title: What Would Dogbert Do Sticker

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You really should try it.

situation: Dogbert tells Ratbert to always ask himself what Dogbert would do and offers him a WWDD bumper sticker as a reminder. Ratbert grabs it, then sticks it onto Dogbert's face. Dogbert protests, and Ratbert says he really should try it.
punchline: Ratbert is following the advice and doing what Dogbert would do, which is exploiting and victimizing someone, so Dogbert becomes the target of his own scheming mindset.
summary: A pet dog hands out a motivational sticker urging imitation of himself, only to have his tiny companion follow the advice by turning the trick back on him.

file: 2000/2000-02-05_limbo_a division of heck_career limbo section_wait to be seated.gif

situation: A devil dressed as a hostess welcomes Dilbert to a place called Limbo and tells him he will be in the Career Limbo section. She then walks off and leaves him standing beside a sign telling him to wait to be seated. Dilbert, still waiting, grumbles that the service is terrible.
punchline: Dilbert complains about poor restaurant service when the whole point of Limbo is that he is stuck waiting forever with no progress, mirroring his stalled career.
summary: A devilish host parks Dilbert in an endless waiting area for stalled careers, and he mistakes eternal limbo for slow restaurant service.

file: 2000/2000-08-01_meeting_men_automatic registartion_product_business.gif
title: Planning Feature That Already Exists

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I plan to spend the next year adding automatic registration to our product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It already has that feature.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Oh.

situation: At a meeting table, a glasses-wearing engineer announces he will spend an entire year building automatic registration for the product. Dilbert points out the product already has that feature. The engineer is left with a flat 'Oh.' while the boss sits by, unbothered.
punchline: Someone has committed a year of work to a feature without ever checking that the product already includes it, showing how disconnected people can be from what they are supposedly working on.
summary: A colleague proudly outlines a year-long project, only to be told the thing he wants to build is already finished.

file: 2000/2000-05-28_fake surveillance camera_chepaer_discourage thefts_treat employees like criminals_leave.gif

transcript.text: Pssst.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Come in and shut the door.

transcript.text: I bought a fake video surveillance camera.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Install it in the break room tonight.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's cheaper than a real camera and it will discourage thefts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you treat employees like criminals, they'll leave.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good point.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'd better hide the fake camera so no one knows it's there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (humming)

situation: The Boss secretly summons Dilbert and asks him to install a cheap fake surveillance camera in the break room to discourage theft. Dilbert warns that treating employees like criminals will make them quit. The Boss agrees with the point, but his conclusion is that the fake camera should simply be hidden.
punchline: The Boss accepts Dilbert's warning about employee morale but responds by hiding the camera, which defeats its entire purpose as a theft deterrent.
summary: A manager plans a bogus security camera for the break room and, when told it will insult staff, decides concealing it solves the problem.

file: 2000/2000-05-02_asset tags_equipment_staplers_not considered equipment_asset tag man_conversation.gif

transcript.text: No one likes to make conversation with the asset tag man.

situation: An employee carrying a clipboard of papers stops at Dilbert's desk and explains that his job is to put asset tags on all equipment. He then offers a trivia fact about staplers not counting as equipment, while Dilbert silently stares at his monitor. In the last panel the man thinks to himself about how nobody enjoys talking to him.
punchline: The asset tag man's dull small talk about staplers shows why nobody wants to converse with him, and he is oblivious that his own boring conversation is the cause.
summary: A tag-labeling worker tries to chat up a coworker with stapler trivia, then sadly wonders why people avoid him.

file: 2000/2000-01-01_bait and switch_assisting eddie_never see again.gif
title: Bait and Switch Consulting Group

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'm assigning Eddie to work on your account. You will never see me again.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, what is it that you do here?

situation: The Boss proudly tells a bald consultant that he hired the Bait and Switch consulting group for their intelligence. The consultant announces he is handing the account to a junior colleague named Eddie and that the Boss will never see him again. The Boss, now sitting across from Eddie, asks what it is that Eddie does there.
punchline: The consulting firm's name describes exactly what it does: it sells the client on its smart senior people, then swaps in a junior staffer who has to be asked what he does.
summary: A consulting firm wins a contract on its experts' reputation and immediately substitutes a lone junior employee for them.

file: 2000/2000-05-18_vp stalks alice_bouquet_pencils_fire secreatry_vp_no flowers.gif
title: VP's Pencil Bouquet Courtship

transcript.text: I brought you a bouquet, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's a bunch of pencils, not a flower bouquet.

transcript.speaker: VP

summary: A boss tries to woo a coworker with a flower arrangement that turns out to be office supplies, then blames and sacks his assistant.

file: 2000/2000-05-04_three bulls points_summarize_project_invent words_new words_splrgy_noobah_pizkwat.gif
title: Three Bullet Points, Invented Words

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been asked to summarize my project into three bullet points.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had to invent some new words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Believe me, you don't want to be any of these things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert stands before an audience holding notes and explains that he was told to boil his whole project down to three bullet points. He says he had to invent new words to do it, then presents a slide listing three nonsense terms and warns that nobody wants to be any of them.
punchline: Condensing a complex project into three bullet points is so reductive that it requires made-up jargon, and the made-up labels sound like insults describing the people involved.
summary: Forced to compress an entire project into a tidy three-item list, Dilbert resorts to gibberish terms that he insists are unflattering to anyone they describe.

file: 2000/2000-09-09_work for losers_commits deadline_winners_respect me less.gif
title: Winners Never Commit to Deadlines

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Work is for losers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A winner says, "That's on my list" and never commits to a deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't people respect me less?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't see how.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch beside Dilbert and advises him that work is for losers. He explains that a winner simply says a task is on his list and never commits to a deadline. Dilbert asks whether people would respect him less, and Dogbert replies that he doesn't see how.
punchline: Dogbert's dry reply implies that Dilbert already commands so little respect that avoiding work and deadlines couldn't possibly lower it further.
summary: Dogbert coaches Dilbert on dodging deadlines to seem successful, then slyly implies Dilbert has no respect left to lose.

file: 2000/2000-08-03_internal clients_tracking_fake bills_helpful.gif
title: Fake Bills Prove Departmental Helpfulness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to start tracking our time spent with internal clients.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I will cleverly send fake bills to other departments to show how helpful we are.

situation: The boss announces that the department will track the time it spends serving internal clients. An employee plans to cleverly send fake bills to other departments to show how helpful they are. Later, on the phone with someone asking for help, he refuses because he is busy with his time sheet.
punchline: The time-tracking system meant to prove the department's helpfulness consumes so much effort that it stops them from actually helping anyone.
summary: A new billing scheme meant to showcase a department's usefulness leaves its staff too busy with paperwork to assist the people they serve.

file: 2000/2000-01-06_data miner_eureka!_correclation_vacation_telecommute_expense vouchers_vouchers_out sick.gif
title: Data Miner Finds Absurd Correlations

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Data Miner

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Eureka! I found a correlation.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you're on vacation, all your employees telecommute.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And 100% of all expense vouchers are signed when you're out sick.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have vouchers?

situation: Dogbert, wearing a miner's hard hat with a headlamp, works at a laptop as a 'data miner' and excitedly reports correlations he has found in company data. He tells the Boss that employees telecommute whenever the Boss is on vacation, and that expense vouchers only get signed when the Boss is out sick. The Boss is surprised by each finding, not knowing about either.
punchline: The correlations Dogbert uncovers are really just evidence of how oblivious the Boss is: he doesn't know his employees telecommute when he's away, or that expense vouchers even exist.
summary: A hard-hatted Dogbert mines company data and unearths findings that mostly reveal how little his clueless manager knows about his own department.

file: 2000/2000-02-09_face time_software_man makes face_imitating worker_discourage from raise_costs money_discouraging_engineering.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: And this is you asking for a raise.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, then the VP's office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he needs 'face time' with the VP and takes him to the VP's office without explaining what it means. Once there, the VP leans back and pulls a silly face with his fingers in his mouth while announcing that this is what Dilbert looks like when he asks for a raise.
punchline: 'Face time' turns out to be literal: the VP uses the meeting to mock Dilbert's raise request with a ridiculous face, showing how little he values it.
summary: A vague promise of valuable executive exposure ends with a VP making a goofy face to ridicule an employee's pay request.

file: 2000/2000-03-16_the psychologist_merger pending_stress_what merger.gif

transcript.speaker: The Psychologist

situation: A psychologist tells his patient, a woman with big brown hair, that stress is normal when a merger is pending. She had no idea about any merger, and he realizes he has once again revealed confidential information he shouldn't have.
punchline: The psychologist has a habit of blurting out secrets he learned from other patients, so his attempt at reassurance leaks news of a company merger that the patient hadn't been told about.
summary: A therapist's comforting remark about stress inadvertently spills a confidential corporate secret to a patient who knew nothing of it.

file: 2000/2000-04-15_evil hr director_offered stock incentives_working hard enogh_beating customers.gif

transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So you admit you're not working hard enough now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Umm...

transcript.text: Lastly, are you still beating up customers?

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, interviews Dilbert across his desk. He asks whether Dilbert would work harder for stock incentives, and when Dilbert says yes, Catbert pounces on this as an admission that Dilbert isn't working hard enough now. He then follows up with an absurd accusation about beating up customers.
punchline: Catbert turns an innocent answer into a damning confession, then tacks on a ridiculous loaded question that Dilbert can't answer without incriminating himself.
summary: An H.R. interrogation twists an honest answer about incentives into an admission of slacking, followed by a loaded question about customer abuse.

file: 2000/2000-09-07_amoeba_boss_cry_cubicle_doing work_gets fired_key board_one cell organism_secrete.gif
title: Firing an Amoeba Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This isn't working out. I have to let you go.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you can get your old job back at Farworks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Great. Now he's going to secrete.

situation: The Boss stands beside a large, shapeless, yellowish amoeba-like employee seated at a computer and tells it he has to fire it. He suggests it try to get its old job back at Farworks. In the last panel the creature starts oozing droplets, and the Boss thinks about the upcoming mess.
punchline: Firing a single-celled organism means dealing with it secreting fluid, so the Boss's real concern is the gooey cleanup rather than the employee's feelings.
summary: A manager dismisses a blobby one-celled worker and quietly dreads the slime that follows.

file: 2000/2000-07-29_computer screen_fuzzy_fiddling_stop working_flu season_clean screen_handkerchief.gif
title: Boss Blames Dilbert for Fuzzy Screen

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks to you, my computer screen is all fuzzy now!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're always fiddling with something that makes something else stop working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't clean your screen with your handkerchief during flu season.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop changing the subject.

situation: The Boss storms up to Dilbert and blames him for his computer screen being fuzzy, claiming Dilbert is always meddling with things and breaking other things. Dilbert calmly points out that the boss shouldn't be wiping his screen with a handkerchief during flu season. The boss accuses Dilbert of changing the subject.
punchline: The boss's fuzzy screen is obviously caused by his own handkerchief-wiping, and when Dilbert points out the real cause, the boss absurdly accuses him of changing the subject, refusing to accept responsibility.
summary: A boss pins the blame for his smeared monitor on an employee, then dismisses the real explanation as a diversion.

file: 2000/2000-06-24_worst date ever_whats on ground_bends over_check out ass_not so good.gif
title: Dilbert's Date Bends Over Awkwardly

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm having the worst date ever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll check.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: What's that on the ground? It looks interesting.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Not so good.

setting: Outdoors on a walk, blue background
situation: A woman on a date with Dilbert talks on her phone, complaining that she's having the worst date ever. Hearing this, Dilbert says he'll check, then she points at the ground and asks what it is, tricking him into bending over. In the last panel Dilbert is bent over, with only his rear visible, and the woman reports 'not so good' into her phone.
punchline: The woman tricks Dilbert into bending over so she can check out his backside, then delivers a deadpan negative review to her friend on the phone, confirming the date really is terrible.
summary: A woman narrates her miserable date to a friend by phone and lures her companion into bending over so she can appraise his rear.

file: 2000/2000-01-12_boss office_coup_parked_reserved spot_scheduled meetings.gif
title: Carol's Parking Space Coup

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, you parked in my reserved space.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I scheduled you to drive to meetings all day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Tomorrow I move my stuff into his office and the coup is complete.

situation: The Boss complains to his assistant Carol that she parked in his reserved space. Carol calmly hands him a schedule that has him driving to meetings all day, so he will be out of the office. In the last panel she privately plans to move into his office the next day.
punchline: Carol uses her control over the Boss's schedule to get him out of the building, quietly taking over his job while he is too clueless to notice.
summary: An assistant gets her boss out of the way with a packed calendar so she can quietly take over his office.

file: 2000/2000-08-22_employees_funerals_evil dierctor_heating costs_too high_company furnace_cremated_business.gif
title: Catbert Proposes Cremating Employees for Savings

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Employees waste too much time at funerals.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: On a related note, our heating costs are too high.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: As a matter of fact, I would mind being cremated in the company furnace.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells a meeting that employees waste too much time at funerals, then adds that heating costs are too high. The implication is that he plans to cremate dead employees in the company furnace. At home, Dilbert's mother, stirring a pot, says she would indeed mind being cremated there.
punchline: Catbert's cost-cutting logic joins two complaints into a ghoulish plan to heat the building by burning dead employees, and Dilbert's mother, who is not even an employee, objects to the idea of ending up in the furnace.
summary: An HR villain links two corporate gripes into a macabre money-saving scheme, and a worried relative objects to being part of it.

file: 2000/2000-04-23_complain about work load_ounce of prevention_pound of assignments_working day and night_projects_assignments_deliverables_must do items_action items_frie drills_dog and pony shows_glare problem.gif
title: Wally Pre-empts Assignments With Workload Complaints

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: ZZZZZ

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Beep beep beep

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's time to complain about my workload.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of assignments.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm working day and night!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've got projects, assignments, deliverables, tasks...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: ...must-do items, action items, fire drills, and dog and pony shows.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I have an assignment for you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I solved my glare problem.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: Wally dozes at his desk until his alarm beeps, then decides to head off work by preemptively complaining about his workload to the Boss. He rattles off a long list of tasks, but the Boss still announces he has an assignment for him. Wally then returns to his desk with a paper over his head, claiming he has solved his glare problem.
punchline: Wally's pre-emptive complaining fails to stop the Boss from handing him work, and he sulks by covering his monitor glare with a paper on his head, showing his minimal effort and focus on trivial matters.
summary: A napping employee tries to dodge extra work by loudly claiming to be overloaded, but his boss assigns him a task anyway.

file: 2000/2000-01-02_can't read_ceo_copies_esearch_hand off_manage data_no copies_smother me_documents.gif
title: Research Lost Down the Chain

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: CEO says...

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: The research supports my strategy.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: You can read the research but don't make copies.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Senior VP says...

transcript.speaker: Senior VP
transcript.text: I can tell you about it but you can't read it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: VP says...

transcript.speaker: VP
transcript.text: I don't remember the reason but I'm sure there is one.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Assistant VP says...

transcript.speaker: Assistant VP
transcript.text: There's no reason.

transcript.speaker: Assistant VP
transcript.text: Our strategy is a huge mistake but we have to do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: After I fall asleep tonight, please smother me with a pillow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My people love me because I manage with data.

setting: Corporate offices and a meeting room, plus Dilbert's home at night
situation: A strategy is passed down the corporate hierarchy, with each level knowing less about the research supposedly supporting it. The CEO claims research backs his plan, and each successive layer of management retains less access to or memory of that research until the assistant VP admits there is no reason and the strategy is a huge mistake. Dilbert, hearing this, asks Dogbert to smother him in his sleep, while the Boss smugly claims to manage with data.
punchline: The supposed data-driven strategy degrades into no reasoning at all by the time it reaches the people who must carry it out, yet management still brags about being data-driven.
summary: Justification for a strategy evaporates at each management level until the people implementing it know it is baseless, driving one employee to despair.

file: 2000/2000-01-28_stuck in assignment_no hope_succeeding_sandwhich.gif
title: Ratbert Laughs, Then Wants Sandwich

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm stuck in an assignment that has no hope of succeeding.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Can I have the first bite of our sandwich?

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on his couch holding a sandwich and confesses to Ratbert that he is stuck in a hopeless work assignment. Ratbert bursts into hysterical laughter at his misfortune. Once he has finished laughing, Ratbert cheerfully asks for the first bite of the sandwich, as if nothing happened.
punchline: Ratbert callously laughs at Dilbert's misery and then immediately asks for a favor, showing he has no real sympathy and is only interested in the sandwich.
summary: A pet lab rat howls with mirth at his owner's career troubles before casually asking to share his lunch.

file: 2000/2000-04-26_engineering liason_project staus_translate for clients_never completed_idiot clients_change requirements.gif
title: Liaison Translates Honest Status as Drunk

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Engineering liaison

transcript.speaker: Engineering Liaison
transcript.text: Tell me your project status and I'll translate for our clients.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The project will never be completed because our idiot clients change the requirements every other day.

transcript.speaker: Engineering Liaison
transcript.text: I'll just say you're drunk.

situation: An engineering liaison, who relays technical information to the clients, asks Dilbert for his project status. Dilbert bluntly says the project will never finish because the idiot clients keep changing the requirements. The liaison, notepad in hand, says she will simply tell the clients he is drunk.
punchline: The liaison would rather tell clients that the engineer is drunk than convey the truth that the clients' constant requirement changes doom the project.
summary: A go-between who sugarcoats engineering news for customers decides the safest way to explain an honest rant is to blame alcohol.

file: 2000/2000-02-17_talking to customore_make up mind_discontinue_product_fill a lull.gif
title: Boss Blurts Out Product Discontinuation

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Let me do all the talking to the customer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Check!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'd better make up your mind fast. We plan to discontinue that product any day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, excuse me for trying to fill a lull in the conversation.

setting: Walking to and sitting in a conference room with a customer
situation: A salesman tells the Boss to let him do all the talking with a customer, and the Boss agrees. In the meeting, the Boss immediately tells the customer to decide quickly because the product is about to be discontinued. Afterward the angry salesman glares at him, and the Boss defensively says he was only filling a lull.
punchline: The Boss agrees to stay quiet, then instantly blurts out damaging information that wrecks the sale, and acts like the salesman is being unreasonable for being upset.
summary: After promising to let the salesman handle a client, the Boss immediately sabotages the pitch by revealing the product is about to be killed off.

file: 2000/2000-05-08_generic self help_consultant_keep a journal_lead by example_business.gif
title: Dogbert Bills People For Journaling

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to become a generic self-help consultant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll tell people to keep a journal of all their thoughts. Then I'll bill them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How would that help anyone?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I lead by example, my friend.

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting at a table with coffee mugs
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he is becoming a generic self-help consultant. His plan is to advise clients to journal all their thoughts and then charge them for the advice. When Dilbert asks how that helps anyone, Dogbert says he leads by example.
punchline: Dogbert's 'example' is that he profits from the scheme, so the only person it helps is the consultant, which is exactly how he is leading.
summary: A scheming dog explains a lazy consulting racket in which clients write down their thoughts while he collects the fees.

file: 2000/2000-02-10_dilbert_dilbert not buying it_excuses_get information_hate people_promise_resentment_saves time_advance.gif
title: Hating People in Advance

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll get this information for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No you won't. You'll wait until I hunt you down and then you'll say you were too busy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I started hating people in advance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It saves time.

setting: A conference table at the office, then Dilbert's living room couch
situation: A coworker promises to get Dilbert some information, and Dilbert flatly predicts the coworker will do nothing until chased and then claim to be too busy. At home, Dilbert tells Dogbert he has started hating people in advance, and Dogbert approves.
punchline: Dilbert has become so cynical about coworkers' broken promises that he preemptively resents them, and Dogbert dryly endorses it as an efficiency gain.
summary: After predicting a colleague's inevitable excuse, Dilbert adopts a new policy of pre-emptive loathing that his dog calls a time-saver.

file: 2000/2000-07-31_outside jobs_control my life_control what i think_evil hr director.gif
title: Catbert Scripts Employee's Rebellion

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You need my approval for any outside jobs.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Oh, my...I have the sudden realization that you control my entire life.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: But you can't control what I think!

transcript.speaker: Note
transcript.text: Employee will say, "You can't control what I think!"

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells an employee he needs approval for any outside jobs. The employee dramatically realizes that Catbert controls his whole life and then declares that at least Catbert can't control what he thinks. In the last panel, Catbert is shown holding a script that predicted exactly what the employee would say.
punchline: Catbert's control is so total that he can even predict the employee's defiant line, proving he does control what the employee thinks.
summary: A defiant worker's last stand of mental independence is exposed as entirely predictable when his manager holds a script of his exact words.

file: 2000/2000-02-27_disgram_shares connected_lines_impressive words_synchronized space_presentation_experiment_disturbing_science.gif
title: Dilbert's Meaningless Buzzword Presentation Experiment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to start with a diagram.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a bunch of shapes connected by lines.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I will say some impressive words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Synchronized incremental digital integrated dynamic e-commerce space.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: May I have a copy of your presentation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The results of my experiment are disturbing.

setting: A conference room during a presentation, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert gives a deliberately empty presentation, showing a meaningless diagram and then reciting a string of buzzwords. Instead of confusion or challenge, the audience has no questions and one attendee asks for a copy of the presentation. Dilbert returns home and tells Dogbert the results of his experiment are disturbing.
punchline: Dilbert's nonsense presentation was received as impressive, which shows that people in business accept and even value meaningless buzzwords without understanding them.
summary: Dilbert tests whether a nonsensical slideshow full of jargon will fool his colleagues and is dismayed when it works.

file: 2000/2000-08-18_conditioning worsening_easiest rounds_home early_layoffs_storm_trick.gif
title: Storm Day Layoff Spotting Trick

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Due to worsening storm conditions, all "non-essential" personnel may go home early.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This will be the easiest round of layoffs ever.

situation: The Boss types an email announcing that non-essential personnel may leave early because of a worsening storm. He then stands at his window with binoculars, watching employees drive out of the parking lot. He realizes he now has an easy way to identify who to lay off.
