punchline: The Boss uses the storm early-release offer as a trap, treating anyone who leaves as proof they are expendable and so saving himself the work of choosing layoff targets.
summary: A manager turns a weather-related early dismissal into a lazy way to pick employees to fire.

file: 2000/2000-06-30_company concierge_diet an dexercise_doctor appointment_sleeping at desk_want pills.gif
title: Boss Sends Dogbert To Doctor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company Concierge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have time for my doctor appointment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go in my place and tell him you're having trouble sleeping at your desk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And don't let him sweet-talk you about diet and exercise. I want pills!

situation: Dogbert, acting as the Company Concierge, sits at a desk while the Boss explains he is too busy for his own doctor appointment. The Boss instructs Dogbert to attend in his place and pretend to have trouble sleeping at the desk. He also tells Dogbert to resist any advice about diet and exercise and insist on getting pills.
punchline: The Boss values his time over his health, sending a proxy to the doctor and demanding a quick pharmaceutical fix instead of the lifestyle changes he actually needs.
summary: A busy executive outsources his medical checkup to a concierge and orders him to come back with medication rather than healthy-living advice.

file: 2000/2000-08-21_boss_hired you_response_ignore chain letters_few more apllcants_in basket.gif
title: Interviewing Applicants With Chain Letters

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I hired you, how would you respond to something like this?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: I usually ignore chain letters.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's try another.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: Did you finish your in basket?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I'll need a few more applicants.

setting: Boss's office during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews a job applicant by handing him a chain letter and asking how he would respond if hired. The applicant says he ignores chain letters, so the Boss moves on to another test. His secretary then asks if he has finished his in basket, and he says he needs more applicants.
punchline: The Boss is using the job interview to get his own paperwork done, treating applicants as free labor to clear his in basket and wanting more of them to finish the job.
summary: A manager disguises his pile of unfinished paperwork as interview questions so that job candidates will do his work for free.

file: 2000/2000-03-04_product to meet demand_lower demand_bah_new startegy_more arrogant_teach.gif
title: Arrogance Strategy To Reduce Demand

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can't make enough of our product to meet demand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new strategy is to be more arrogant. We hope that will lower demand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you teach me to be arrogant?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bah!

setting: Conference room, then Dilbert's home or office
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the company cannot produce enough product to satisfy customer demand. His solution is to act more arrogant so customers will want the product less. Dilbert then asks Dogbert to teach him how to be arrogant, and Dogbert dismissively replies 'Bah!'.
punchline: The company tries to fix a supply shortage by deliberately alienating customers, and Dogbert's dismissive 'Bah!' shows he is already an expert at the arrogance being sought.
summary: Management responds to overwhelming customer demand by choosing to be insufferable, and Dilbert seeks lessons from the most condescending creature he knows.

file: 2000/2000-09-01_technical certificate_new power_better job_different comaony_hired you.gif
title: Certified Employee Quits For Better Job

transcript.speaker: Certified Employee
transcript.text: Ha ha! You never should have let me get a technical certification.

transcript.speaker: Certified Employee
transcript.text: I used my new power to get a better job at a different company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me again why I hired you?

situation: An employee in a blue shirt marked with a 'C' and a red cape gloats to The Boss that the technical certification he was allowed to earn has given him the power to land a better job elsewhere. He arrives with a briefcase, clearly on his way out. The Boss, seated at his desk, is left asking why he hired this person.
punchline: The Boss paid for or permitted the employee's certification, which only made him more marketable, so the company trained its own departing worker, and the Boss ironically blames the hiring instead of his own decision.
summary: A newly credentialed worker crows that his qualification won him a job with a rival firm, leaving his bewildered manager to question his hiring choices.

file: 2000/2000-07-10_perfromance evaluation_3% raise_earn a billion_steals as much.gif
title: Self-Written Evaluation Gets Honest Honesty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write a performance evaluation for yourself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shoot for about a 3% raise...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because that's what you're getting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dilbert's inventions will earn a billion dollars. But we think he steals almost as much.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to write his own performance evaluation, then instructs him to aim for a 3% raise because that is all he will be given. Dilbert then types an evaluation that says his inventions will earn a billion dollars but that he probably steals nearly as much.
punchline: Told the raise is fixed at 3% regardless, Dilbert writes a deliberately self-incriminating review, showing that the self-evaluation is a meaningless formality he can mock.
summary: A manager hands the review process to his employee while pre-announcing the pitiful raise, so the employee turns in a sarcastic write-up about his own worth and theft.

file: 2000/2000-08-28_self service consulting_strategy_massive bills_hoping to print.gif
title: Self-Service Consulting With Massive Bills

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I now offer self-service consulting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Write down your strategy and I'll send you massive bills.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a card?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was hoping you'd print some for me.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert standing on his desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, announces a new self-service consulting offering to the Boss. His only contribution is that the client writes down their own strategy, after which Dogbert will bill them heavily. When the Boss asks for a business card, Dogbert says he expects the client to print those too.
punchline: Dogbert has stripped consulting down to pure billing, so the client does all the work, even making Dogbert's business cards, while he collects the fees.
summary: A canine consultant pitches a do-it-yourself service in which the customer supplies the strategy and even the stationery, while he supplies only the invoices.

file: 2000/2000-08-29_self service consulting_crate of anvils_centralized_decentralized_strategy.gif
title: Consultant Insults Clients, Asks Basic Question

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Self-service consulting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was hired because you're all dumber than a crate of anvils.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now, can anyone tell me if your operations are centralized or decentralized?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh! Ooh! I just thought of a strategy!

setting: Conference room during a consulting session
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, opens a meeting by telling the assembled managers they are dumber than a crate of anvils. He then asks a basic question about whether operations are centralized or decentralized. Instead of answering, the Boss excitedly raises his hand to announce he has thought of a strategy.
punchline: The Boss proves Dogbert's insult right by ignoring a simple factual question and eagerly blurting out an irrelevant 'strategy' instead.
summary: A canine consultant insults his clients' intelligence, asks them a simple question, and gets an eager but off-topic reply that confirms his low opinion.
keywords: dumber than a crate of anvils

file: 2000/2000-07-30_candidate for engineering_resume_invented e-commerce_hire now_team that invented_teach paul_to invent things.gif
title: Boss Hires Candidate Who Invented E-Commerce

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Help me interview a candidate for engineering.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think he's terrific!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to your resumé, Paul, you invented e-commerce.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to hire him right now!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hold on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Paul, you didn't really invent e-commerce, did you?

transcript.speaker: Paul
transcript.text: Well...

transcript.speaker: Paul
transcript.text: Maybe I was... um... part of the team that invented it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one invented e-commerce!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When can you start?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why am I here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe Paul can teach you how to invent things.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to help interview an engineering candidate, then gushes over the man's resumé claiming he invented e-commerce. Dilbert points out that no one invented e-commerce and the candidate quickly backpedals, but the Boss hires him anyway. When Dilbert asks why he was even there, the Boss suggests the fraud can teach Dilbert how to invent things.
punchline: The Boss ignores obvious resume exaggeration and rewards it, even implying that the dishonest candidate should train the honest engineer.
summary: A manager is so dazzled by an applicant's absurd resume boast that he hires him on the spot and dismisses the engineer who exposed the lie.

file: 2000/2000-07-22_resume_sarcasm_slave to company_supportiveness_undesirable location_potential slave.gif
title: Resume Done, Sarcasm or Support

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There... my résumé is done. I will no longer be a slave to my company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah! Now you're a potential slave for a company in an undesirable location!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was that sarcasm or supportiveness?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You only think there's a difference.

situation: Dilbert finishes typing his résumé and announces that he will no longer be a slave to his company. Dogbert, sitting on his desk, cheerfully points out that he is merely a potential slave for some other company in a bad location. When Dilbert asks whether that was sarcasm or support, Dogbert says there is no real difference.
punchline: Dogbert's encouragement is indistinguishable from mockery, and he implies that changing jobs just swaps one form of workplace servitude for another.
summary: After updating his résumé to escape his employer, Dilbert gets a cheerful but deflating reminder from Dogbert that any new job is just more of the same.

file: 2000/2000-04-29_bucky the project manger_assignment_painfully difficult_unnecessary_complaining to boss.gif
title: Project Manager Pre-Complains About Assignment

transcript.speaker: Bucky
transcript.text: I'm Bucky, the project manager.

transcript.speaker: Bucky
transcript.text: Your assignment is painfully difficult and probably unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: Bucky
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be complaining about you to your boss.

situation: A project manager named Bucky walks up to Dilbert's desk, introduces himself, and hands over a sheet of paper describing Dilbert's new assignment. He admits the task is very hard and likely pointless, then announces that he'll be off complaining about Dilbert to Dilbert's boss rather than helping.
punchline: The project manager offers no support and instead plans to badmouth the very person he has just given an impossible, pointless task, so the only 'management' he provides is blame.
summary: A new project manager dumps a dreadful job on Dilbert and promptly leaves to grumble about him to the higher-ups.

file: 2000/2000-04-19_life misrable_thwart move_new sadist_old one_sadist paradise_auditing department.gif
title: New Sadist Replaces Old One

transcript.speaker: Sadist
transcript.text: I'll make your life miserable! I'll thwart your every move!

transcript.speaker: Sadist
transcript.text: Hi. I'm the new sadist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happened to the old one?

transcript.speaker: Sadist
transcript.text: He went to sadist paradise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The auditing department?

situation: A bald, scowling coworker storms up to Dilbert's cubicle and threatens to make his life miserable and thwart his every move. In the next panel he introduces himself as the new sadist, and Dilbert asks what became of the previous one. The sadist says his predecessor went to sadist paradise, and Dilbert guesses that means the auditing department.
punchline: Dilbert implies that the auditing department is where sadists find their ideal job, since auditors exist to make other employees' lives miserable.
summary: A menacing newcomer announces himself as the replacement tormentor, and Dilbert deduces that his predecessor was promoted to the one department that rewards cruelty.

file: 2000/2000-07-01_company concierge_alibi_lye_a barrel_police_break you_legal.gif
title: Concierge Services for Covering Up Murder

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company concierge

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: I need an alibi.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The police will try to beat the truth out of you, but don't let them break you!

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: I also need lye... and a barrel...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Better yet, make that two barrels.

setting: Dogbert's company concierge desk in an office
situation: Dogbert works as the company concierge and an employee asks him for an alibi. Dogbert cheerfully coaches him on how to withstand police interrogation. The employee then asks for lye and a barrel, and Dogbert upsells him to two barrels.
punchline: Dogbert treats a request that implies murder and disposing of a body as ordinary customer service, even upselling to two barrels, which implies a second victim.
summary: A helpful concierge supplies an alibi, interrogation tips and body-disposal supplies without a moment's concern, then tries to sell extra barrels.

file: 2000/2000-05-14_live person_attracted to idea_drain on morale_voice mail_secretary in action_answering phone.gif
title: Boss Bans Voice Mail, Dilbert Calls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, from now on, I want a live person answering my phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What attracted you to that idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was it the inefficiency or the drain on morale?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Important executives don't use voice mail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have some information for you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Call me.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Beep Boop Beep Beep Boop Beep Beep

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He's not here. Do you want to leave a detailed message?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Well, you can't!!!

setting: Office, at Carol's desk outside the Boss's area
situation: The Boss orders Carol to personally answer his phone instead of using voice mail, since important executives supposedly don't use it. Dilbert, who has information for the Boss, is told to call him, so he dials from his cell phone. Carol answers, and when Dilbert wants to leave a detailed message, she refuses.
punchline: Carol, forced to act as a live voice mail replacement, spitefully refuses to take a detailed message, showing that the Boss's inefficient policy leaves him with no way to receive information.
summary: After the Boss replaces voice mail with his secretary, she gets her revenge by refusing to take messages from callers.

file: 2000/2000-05-06_learn new technology_sales person_everything he knows_moist towelettes_sponge bath.gif
title: Vendor Training: Three Moist Towelettes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to take a class to learn the new technology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our vendor's sales person will teach you everything he knows.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson
transcript.text: You only need three "moist towlettes" to give yourself a sponge bath.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he needs a class to learn the new technology. The boss, reading a trade magazine, says the vendor's salesperson will teach him everything he knows. In a meeting, the salesperson offers only a tip about using three moist towelettes for a sponge bath, with nothing about the technology.
punchline: The salesperson's total knowledge turns out to be irrelevant hygiene trivia, showing that free vendor training is worthless.
summary: A cheap-minded manager substitutes a vendor's salesperson for real training, and the salesperson's wisdom proves to be about bathing rather than technology.

file: 2000/2000-06-28_loofah_new company concierge_personal_any errand.gif
title: Ratbert Concierge Will Lather Anyone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ratbert is our new company concierge.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I will perform any errand, no matter how personal or degrading it is.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need a loofah.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Lather me up!

setting: Conference room, then Ratbert's concierge desk in the office
situation: The Boss introduces Ratbert to a meeting as the new company concierge, and Ratbert eagerly promises to do any errand, however personal or degrading. A coworker then walks up to his desk and asks for a loofah, and Ratbert enthusiastically replies with a line that misreads the request as an invitation to be washed.
punchline: Ratbert's eagerness to do anything backfires when he answers a simple request for a loofah with an inappropriate offer to be lathered up himself, turning his job promise into an unintentionally suggestive and degrading joke.
summary: A newly appointed office concierge boasts he will do any humiliating task, then responds to a request for a bath sponge by offering himself up to be soaped.

file: 2000/2000-05-27_random drug tests_unpleasent_offer free cashews_charlie brown.gif
title: Drug Test Cashews Evoke Charlie Brown

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We know these random drug tests are unpleasant for employees.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: That's why we offer free cashews.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Suddenly I thought about Charlie Brown but I don't know why.

setting: Office, during a workplace drug test
situation: A manager hands Dilbert a sample cup for a random drug test and tries to make it more pleasant by offering a bowl of free cashews. Dilbert, who has apparently just been dosed with something, suddenly thinks of Charlie Brown for no reason while Dogbert lies on a red couch nearby.
punchline: The free cashews were apparently laced with drugs or the test is rigged, as Dilbert's sudden, inexplicable thought of Charlie Brown suggests he has been drugged, undermining the 'perk' as a trap.
summary: A company sweetens its random drug testing with free nuts, and the snack seems to have an unexpected psychoactive effect on Dilbert.

file: 2000/2000-04-10_skydiving_planting false memories_subconscious_college_education.gif
title: Dogbert Plants False Skydiving Memories

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Remember the time you went skydiving?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You will. I'm planting false memories in your subconscious.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It won't work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But you believe you went to college, right?

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on his couch holding a remote while Dogbert asks if he remembers going skydiving. When Dilbert says no, Dogbert announces he is planting false memories in Dilbert's subconscious. Dilbert insists it won't work, and Dogbert replies by asking whether he believes he went to college.
punchline: Dogbert implies that Dilbert's memory of attending college is itself a false memory he planted, which means it proves the technique works.
summary: A scheming dog tries to implant an imaginary adventure in his owner's mind, then casts doubt on the man's whole education when challenged.

file: 2000/2000-08-05_booby trap cucbilce_borrow guest chair_in slices cubicle_dilbert snagged_upside down_hanging_rope_innocent_trapped.gif
title: Dilbert Caught in Alice's Trap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice, did you booby-trap your cubicle?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The question is, why are you in my cubicle?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I promise to never again borrow your guest chair?

situation: Dilbert is dangling upside down from a rope, apparently snared by a trap in Alice's cubicle. He accuses her of booby-trapping the space, but Alice calmly turns the question around and asks why he is there at all. Dilbert then tries to bargain for his release by promising to stop borrowing her guest chair.
punchline: Dilbert's trespassing to steal her guest chair got him caught in a trap, and Alice's calm deflection leaves him bargaining from a position of total weakness.
summary: A man hanging upside down from a rope in a colleague's cubicle tries to talk his way out by offering a promise about furniture.

file: 2000/2000-02-19_prison morse code_communicate_secret message_cubicle wall_sent email_futile_tapping out_language.gif
title: Prison Tap Code Between Cubicles

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I created a prison Morse code so we can communicate during the day.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Tap your secret messages on the cubicle wall.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Tap tap tap

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I sent you email.

situation: A coworker holding a slip of paper proudly announces that he invented a prison-style tap code so he and his bald cubicle neighbor can talk secretly through the wall. He instructs the neighbor to tap messages on the cubicle wall. In the last panel, the neighbor taps away on the wall while the first coworker, standing nearby, thinks that the message simply says he sent him an email.
punchline: The elaborate, laborious secret tapping code is used to relay something that email already handles, making the whole system pointless.
summary: A man devises a clandestine wall-tapping language for his cubicle neighbor, only for the first message to be a note about an email he already sent.

file: 2000/2000-09-04_feel harassed_multi celled life form_resume_shake hands_yelp.gif
title: Hiring an Amoeba-Like Job Candidate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your résumé says you're a multi-celled life form.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's exactly what we're looking for!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm trying to shake hands. If you feel harassed in any way just let out a yelp.

setting: The Boss's office during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews a shapeless blob-like creature seated across his desk. He reads from its résumé that it is a multi-celled life form and enthusiastically says that is exactly what the company wants. He then awkwardly tries to shake its hand, nervously telling it to yelp if it feels harassed.
punchline: The Boss is so eager to hire a candidate with the barest qualification, and so fearful of a harassment complaint, that he treats a mindless blob as a normal job applicant.
summary: A manager happily interviews a spongy blob of a candidate and warily reaches out to shake its non-existent hand.

file: 2000/2000-06-10_mahage_sadistic game show host_insane_didn't work_rather have performance_pecked to death_trained birds.gif
title: Performance Review Or Pecking Birds

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to manage like a sadistic game show host.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because it would be insane if I kept doing what didn't work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you rather have a performance review or be pecked to death by trained birds?

situation: The Boss stands beside Alice at her desk and announces he is switching to a management style modeled on a sadistic game show host. He justifies it by saying it would be insane to keep doing what didn't work. He then offers her a game-show-style choice between a performance review and being pecked to death by trained birds.
punchline: The Boss thinks changing his management style to a cruel game show format is a sane response to failure, and the choice he offers makes a performance review sound as bad as death by birds.
summary: After deciding that repeating failed methods would be crazy, a manager adopts a cruel game-show approach and forces an employee to pick between two awful fates.

file: 2000/2000-07-16_impractical plan_philosophy_hard_worth doing_walk around_hop on one foot_reasoning capabilities.gif
title: Hopping Boss Defeated By Own Philosophy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This plan is impractical.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My philosophy is that if it isn't hard, it isn't worth doing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's easy to say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So according to your philosophy, you shouldn't have said it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it's easy to walk around. Maybe you should hop on one foot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or would it be better to recant your absurd philosophy...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and bow before my superior reasoning capabilities?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (No dialogue: The Boss hops away on one foot.)

setting: Dilbert's cubicle or office, with the boss standing nearby
situation: Dilbert tells the boss that a plan is impractical, and the boss replies that anything easy isn't worth doing. Dilbert turns the boss's philosophy against him, pointing out that saying it was easy and suggesting he hop on one foot instead of walking. The boss, trapped by his own logic, hops away rather than admit he is wrong.
punchline: The boss would rather hop around on one foot than concede that his 'if it isn't hard, it isn't worth doing' philosophy is absurd.
summary: A boss who insists only difficult things are worthwhile gets his own logic used against him and ends up hopping away to avoid admitting defeat.

file: 2000/2000-06-27_18 hour days_industry_competitors die trying_match.gif
title: Bluffing About Eighteen Hour Days

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You've got to work eighteen hours a day to compete in this industry!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's just SAY we work eighteen hours a day. Maybe our competitors will die trying to match us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would that work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It almost worked on us.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that employees must work eighteen hours a day to stay competitive. He then changes his mind and proposes merely claiming to work that long, hoping rivals will wear themselves out trying to match it. He asks if the ruse would work, and Dilbert replies that the idea almost killed his own team.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan reply reveals that the punishing eighteen-hour schedule has nearly killed his own employees, so it could plausibly kill competitors too.
summary: A manager floats a plan to fake a brutal work schedule so rivals exhaust themselves, and his employee notes that the real thing nearly did that to them.

file: 2000/2000-07-14_rendered useless_stress_bad management_secret_quiet_blare.gif
title: Don't Say Bad Management Out Loud

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This week I was rendered useless by the stress of bad management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's something we only say in the cafeteria.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You're doing a terrific job!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try to find a middle range.

setting: Conference room meeting with the boss
situation: In a meeting with the boss, Asok blurts out that bad management has left him useless, and Dilbert nudges him and warns that such things are only said in the cafeteria. Asok overcorrects by gushing that the boss is doing a terrific job, so Dilbert tells him to find a middle range between brutal honesty and flattery.
punchline: Employees can only voice their real opinions of management out of earshot, and in front of the boss the choices are tactless honesty or absurd flattery, with nothing sensible in between.
summary: A naive young engineer fumbles between insulting his boss and fawning over him, while a colleague coaches him on workplace diplomacy.

file: 2000/2000-04-11_bounced back into plane_didn't open_false memory_parachute_skydiving_tell story_trampoline_planted by dogbert.gif
title: Skydiving Story Is Probably Implanted Memory

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I ever tell you about the time I went skydiving?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That sounds like a false memory planted by Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bah!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My parachute didn't open. Luckily, I landed on a trampoline and bounced back into the plane.

setting: Office break room table during lunch
situation: Dilbert starts to tell a coworker a skydiving story while they eat lunch at a table. Alice suggests the memory is a false one implanted by Dogbert, and Dilbert dismisses the idea. The final panel reveals the story he recalls, in which a failed parachute is saved by a trampoline that bounces him back into the plane.
punchline: Dilbert's skydiving story is so physically impossible that Alice's theory of a false memory planted by Dogbert seems entirely plausible.
summary: A man's tale of surviving a skydive gone wrong is so absurd that his coworker blames a mischievous dog for fabricating the memory.

file: 2000/2000-05-09_lose weight_write down meals_patented weight loss pencil.gif
title: The Patented Weight-Loss Pencil

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You can lose weight if you write down all of your meals in a journal.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's all I need to do?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yes, if you use our patented weight-loss pencil.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Wally struggles to carry an enormous pencil down the street.)

setting: Office area and a city sidewalk
situation: Ratbert, standing on a box, tells Wally that he can lose weight simply by writing down his meals in a journal. When Wally asks if that's all he needs to do, Ratbert says yes, as long as he uses their patented weight-loss pencil. In the last panel Wally is shown hauling a gigantic pencil on his shoulder.
punchline: The 'patented' pencil is a giant, heavy pencil, so the weight loss comes from the exhausting effort of lugging it around rather than from the food journal.
summary: A tiny pitchman sells a bald employee on an easy diet trick that turns out to require carrying around an absurdly oversized writing tool.

file: 2000/2000-01-15_alice_eating_lettuce_grabbed food_inhaled food_old lady_break room.gif
title: Coworker Sniffs Away Alice's Lunch

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey Alice, what are you eating? Let me have a sniff.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: SNIFF!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My lettuce is gone!

setting: Office cubicle or break room table
situation: A gray-haired female coworker walks up to Alice, who is eating a sandwich, and asks to have a sniff of her food. She leans in and inhales so hard that the lettuce vanishes from Alice's lunch. The coworker walks away looking smug while a stunned Alice discovers the lettuce is gone.
punchline: The coworker's sniff is so powerful that she literally inhales the lettuce right out of Alice's sandwich, turning a polite request into lunch theft.
summary: A nosy colleague's request to smell Alice's lunch turns out to be a vacuum-powered snack heist.

file: 2000/2000-08-26_converging_corate slogan_future_power of internet_psoriasis_goose bumps.gif
title: Slogan Causes Skin Conditions Instead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new corporate slogan is...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "The power of the Internet lies in converging the future with the here and now."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Goose-bumps?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Psoriasis.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss reads aloud a new corporate slogan about the power of the Internet converging the future with the here and now. Instead of praising it, two meeting attendees respond with the names of skin conditions, goose-bumps and psoriasis.
punchline: The slogan is such empty buzzword jargon that the staff's only reaction is physical discomfort, sarcastically comparing it to skin ailments.
summary: A manager unveils a grandiose Internet-era slogan and his audience can only answer with names of itchy skin complaints.

file: 2000/2000-02-15_ceo selling stock_portfolio_routine diversification_sell_sudden panic_employees_boss_ceo_business.gif
title: Boss Panic-Sells Despite Reassurance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yikes! Our CEO is selling his stock!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry. It's routine diversification of his portfolio.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh...I guess that's okay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sell, sell, sell.

setting: Dilbert's office and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert worries after noticing the CEO is selling his company stock. The Boss calmly tells him it's just routine portfolio diversification, then, once Dilbert leaves reassured, the Boss frantically sells his own shares at his computer.
punchline: The Boss's soothing explanation is a lie: he is secretly panicking and dumping his own stock, which shows the CEO's sale is anything but routine.
summary: A manager downplays an executive's share sale to a worried employee while privately rushing to offload his own holdings.

file: 2000/2000-01-23_cash balance_pension plan_make more competetive_good for young emplyees_not good for old_change back.gif
title: Pension Change Sparks Generational Brawl

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're changing to a cash balance pension plan.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It will make the company much more competitive.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: Yippee!!! A cash balance plan is good for young employees!

transcript.speaker: Older Employee
transcript.text: Oh, yeah? Well it's not so good for me!

transcript.speaker: Older Employee
transcript.text: I demand that you change it back!

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: No!

transcript.speaker: Older Employee
transcript.text: I'll snap you like a dried twig, you little zygote!

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: Ouch! Stop clubbing me with your artificial hip!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On the plus side, they do seem more competitive.

situation: The Boss and Catbert announce a switch to a cash balance pension plan at a meeting. A young employee cheers because it benefits him, while an older employee objects that it hurts him, and the two get into a physical fight. Afterward, the Boss notes that the employees now seem more competitive.
punchline: The Boss and Catbert claimed the plan would make the company more competitive, and the plan did, literally, by making employees fight each other.
summary: A pension overhaul pits a gleeful young worker against an angry older one, ending in a scuffle that management cheerfully counts as improved competitiveness.

file: 2000/2000-07-13_bean with golf ball_clubhouse_golf with ceo_million dollars_wears helmet_dogbert consults.gif
title: Dogbert Offers CEO Golf Assassination

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I golf with your CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a million dollars I can accidentally bean him with a golf ball.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He always wears a helmet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not in the clubhouse.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert sitting on the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that he golfs with the company's CEO. He offers to 'accidentally' hit the CEO with a golf ball for a million dollars. When the Boss objects that the CEO always wears a helmet, Dogbert replies that he doesn't wear one in the clubhouse.
punchline: Dogbert's plan to harm the CEO isn't deterred by the helmet, since he'll simply attack where the CEO is unprotected, revealing how casually he treats paid sabotage.
summary: A consulting dog proposes a pricey 'accident' on the golf course for the CEO and shrugs off the helmet objection by moving the attack indoors.

file: 2000/2000-03-29_anne l. retentive_anal retentive_typo killed_comma_coma.gif
title: Anne Retentive Dies From Typo

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Anne, I need you to review my first draft.

transcript.speaker: Anne
transcript.text: Typo! Aaagh! My world is flying apart!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You killed Anne L. Retentive with a typo?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, she's in a comma.

situation: Dilbert hands his first draft to a coworker named Anne L. Retentive for review. She spots a typo and has a dramatic meltdown, and she ends up collapsed on the floor. Wally asks if Dilbert killed her with a typo, and Dilbert replies that she's merely in a 'comma'.
punchline: Dilbert puns on 'coma' versus 'comma', suggesting the punctuation-obsessed coworker collapsed from her own perfectionism over a typo.
summary: A meticulous proofreader is so thrown by an error in a colleague's draft that she collapses, prompting a grammar-themed pun about her condition.

file: 2000/2000-03-27_cd rom business card_character flaw_film archive.gif
title: CD-ROM Business Card of Flaws

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my CD-ROM business card.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It has a film archive of all my character flaws.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Including this one?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's number 34.

setting: A social gathering or party, with both holding wine glasses
situation: Dilbert meets a woman at a party and hands her a CD-ROM business card, boasting that it contains a film archive of all his character flaws. She asks whether it includes this very moment, and he deadpans that the awkward behavior is flaw number 34.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to impress someone with a high-tech business card becomes itself a documented character flaw, showing how routinely he embarrasses himself.
summary: At a party, a man hands over a disc cataloguing his own failings and is told that this clumsy introduction already qualifies as one of them.

file: 2000/2000-07-12_dogbert consults_consulting report_exclusive rights_microsoft_dos_good feeling_behind the times.gif
title: Used Consulting Report Recommends DOS

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I saved some money by buying a used consulting report.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to give the exclusive rights for something called DOS to something called Microsoft.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a good feeling about this.

setting: Conference room during a Dogbert consulting session
situation: The Boss proudly tells Dogbert and the staff that he saved money by purchasing a used consulting report. He then reads out its outdated recommendation to give exclusive rights for DOS to a company called Microsoft, treating it as fresh strategic advice. He ends by saying he has a good feeling about the decision.
punchline: The used consulting report is decades out of date, so the Boss is excitedly acting on ancient advice about DOS and Microsoft as though they were unknown, and his cheapness has made him hopelessly behind the times.
summary: A frugal manager acts on a secondhand consulting report so old that it treats Microsoft and DOS as brand-new curiosities.

file: 2000/2000-08-17_salary_115%_mid point_supervisors package_no peeking_money.gif
title: Salary Review Exposes Unreachable Pay Range

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your salary is 115% of the midpoint for your range. Isn't that exciting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't you say it's 115% below the top of the range which can never be achieved under our system?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No peeking at the supervisor's page.

setting: The Boss's office, during a salary review meeting
situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Dilbert that his salary is 115% of the midpoint of his pay range. Dilbert, holding a sheet of paper, points out that this is spun positively and that the top of the range can never actually be reached under the company's system. The Boss's only reaction is to scold Dilbert for looking at the supervisor's page of the document.
punchline: The Boss doesn't dispute that the pay system is rigged to keep raises out of reach; he is only upset that Dilbert saw the supervisor-only information that revealed it.
summary: A manager presents a pay figure as good news, but his employee sees through the spin, and the manager just complains about the employee reading confidential pages.

file: 2000/2000-04-14_quit job_next year_extra week vacation_every ten years.gif
title: Vacation Perk Pays Off Eventually

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd quit this job, but next year I'll get an extra week of vacation.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If you get an extra week for every ten years of service...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ...you'll be happy in 480 years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good plan.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Shut up.

setting: Office, in a cubicle and at a desk
situation: Alice tells Dilbert she would quit but is holding out for an extra week of vacation next year. Dilbert points out that the benefit only grows by one week per ten years of service, so it would take 480 years to make her happy. Alice sulks at the desk, and when Dilbert calls it a 'good plan' she tells him to shut up.
punchline: Alice's reason for staying is so trivial that Dilbert's math shows her happiness is centuries away, and his sarcastic 'good plan' makes her snap.
summary: A worker clings to a tiny vacation perk as a reason to stay, until a coworker calculates how far off real contentment would be.

file: 2000/2000-02-08_bury_bury them_dig_eight patent ideas_hiding_literally_not growing_shivel_intern_free time_appearences.gif
title: Burying Asok's Patentable Ideas

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! You've developed eight patentable ideas, Asok.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll have to bury them or else it will look like we have too much free time.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Then I said, "Literally?" And then he said...

setting: Boss's office, then an outdoor grassy area under a tree
situation: The Boss is impressed that intern Asok has come up with eight patentable ideas. He then decides they must be hidden so the company won't appear to have too much free time. In the last panel, Asok is outdoors with a shovel, literally burying the ideas while chatting to himself or a bird.
punchline: The Boss meant 'bury' as a figure of speech for suppressing the ideas, but Asok takes it literally and digs a hole to bury them.
summary: A manager praises a gifted intern's inventions, then orders them hidden to avoid looking idle, and the intern obeys by digging a hole in the yard.

file: 2000/2000-04-16_sales call_long distance_how long_50 miles long_don't know anyone.gif
title: Long-Distance Service Measured In Miles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Again? That thing rang last week, too.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Ring ring

transcript.speaker: Telemarketer
transcript.text: Hello. May I interest you in long-distance phone service?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long is it?

transcript.speaker: Telemarketer
transcript.text: Umm... it's very long. Extremely long.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to know exactly how long it is!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If it's too short I'll have to shout the last mile! I hate that.

transcript.speaker: Telemarketer
transcript.text: Okay... it's fifty miles long.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, thanks. I don't know anyone fifty miles away.

setting: The Boss's office and a telemarketer's call-center cubicle
situation: The Boss, reading a newspaper, gets a phone call from a telemarketer offering long-distance phone service. He misunderstands 'long-distance' as a physical length and insists on knowing exactly how long it is, worrying he'd have to shout the last mile. When told it is fifty miles long, he declines because he knows nobody that far away.
punchline: The Boss takes 'long-distance service' literally as a physical line of a fixed length, and rejects it because he has no friends living exactly fifty miles away.
summary: A clueless executive treats a long-distance phone plan like a physical cable and turns it down because it only reaches fifty miles.

file: 2000/2000-01-05_data_make face_quite shoccking_sales higest_mining data.gif
title: Data Mining Reveals Silly Sales Pose

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our consultant has been mining data all day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The results are quite shocking.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to the data, sales are always highest when I do this...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (The Boss contorts his face and covers his head with his hands in a bizarre pose.)

situation: The Boss announces to the meeting that the consultant, Dogbert, who is wearing a miner's helmet, has been mining data all day. He reads out the results, saying sales are highest whenever he does a certain thing, and then strikes a ridiculous contorted pose while Dilbert looks on.
punchline: The consultant's data mining has produced a meaningless correlation, that sales peak when the boss makes a silly face, showing how spurious statistics can be presented as insight.
summary: A consultant's literal data mining turns up an absurd link between the boss's goofy gesture and rising revenue.

file: 2000/2000-02-24_technology demo_software_user interface_not working_gotta get some_any questions_engineering.gif
title: Demoing Software With No Interface

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The technology demo

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The software isn't 100% complete.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it had a user interface you would see something here... here... and sometimes here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And then you'd be saying, "I gotta get me some of that."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Any questions?

setting: Conference room during a technology demonstration
situation: Dilbert presents a technology demo to a small audience, admitting the software isn't finished. He points at a blank screen, describing where a user interface would appear if it existed. He then asks for questions as though the demo had been impressive.
punchline: Dilbert tries to sell an unfinished product by describing what the audience would see on a blank screen, then cheerfully asks for questions as if the demo was a success.
summary: An engineer gives a demonstration of unfinished software by gesturing at an empty screen and imagining how impressed everyone would be.

file: 2000/2000-05-05_inferiority complex_feel better_wicked wag.gif
title: Dogbert Therapist Confirms Dilbert's Inferiority

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm starting to get an inferiority complex.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If it makes you feel better, that isn't a complex.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now if you'll excuse me, I gotta take a wicked wag.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch, in a therapy-style session
situation: Dilbert sits on a couch holding a mug, confiding in Dogbert, who is reclined like a therapist's patient-turned-analyst. Dilbert says he is developing an inferiority complex, and Dogbert reassures him in a backhanded way. Dogbert then leaves abruptly to take a wag, the dog equivalent of a joke about going to the bathroom.
punchline: Dogbert 'comforts' Dilbert by saying his feelings of inferiority aren't a complex because he really is inferior, then dismisses him with a crude pun on 'wicked wag' (a play on taking a wicked whiz).
summary: A man worried about feeling inferior gets an insultingly honest reply from his dog, who then bolts for a bathroom-style break.

file: 2000/2000-01-26_wally report_serious threat_productivity_new things_brain full_forget fifth grade_more information_can't sustain information.gif
title: Wally Forgets Fifth Grade Instead

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In this week's Wally report, I'll discuss a serious threat to my productivity.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: By Tuesday my brain was so full that I had to forget things to make room for new things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I have some information for you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Great. I'll just forget the fifth grade.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: Alice reads out her weekly report on Wally's behalf, explaining that her brain filled up so much that she had to forget old things to make room for new ones. The Boss then tells Wally he has some information for him. Wally cheerfully responds that he will simply delete his memory of the fifth grade to make room.
punchline: Wally treats his brain like a full hard drive, casually sacrificing a whole school year of memories to accommodate a trivial piece of workplace information.
summary: A colleague jokes that her overstuffed mind forces her to erase old memories for new data, and when handed more information she volunteers to dump an entire school year.

file: 2000/2000-06-13_share knowledge_new intranet_collaboration software_knowledge to share_hurst_true_hoarding.gif
title: Hoarding Knowledge Instead of Sharing It

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Who wants to share knowledge with me via our new intranet collaboration software?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't have any knowledge to share.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ouch. It hurts because it's true.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm hoarding my knowledge in case I ever need it.

situation: Asok eagerly asks coworkers to share knowledge with him through the company's new intranet collaboration software. Dilbert bluntly tells him he has no knowledge of his own to share, and Asok admits the insult stings because it's accurate. Wally then explains that he keeps his knowledge to himself in case he needs it later.
punchline: Wally treats knowledge as a private stockpile to protect his own job security, which undercuts the whole purpose of collaboration software.
summary: A junior employee's call for knowledge sharing is met with insults and with a coworker who stockpiles what he knows as a personal safety net.

file: 2000/2000-01-10_completed assignments_service_wrinkled paper.gif
title: Boss Assigns Work From Trash Can

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I completed all my assignments. How may I be of service now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I have something in here.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My other assignments were on wrinkled paper, too.

setting: The Boss's office, then Asok's desk
situation: Asok, an eager young employee, tells the Boss he has finished all his assignments and asks for more. The Boss rummages through his wastebasket looking for something to give him. Asok, now at his desk holding a crumpled sheet of paper, thinks that his earlier assignments also came from the trash.
punchline: The Boss's work assignments are literally pulled from the garbage, implying management hands out random, worthless tasks without any real planning.
summary: A keen employee asks for more work and watches his boss dig a new task out of the wastebasket, realizing that is where all his previous tasks came from.

file: 2000/2000-02-06_product is defective_expect delivery_quality s primary goal_opposite of philosophy_rich philosophers_swiss bank.gif
title: Ship Defective Product, Book Revenue

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My tests prove our product is defective.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Customers expect delivery tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our corporate philosophy is "Quality is our primary goal."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you want me to delay shipment until we fix the problems?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to ship now so we can book the revenue.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa! That's the opposite of our philosophy!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now you know why there aren't any rich philosophers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There used to be one, but he believed I was a Swiss bank.

setting: Office, then Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that his tests show the product is defective, but the boss insists on shipping on time. When Dilbert cites the company's quality-first philosophy, the boss says he wants to ship now to book the revenue. In the final panel Dilbert, at home in a robe on the couch with Dogbert, delivers a bitter quip about philosophers and money.
punchline: The boss dismisses the company's stated philosophy as irrelevant to making money, and Dilbert sarcastically implies that the only philosopher who was ever rich got that way by taking money from a gullible mark (Dogbert posing as a Swiss bank).
summary: A manager overrides an engineer's warning about faulty goods so the company can record sales immediately, and a closing gag mocks the profitability of ethics.

file: 2000/2000-09-03_funny in purple_important decsions_missile defense networks_naps_french people_touching with cigarette.gif
title: Dilbert Naps While Making Decisions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it okay if I take naps during the day?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or would you prefer that I make important decisions while groggy and delusional?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Either way is okay with me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's your call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He looks funny all purple.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must... stay... awake.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Make... impor-tant... decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must replace optical switches with dancing lemurs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa! French people are touching me with cigarettes!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope that's how engineers design missile defense networks.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether he may nap during the day, pointing out the alternative is that he makes important decisions while groggy and delusional. The boss doesn't answer, and Dilbert fights sleep at his desk, then dozes off and has a bizarre dream and wakes up shouting. The boss, watching, wonders if this is how engineers design missile defense networks.
punchline: Dilbert's sleep-deprived, delusional decision-making is so absurd that the boss jokes it must be how critical systems like missile defense networks actually get designed.
summary: A tired engineer warns his boss that he will either nap or make absurd decisions while half asleep, then proves the point by dozing off and babbling nonsense.

file: 2000/2000-08-12_casserole_surgery_ten year service party_medical.gif
title: Casserole for Your Own Party

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Ted, your ten year service party will be on Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'm having surgery Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Maybe you could drop off a casserole on your way.

situation: Carol, the boss's assistant, announces to Ted that his ten year service party is scheduled for Tuesday. Ted says he has surgery that day, and Carol responds by suggesting he bring a casserole to the party on his way to the hospital.
punchline: Carol is so indifferent to Ted's medical situation that she expects him to supply food for his own service party on the day of his surgery.
summary: A coworker's surgery fails to interrupt the planning of his own anniversary party, and he is still expected to contribute food.

file: 2000/2000-05-10_melt polar ice caps_doom humanity_part of humanity_marketing_help destroy planet_free t shirts_business.gif
title: Marketing Sold Out For T-Shirts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This product would melt the polar ice caps and doom humanity.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: That's okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're part of humanity.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: No, I'm in marketing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I won't help you destroy the planet.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: That's what I said until I saw the free t-shirts.

situation: Dilbert warns a marketing colleague that the product they are promoting would melt the polar ice caps and doom humanity. She shrugs it off, jokes that being in marketing exempts her from humanity, and then admits that free t-shirts overcame her earlier objection to destroying the planet.
punchline: The marketer's ethical stance on destroying the planet evaporated the moment she was offered free promotional t-shirts, showing how cheap corporate loyalty and conscience can be bought.
summary: A marketer waves away a warning about global catastrophe, claiming she isn't really human, and confesses that free swag cured her scruples.

file: 2000/2000-02-11_cynics annonymous_fluorescent lights_higher power_naive optimism_perfect emplyee.gif
title: Cynics Anonymous Higher Power Fix

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Dilbert, you've become too aware of reality. I'm sending you to "Cynics Anonymous."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: A higher power will help you regain the naive optimism that once made you a perfect employee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why can't the higher power change me while I'm sitting here?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Fluorescent lights block his power.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Dilbert he has become too aware of reality and is being sent to a "Cynics Anonymous" program. He explains that a higher power will restore Dilbert's naive optimism so he can be a perfect employee again. Dilbert asks why the higher power can't just change him right there in the office.
punchline: Catbert's flimsy excuse that fluorescent office lights block the higher power's abilities shows the mandated program is an arbitrary, nonsensical way to force employees into cheerful compliance.
summary: The company's scheming HR chief orders a clear-eyed engineer into a twelve-step-style program to make him gullible again, then dismisses his logical objection with an absurd excuse.

file: 2000/2000-01-22_huge liars_management in person_dogbert investments.gif
title: Dogbert Doesn't Actually Meet Management

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Investments

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Before I invest in a stock, I talk to the management in person.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: What good is that? They're all huge liars.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You believe I really talk to them, right?

situation: Dogbert, running an investment business, tells a client that he personally interviews a company's management before buying its stock. The client objects that executives are all liars, so the meetings are worthless. Dogbert responds by asking whether the client really believes he talks to them at all.
punchline: Dogbert admits, by implication, that his claimed due diligence is a lie, proving he is just as dishonest as the executives he supposedly interviews.
summary: A fraudulent investment advisor gets caught out when his claim of careful research is met with doubt, and he cheerfully hints that he made the whole thing up.

file: 2000/2000-07-06_filing system_reorganized files_stress is gone_lulu_meeting_boss_dilbert_business.gif
title: Reorganizing Files Instead of Fixing Project

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My project was in a death spiral.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I leapt into action and reorganized my filing system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did that help?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My stress is gone!

situation: A coworker at a meeting table explains that his project was failing badly, so he reorganized his filing system. The Boss asks if that helped, and the coworker cheerfully reports his stress is gone. Dilbert sits beside him listening.
punchline: The coworker only fixed his own stress by doing a trivial task, while the actual project is still in a death spiral.
summary: A worker tackles a collapsing project by tidying his files and is delighted that he feels calmer, ignoring that nothing real has been fixed.

file: 2000/2000-06-16_server named pointy_over loaded_moving_haired and idiot_cluless_purchase order.gif
title: Servers Named After the Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our server named "Pointy" is overloaded.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So we're moving some of the load to "Haired" and "Idiot."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But we still need a new server.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He signed the purchase order for "Clueless".

setting: Conference room with a chalkboard, then an office cubicle area
situation: Dilbert explains to a meeting at the chalkboard that the server named "Pointy" is overloaded and that work is being shifted to servers named "Haired" and "Idiot." He notes a new server is still needed. In the last panel, he holds up a purchase order the boss signed, saying it is for a server to be named "Clueless."
punchline: The servers are named so that together they spell out an insult to the boss (Pointy, Haired, Idiot, Clueless), and the boss unknowingly signs the purchase order for the one that completes the joke.
summary: Engineers quietly mock their manager by naming the company's servers with a string of insulting words, and he obliviously approves the purchase of the next one.

file: 2000/2000-04-24_project plan_without input_lied to me_skipped that step_already assigned blame_for failure.gif
title: Blame Assigned Before Project Begins

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I finished the project plan without your input.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You would have lied to me anyway, so I just skipped that step.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've already assigned blame for failure, but don't worry, it's just preliminary.

setting: Office meeting area at a conference table
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a finished project plan that he wrote without consulting anyone. He explains he skipped asking for input because he assumes Dilbert would lie. He then reveals he has already decided who will take the blame when the project fails.
punchline: The Boss plans for the project's failure from the start and pre-assigns blame, treating it as a minor, provisional detail.
summary: A manager imposes a plan on his team without consultation, distrusts their honesty, and has already picked the scapegoat for the inevitable flop.

file: 2000/2000-02-02_stay at job_easy commute_risk everything_fast paced start up_yakking_ipo.gif
title: Therapist Beats Dilbert to Startup Riches

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I stay at my current job where the commute is easy?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or should I risk everything and join a fast-paced start-up company?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: I joined a fast-paced start-up company while you were yakking.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Mine went IPO.

situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair, talking aloud through his career dilemma about staying at his easy-commute job or risking a start-up. While he rambles, his therapists, a small yellow creature (Ratbert) and a green dinosaur, act on the idea themselves. The dinosaur reveals he already joined a start-up during Dilbert's monologue, and Ratbert's start-up has already gone public.
punchline: Dilbert dithers so long over a decision that the people listening have already made the move and cashed in on it.
summary: While a man agonizes aloud about a career gamble, the listeners quietly act on it and strike it rich first.

file: 2000/2000-02-01_more money else where_good coffee_why stay.gif
title: Why Dilbert Stays Despite Lower Pay

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know I could earn more money at another company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So why do I stay?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe the coffee is good and you enjoy watching the antics of feeble, unaware losers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I don't think that's...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This coffee is good.

setting: Dilbert's home or office table with papers and a coffee cup
situation: Dilbert muses aloud that he could make more money at another company and wonders why he stays. Dogbert offers two guesses: the coffee is good, and Dilbert enjoys watching feeble, unaware losers. Dilbert starts to dismiss the idea, but Dogbert, sipping from the cup, simply confirms the coffee is good.
punchline: Dogbert's insulting theory implies Dilbert likes feeling superior to his clueless coworkers, and Dogbert slyly sidesteps Dilbert's denial by agreeing only with the harmless part about the coffee, leaving the insult hanging.
summary: A dog tosses out a backhanded explanation for why his owner remains in an underpaying job, then retreats to praising the beverage.

file: 2000/2000-03-18_many tasks_better_never born_technically true_slap later.gif
title: Technically, My Existence Is Net Negative

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I performed many tasks, but I can not claim any accomplishments.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Because things might have turned out better had I never been born.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Technically, it's true.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remind me to slap you later.

situation: Seated at a meeting table with Dilbert and the boss, Asok announces that although he completed many tasks he cannot claim any accomplishments. He explains that things might have turned out better if he had never been born. Dilbert concedes the point is technically true and asks to be reminded to slap him later.
punchline: Asok's absurdly self-deprecating logic is so dismal that Dilbert can only agree it is technically correct, while also being annoyed enough to want to slap him.
summary: A junior employee gloomily argues that the world would be better off without him, and a coworker grudgingly agrees before threatening to hit him.

file: 2000/2000-01-19_dogcart investment fund_higher fees_best fund_diversified_suckers_all types.gif
title: Dogbert's Fund Has Highest Fees

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Wow! The Dogbert Investment Fund has higher fees than any other!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's true!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's how you can tell it's the best fund.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm in.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Are you diversified?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, I have suckers of all types.

situation: A woman reading a brochure tells Dogbert, who is running an investment fund, that his fees are higher than any other fund's. Dogbert claims high fees prove it's the best, and she agrees to invest. She then asks whether the fund is diversified, and he answers that he has all kinds of suckers.
punchline: Dogbert reveals that his only diversification is in the variety of gullible customers he has fleeced, not in any investments.
summary: A cheerfully gullible investor falls for a pitch that treats exorbitant charges as a mark of quality, then learns the fund's only real diversity is its victims.

file: 2000/2000-04-05_disablity_jiggle the camera_test_walls claim_sneak_camera_caught_spy_window_unsuspecting.gif
title: Asok Spies On Wally's Disability

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally's claim of disability will be put to the test.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Here we go... Oh, yeah... Come to Asok... Go, baby, go!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Does he ever move?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It looks that way when I jiggle the camera.

setting: Outdoors, in bushes outside Wally's house, filming through a window
situation: Asok crouches outside a window with a camcorder, secretly filming Wally to see whether his disability claim is genuine. Wally sits motionless in a recliner with his feet up. Catbert asks if Wally ever moves, and Asok admits that he only appears to move when Asok jiggles the camera.
punchline: Wally is so lazy that the only way to make him look active on the surveillance footage is to shake the camera, so Asok's spying proves nothing about fraud.
summary: A junior employee stakes out a coworker's house to catch him faking a disability, but the target is so inert that the footage only shows motion when the camera shakes.

file: 2000/2000-08-30_tom peters advice_become own brand_get me some.gif
title: Wally's Personal Brand Flops

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm going to follow Tom Peters' advice and become my own brand.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The phrase you're least likely to hear is, "I gotta get me some of that."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Day one: not so good.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Wally announces to Alice at the coffee machine that he will follow Tom Peters' advice and turn himself into a personal brand. Alice bluntly tells him nobody will ever want a piece of him. Wally, holding his coffee mug, reflects that his first day has not gone well.
punchline: Alice's insult points out that no one would ever want what Wally has to offer, so his personal branding effort is doomed from the start, and Wally takes it as a day-one failure.
summary: A coworker's plan to market himself as a personal brand is crushed by a colleague's blunt observation that nobody would ever desire what he's selling.

file: 2000/2000-05-15_meeting with boss_speak frankly_problems in dept_ask out.gif
title: Consultant Plans to Date Boss

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I scheduled a meeting with your boss.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: He'll probably ask me to speak frankly about any problems in the department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This couldn't get any worse.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: He's cute. I might ask him out.

setting: The Boss's office, at his desk
situation: A woman with big curly hair tells the Pointy-Haired Boss that she has scheduled a meeting with his boss, where she expects to be asked to speak frankly about the department's problems. The Boss grows increasingly anxious, thinking things can't get worse. She then adds that she finds his boss cute and might ask him out.
punchline: The Boss thinks nothing could be worse than her candidly reporting his department's problems, but her romantic interest in his superior shows it can, since a personal relationship could give her even more influence over his fate.
summary: A visitor's plan to give honest feedback to the big boss turns even more threatening when she admits she may also date him.

file: 2000/2000-08-23_pay slip_increased complexity_won't know_rip off_clueless_in the dark_happy to be evil_cheat_evil catbert.gif
title: Catbert Complicates Pay Slips to Cheat

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We increased the complexity of your pay slip.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Now you'll never know when we rip you off!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yeeha! Yeeha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only part that really bugs me is the yeehas.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, holds up a pay slip and gleefully tells the employees at the conference table that the pay slip has been made more complex. He explains this means they can no longer tell when the company is shortchanging them, and celebrates with yeehas. Dilbert calmly remarks that the celebratory yeehas are the only part that bothers him.
punchline: Dilbert shrugs off the openly admitted wage theft and complains only about Catbert's gloating, implying employees have resigned themselves to being cheated.
summary: The malicious personnel chief boasts that confusing paychecks will hide his underpayment schemes, and the resigned staff only object to his whooping.

file: 2000/2000-03-22_future me_came to help_project_miserable_sewerage_got bad assignments.gif
title: Future Dilbert Insults Present Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A future me built a time machine and came to help on my project.

transcript.speaker: Future Dilbert
transcript.text: Hello, you miserable pile of solid sewerage.

transcript.speaker: Future Dilbert
transcript.text: You always got bad assignments after today.

setting: Office, in front of the boss
situation: Dilbert introduces a future version of himself who built a time machine to help on his project. The future Dilbert greets him with a harsh insult. He then explains that Dilbert will keep getting bad assignments from now on, implying the boss will keep dumping on him.
punchline: Even a time traveller from the future has no good news: Dilbert's bad assignments will continue, and the boss is the cause of it.
summary: A time-travelling older Dilbert arrives to help, but only brings insults and the grim news that his work life will never improve.

file: 2000/2000-06-15_fixed bug_meeting_not inviting_scheduling people_accomplishment_fixed the bug_inviting_business.gif
title: Fixing Bug Before Fifty-Person Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My accomplishment this week was scheduling fifty people to discuss the bug in our product.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I fixed the bug this morning.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And thanks for not inviting me to the meeting.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss proudly announces his weekly accomplishment: scheduling fifty people to discuss a bug in the product. Alice calmly reveals she already fixed the bug that morning. She then sarcastically thanks him for leaving her out of the meeting.
punchline: The boss's only 'accomplishment' is organizing a huge meeting about a problem that Alice, who was conveniently not invited, has already solved, and her thanks is pointed sarcasm.
summary: A manager brags about convening a crowd to discuss a defect, only for a coworker to say she has already repaired it and wryly thank him for the non-invitation.

file: 2000/2000-05-19_perfromance review_no initiative_fault_creating atmosphere_fear and distrust.gif
title: Boss Responds to Fear Accusation

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't show any initiative this year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's your fault for creating an atmosphere of fear and distrust.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You, you, you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Note to self: increase fear.

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert during his performance review that he showed no initiative this year. Dilbert replies that the lack of initiative is the Boss's fault for fostering an atmosphere of fear and distrust, pointing accusingly at him. The Boss, instead of reflecting, thinks to himself that he should increase the fear.
punchline: The Boss takes legitimate criticism of his fear-based management as a strategy tip and resolves to make the intimidation even worse.
summary: An employee blames his boss's intimidating management for his lack of initiative, and the boss responds by planning to intimidate people even more.

file: 2000/2000-01-30_anti spam software_incoming email_key words_advertisement_accidental emails_sale.gif
title: Spam Filter Fooled By Spelling

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My anti-spam software is complete.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It checks my incoming e-mail for key words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then it deletes anything that looks like an advertisement.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Suppose a beautiful woman sends you a message saying...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "I am a model for Victoria's Secret. I want to date you on my sailboat."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But she spells sail S-A-L-E.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What then?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
