file: 2000/2000-08-20_good manager_hires samrter_boss dumber_ceo_dumbest person_bad managers_doomed_motivational meeting_high five.gif
title: Smarter Hires Make the CEO Dumbest

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good manager hires people who are smarter than he is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... your boss is dumber than you?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And your boss's boss is dumber yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to your theory, our CEO is the dumbest person in the company.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Unless all of you are bad managers.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Truly we are doomed either way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This concludes the motivational part of the meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd give you a high five but I don't like to move.

situation: The Boss opens a meeting with the motivational claim that a good manager hires people smarter than himself. Dilbert and Alice follow the logic up the management chain and conclude the CEO must be the dumbest person in the company, unless everyone is a bad manager. The Boss ends the meeting with no reaction, declining even a high five out of laziness.
punchline: The Boss's own motivational theory logically proves that either the CEO is the dumbest person at the company or the management is bad, and he responds with indifference and laziness.
summary: A manager's inspirational hiring maxim collapses under his employees' simple logic about what it implies for the company's leadership.

file: 2000/2000-04-02_sing or dance_resigned_huge resignation_manifesto_video clips_humorous sound files_website_broadway theater prodcution_first motivated employee_technology.gif
title: Resignation Manifesto Becomes Broadway Production

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Can you sing or dance?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ted? I thought you resigned in disgust two weeks ago.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Well... I wrote a huge resignation manifesto that I planned to e-mail to the entire company.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: But I thought it needed pictures.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Before long I was adding video clips and humorous sound files.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Then I thought, hey, why not put it all on a web site?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Now I'm turning the whole thing into an off Broadway theatre production.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I saw my first motivated employee today.

situation: Ted, who supposedly resigned in disgust two weeks earlier, shows up at Dilbert's cubicle and asks if he can sing or dance. He explains that his resignation manifesto kept growing from an email into a multimedia website and now an off Broadway show. Afterward Dilbert tells Dogbert he has just seen his first motivated employee.
punchline: Ted's bitterness has turned into the most enthusiastic, creative effort anyone at the company has put in, so the only motivated employee Dilbert has ever seen is one who quit in disgust.
summary: A man who quit angrily keeps inflating his farewell rant into ever grander media projects, leaving a coworker to note it's the most driven anyone has been.

file: 2000/2000-05-23_ad campiagn_festured_new ceo_powerful woman_indutry_than lines.gif
title: Consultant's Ad Campaign Flattery Backfires

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My consultant thinks you should be featured in our ad campaign.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Is that because I'm your new CEO and the most powerful woman in our industry?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... Yes, that's why.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Remember to ask about tan lines.

situation: The Boss tells the new CEO that his consultant, Dogbert, thinks she should appear in the company's ad campaign. She sees through it and asks if it's because she is the new CEO and the most powerful woman in the industry. The Boss sheepishly agrees, and Dogbert prompts him to ask about her tan lines.
punchline: Dogbert's prompt to ask about tan lines reveals that the ad campaign pitch is really a crude, inappropriate come-on, and the consultant is coaching the Boss into it.
summary: A boss pitches an advertising role to his new female CEO, but his consultant is secretly steering him toward an awkward and inappropriate line of questioning.

file: 2000/2000-02-13_marketing to planning meeting_sabotage implementation_hose the plan_implementation_same reason for children.gif
title: Marketing Dooms Plan Either Way

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't invite Marketing to the planning meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I don't, they'll sabotage the implementation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but if you DO include them in the planning...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...They'll hose the plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And they'll still botch the implementation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we know it's doomed, why do we bother?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's the same reason I had kids.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least there's a reason.

situation: Dilbert advises the Boss not to invite Marketing to the planning meeting, but the Boss says excluding them means they'll sabotage the implementation. They work through the dilemma and conclude that Marketing will ruin the plan if included and botch the implementation regardless. When Dilbert asks why they bother, the Boss gives a flippant answer comparing it to why he had kids.
punchline: The Boss admits the project is doomed either way and justifies doing it with the same non-reason he had for having children, leaving Dilbert to reflect that at least there's a reason.
summary: A pair of managers realize that every option involving the marketing department ends in failure, and the boss shrugs it off with a bleak parenting comparison.

file: 2000/2000-05-03_cep_obscenely wealthy_guest house_build house_speech writer_workers_made him rich_bragging_condescending_truth.gif
title: CEO Brags, Needs Better Speechwriter

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: As CEO, I thank you for making me obscenely wealthy.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Yesterday I built a guest house using bundles of cash as bricks.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I need a new speech writer.

setting: Company auditorium during an employee address
situation: A CEO at a podium addresses employees, thanking them for making him obscenely wealthy. He then boasts about building a guest house out of bundles of cash while Alice, Wally and Dilbert listen in the audience. Realizing how tone-deaf his speech sounds, he privately thinks he needs a new speechwriter.
punchline: The CEO only realizes his speech is offensively boastful after delivering it, and blames his speechwriter rather than his own attitude toward the employees who made him rich.
summary: A tycoon executive flaunts his wealth to the very workers who earned it for him, then blames his speechwriter for the awkward result.

file: 2000/2000-02-21_paul tergeist_technology_new lab partner_pen hovering.gif
title: Poltergeist Lab Partner Wrecks Technology

transcript.speaker: Paul Tergeist
transcript.text: My name is Paul Tergeist.

transcript.speaker: Paul Tergeist
transcript.text: I have a way with technology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you met your new lab partner?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My pen is hovering!

situation: A new coworker introduces himself as Paul Tergeist while Dilbert's computer shows an error and then a system failure. The Boss asks Dilbert if he has met his new lab partner, and Dilbert's pen is floating in mid-air.
punchline: The new lab partner's name sounds like 'poltergeist', and he literally has a way with technology because he is a ghost who causes computer errors and makes objects hover.
summary: Dilbert's new lab partner turns out to be a poltergeist whose haunting wreaks havoc on the computers and levitates a pen.

file: 2000/2000-06-19_asks on date_away_faq section_ignorant_without merit_website_technology.gif
title: Ming Rejects Suggestion, Then Gets Asked Out

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ming, our web site needs a FAQ section.

transcript.speaker: Ming
transcript.text: I find your suggestion ignorant and without merit.

transcript.speaker: Ming
transcript.text: Away with you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So...are you doing anything this weekend?

transcript.speaker: Ming
transcript.text: Gaaa!!

setting: Office, at Ming's desk with a computer
situation: Dilbert holding a coffee mug suggests to Ming, the web developer, that the company web site needs a FAQ section. She harshly dismisses the idea as ignorant and without merit and tells him to go away. Undeterred, Dilbert immediately asks whether she is free this weekend, and she recoils in horror.
punchline: Dilbert shrugs off a brutal insult as if it were nothing and moves straight to asking her out, which horrifies her.
summary: After being scornfully brushed off by a coworker over a web site idea, a man cheerfully asks her on a date as though nothing happened.

file: 2000/2000-08-16_slide 387_powerpoint_poisoning.gif
title: Powerpoint Poisoning Diagnosed After Slide 397

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you can clearly see in slide 397...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Gaaaah!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: "Powerpoint" poisoning.

situation: Dilbert presents a convoluted diagram and is already on slide 397. His audience has fallen asleep or is screaming in agony. A coworker examines the victims and diagnoses them with "PowerPoint" poisoning.
punchline: The audience has been so overwhelmed by an endless slide presentation that their collapse is treated as a medical condition, mocking death by PowerPoint.
summary: A presenter's marathon slide deck leaves his listeners unconscious and howling, and an observer calmly names the ailment.

file: 2000/2000-01-03_dogcart consults_data mining_uncover sales_mine data_messages_tie and shirt_messages from god.gif
title: Data Mining Finds Messages From God

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need to do data mining to uncover hidden sales trends.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you mine the data hard enough, you can also find messages from God.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...Sales to left-handed squirrels are up...and God says your tie doesn't go with that shirt.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, explains data mining to the Boss as a way to find hidden sales trends. He adds that mining data hard enough also produces messages from God. He then reads out a ridiculous sales finding followed by divine fashion criticism of the Boss's tie.
punchline: Dogbert mocks data mining by suggesting that if you torture the data long enough you can 'find' anything, including absurd trends and a fashion critique from God.
summary: A consultant dog pitches data mining to his boss, then demonstrates that sufficiently aggressive analysis will turn up anything, even heavenly wardrobe advice.

file: 2000/2000-09-02_kicking me_least valuables_manager_most valuable emplyees_turnover_increase turnover.gif
title: Managing Turnover: Keep Best, Lose Worst

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As a manager, it's my job to reduce the turnover of our most valuable employees...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...and to increase turnover of our least valuable employees.

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: Ow! For the jillionth time, who keeps kicking me?!

situation: The Boss explains at a meeting that a manager's job is to reduce turnover of the most valuable employees and increase turnover of the least valuable ones. In the last panel a balding coworker in glasses complains that someone keeps kicking him under the table, apparently reacting to the idea of being among the least valuable.
punchline: The coworker being repeatedly kicked under the table implies he is the one the boss has in mind as a low-value employee to be pushed out, or that someone is sending him a pointed message.
summary: A manager lays out a plan to keep star performers and shed weak ones while a nearby coworker keeps getting mysteriously kicked under the table.

file: 2000/2000-03-03_against company policy_date skeleton_chipped tooth_date a skeleton_skeleton in closet.gif
title: Asok Dating a Closet Skeleton

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Asok, it's against company policy to date a skeleton you found in a closet.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: We're just friends! I swear!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Eh! Eh!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: (thought) It's just as well; I think I chipped a tooth.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, confronts Asok about violating company policy by dating a skeleton he found in a closet. Asok nervously insists they are just friends. In his thoughts, Asok admits it is just as well the relationship isn't romantic because he chipped a tooth, implying he had actually been kissing the skeleton.
punchline: Asok's private thought reveals he was lying to HR and had in fact been kissing the skeleton, as shown by the tooth he chipped.
summary: An HR cat accuses a young employee of an forbidden romance with a skeleton from the closet, and his inner thoughts give away what he really got up to.

file: 2000/2000-08-11_hire another engineer_last minute_cost saving s awards_plan to hire_work twice as hard.gif
title: Doubling Workload Instead of Hiring

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had planned to hire another engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At the last minute I remembered I could just make you work twice as hard.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could nominate me for one of those cost-saving awards.

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert at his desk and explains that he had meant to hire a second engineer. He then decides to simply make Dilbert work twice as hard instead. He finishes by suggesting Dilbert nominate him for a cost-saving award for the idea.
punchline: The Boss takes credit for 'saving costs' by doubling Dilbert's workload for free, and cheerfully asks the person being exploited to nominate him for an award.
summary: Rather than adding headcount, a manager piles twice the work onto one engineer and then angles for recognition for the savings.

file: 2000/2000-04-09_fly to austin_customer_call big cutsomers_go inperson_telephone_show you care_concept of phone.gif
title: Don't Call Big Customers, Fly There

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fly to Austin and answer some questions for a big customer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doesn't this customer have a telephone?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't call big customers!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Why not?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to go in person to show that you care.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, that would show that I don't understand the concept of the telephone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just go.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Do they have these where you come from?

setting: The Boss's office and then a meeting room at the customer's site in Austin
situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to fly to Austin to answer questions for a big customer instead of simply phoning them. Dilbert points out that a telephone would do the job, but the Boss insists that travelling in person shows you care. Dilbert goes, and the customer holds up a mobile phone and mocks him for flying out.
punchline: Dilbert's pointless, costly trip proves his point, as the customer sarcastically asks whether Dilbert's home turf even has telephones.
summary: A manager sends an employee on a flight to answer a client's questions that a quick phone call could have handled, and the client ends up ridiculing the needless journey.

file: 2000/2000-08-15_disaster recovery plan_help! help!_hope to have budget.gif
title: Disaster Recovery Plan Without Budget

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Our disaster recovery plan goes something like this...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Help! Help!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Someday we hope to have a budget.

situation: Carol presents the company's disaster recovery plan to The Boss. She points at an illustration of a panicking Dilbert crying for help, then explains that the actual plan depends on someday getting a budget.
punchline: The company's disaster recovery plan is really just helpless panic and a vague hope for funding, meaning there is effectively no plan at all.
summary: A staffer outlines a disaster plan that amounts to someone screaming for help while waiting on money that may never arrive.

file: 2000/2000-03-23_me from future_next holiday party_never drank agina_predicting future.gif
title: Future Dilbert Warns About Holiday Party

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice, this is me from the future.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Future Dilbert
transcript.text: At the next holiday party, she's all over you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that true?

transcript.speaker: Future Dilbert
transcript.text: No, but after today she never drank again.

situation: Dilbert introduces Alice to a duplicate of himself who claims to be from the future. The future Dilbert tells her that at the next holiday party she will be all over him. When present Dilbert asks if that is true, the future version admits it is not, but says the mortifying prediction made her swear off alcohol permanently.
punchline: The future Dilbert's made-up prediction was designed to embarrass Alice so badly that she quit drinking, a cruel prank framed as time-travel foresight.
summary: A supposed visitor from tomorrow humiliates a coworker with a fabricated prediction about her drunken behavior at the company party.

file: 2000/2000-03-10_pot luck_drop dish_groceries_employee appreciation luncheon.gif
title: Potluck Appreciation Luncheon Grocery Scheme

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The employee appreciation luncheon will be potluck.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Drop off your dish at my house on your way to work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If this works, I'll never need to buy groceries again.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss announces over the computer that the employee appreciation luncheon will be a potluck. He then instructs Dilbert to drop off his dish at the Boss's house on the way to work. In the last panel the Boss privately schemes that this could supply him with free food indefinitely.
punchline: The employee appreciation luncheon is really a ploy for the Boss to get free meals from his staff, so the 'appreciation' is paid for by the employees themselves.
summary: A manager turns a staff thank-you event into a way to have his workers stock his kitchen for free.

file: 2000/2000-06-06_report to mordac_obligated to hate_works.gif
title: Web Mistress Reassigned to Mordac

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ming, I'm moving your web mistress function to I.S. You'll report to Mordac.

transcript.speaker: Ming
transcript.text: No-o-o-o-o!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can still date but I feel obliged to hate your guts now.

transcript.speaker: Man in suspenders
transcript.text: It works for me.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces to Ming that her web mistress function is being moved to I.S. and she will now report to Mordac. She screams in despair. The Boss then says they can still date, but he feels obliged to hate her now, and a coworker says that suits him fine.
punchline: The Boss treats an office romance as unaffected by a reorganization, apparently content to keep dating someone he is now obliged to hate, and a coworker agrees that arrangement works for him.
summary: A reorganization sends a woman to the dreaded Mordac, while her boss cheerfully says their dating can continue alongside mandatory hatred.

file: 2000/2000-01-24_extroverted thinker_human resources_myers briggs personality_quiet dumb guy_personality types_business.gif
title: Assigning Personalities by Myers-Briggs Type

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, all teams will be formed on the basis of Myers-Briggs personality types.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you do not have a personality, one will be assigned to you by Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We need a quiet dumb guy to pair with an extroverted thinker.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces to the assembled employees that teams will now be formed by Myers-Briggs personality types, and that anyone lacking a personality will be given one by Human Resources. Catbert, the HR director, then reads from a sheet of paper that they need a quiet dumb guy to pair with an extroverted thinker.
punchline: HR treats personalities as assignable commodities and casually reduces employees to stereotypes like 'quiet dumb guy', mocking the pseudo-scientific use of personality tests in team building.
summary: Management announces a personality-based team formation scheme, and the evil HR director cheerfully requests a specific dim, silent employee to fill a slot.

file: 2000/2000-08-07_secretary works harder_paid less_many like you_kill boss eventually_fewer bosses.gif
title: Why Bosses Earn More Than Workers

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I work harder than you. Why do I get paid a fifth of what you make?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's because there are many people like you but few people like me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe that's because the people like me eventually kill the people like you.

situation: Alice, holding a document, confronts the Boss at his desk and says she works harder than he does yet earns only a fifth of his pay. The Boss replies with a supply-and-demand argument: workers like her are plentiful while managers like him are rare. Alice responds with a veiled threat that people like her eventually kill people like him.
punchline: Alice turns the Boss's scarcity argument around by suggesting the reason there are few bosses is that frustrated, underpaid workers eventually murder them.
summary: An underpaid employee answers her manager's justification for his high salary with a chilling suggestion about why managers are scarce.

file: 2000/2000-05-13_dogcart consults_e commerce sight_well documented_flying pigs_coolest part.gif
title: Documentation Delivered by Flying Pigs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My team can build an e-commerce site for you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It will be so well-documented that your I.S. group can easily maintain it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But the coolest part is that the documentation will be delivered by flying pigs!

setting: Conference room during a consulting pitch
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, pitches the Boss on building an e-commerce site. He promises the work will be thoroughly documented so the company's I.S. group can maintain it. He then adds that the documentation will arrive via flying pigs, while Wally and Alice sit at the table listening.
punchline: By saying the documentation will be delivered by flying pigs, Dogbert admits it will never happen, since consultants never provide usable documentation.
summary: A consultant dog sells a website project with a promise of perfect documentation, then gives away the lie by saying it will arrive on flying pigs.

file: 2000/2000-03-24_know every tragedy_future_spilled hot coffee_crotch_happen in the future.gif
title: Predicting Dilbert's Coffee Spill Tragedy

transcript.speaker: Psychic
transcript.text: I know every tragedy that will happen in your future.

transcript.speaker: Psychic
transcript.text: Here it comes!!!

transcript.speaker: Psychic
transcript.text: I'll never forget the day I spilled hot coffee on my crotch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ow ow ow!

setting: A waiting room or lounge with teal armchairs, drinking coffee, with a window onto the street outside
situation: A man claiming to foresee every tragedy in Dilbert's future sits beside him as they hold coffee mugs. He suddenly warns that a tragedy is coming and points as Dilbert's coffee spills. In the last panel the man looks out the window as Dilbert runs down the street yelling in pain, and the man recalls the spill as if it were his own memory.
punchline: The man's 'prediction' of the tragedy is actually a plain recollection of his own past coffee-spill accident, and he tells it with grim irony as Dilbert scalds himself.
summary: A self-proclaimed seer of misfortune cries out a warning, and a scalding coffee mishap promptly befalls the man next to him.

file: 2000/2000-05-17_alice date_cafe_dinner date_drive boss nuts_honesty_indifference arouses_using you_vp and engineer.gif
title: Alice Dates VP to Annoy Boss

transcript.speaker: VP
transcript.text: Alice, maybe we shouldn't date. I'm a VP and you're an engineer in my division.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sheesh. Get over yourself. I'm just using you to drive my boss nuts.

transcript.speaker: VP
transcript.text: Your indifference arouses me! I will make you mine!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: VPs.

setting: Restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: A vice president on a dinner date with Alice worries that dating a subordinate engineer in his division is inappropriate. Alice bluntly says she is only using him to annoy her boss. Instead of being offended, the VP is excited by her indifference and vows to win her over, while Alice thinks to herself about VPs.
punchline: Alice's insulting honesty makes the vain VP more attracted to her, confirming her low opinion of vice presidents.
summary: A dinner date takes a turn when an engineer's blunt admission of ulterior motives only fuels her executive date's ardor.

file: 2000/2000-07-24_ahead of schedule_calendar_eight revision_original schedule_meeting_co workers_business.gif
title: Eighth Revision Schedule Is Just Calendar

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: And we finished ahead of schedule.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you referring to the original schedule or the eighth revision?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Schedules can change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would be called a "calendar".

situation: At a project meeting, a coworker proudly announces the team finished ahead of schedule. Dilbert raises his hand and asks whether she means the original schedule or the eighth revised version. When she says schedules can change, he retorts that a schedule that keeps changing is really just a calendar.
punchline: A schedule that gets revised until it is met is meaningless, so Dilbert sarcastically says it is merely a calendar recording when things happened.
summary: A claim of beating the deadline falls apart when Dilbert points out the timeline was rewritten eight times along the way.

file: 2000/2000-08-08_internet start up_business plan_vc and b and b.gif
title: Boss Mishears Venture Capital News

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should create my own little Internet start-up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All I need is a business plan.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: The V.C. are sick of B to B.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Viet Cong are sick of breakfast in bed?

situation: The Boss sits in his chair daydreaming about launching his own internet start-up and decides all he needs is a business plan. His secretary informs him that the V.C. are tired of B to B, and he misinterprets the abbreviations as the Viet Cong being sick of breakfast in bed.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless about dot-com jargon that he mistakes venture capitalists and business-to-business for the Viet Cong and bed-and-breakfast, showing he is unfit to run an internet start-up.
summary: A manager dreaming of dot-com riches reveals his ignorance when he misreads startup buzzwords as something entirely absurd.

file: 2000/2000-02-28_bv day_boss vacation_pretend working_all day with binder.gif
title: Boss Vacation Means No Pretending

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't meet next Tuesday because that's a B.V. day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: B.V.?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Boss vacation.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't need to pretend I'm working that day.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And on Wednesday I'll be walking around all day with a binder.

situation: A balding, bespectacled employee checking a handheld organizer tells a colleague he can't meet next Tuesday because it's a 'B.V. day.' He explains it means the boss is on vacation, so he won't have to pretend to work. He adds that on Wednesday he'll be carrying a binder around all day to look busy.
punchline: Employees only bother to look busy when the boss is around, so a boss's absence is a free day off and his return requires props like a binder to fake productivity.
summary: A worker cheerfully explains that his boss's time off frees him from faking work, though he'll resume the charade with a prop once the boss returns.

file: 2000/2000-02-16_employees fertilizer_management_organism_plant_survive and grow_weasels_dogbert consults.gif
title: Dogbert Calls Boss a Weasel

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Management is like an organism that needs to survive and grow.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Employees are your fertilizer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I'm like a well-fertilized plant?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, and sadly, weasels don't need fertilizer.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, explains to the seated Boss that management is an organism that needs to survive and grow, with employees serving as its fertilizer. The Boss flatteringly assumes this makes him a well-fertilized plant. Dogbert corrects him by saying he is not a plant but a weasel.
punchline: Dogbert politely insults the Boss by implying he is a weasel, and that a weasel doesn't benefit from the fertilizing employees he exploits.
summary: A consulting dog compares management to a living thing fed by its workers, then slyly reveals what kind of creature the boss really is.

file: 2000/2000-05-16_favorite stories_meeting with boss_urban legends_we laughed_told stories_boss.gif
title: Boss's Stories Become Urban Legends

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... How was your meeting with my boss?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We each told our favorite stories about you. Then we laughed and laughed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He has stories about me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He thought they were urban legends.

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss nervously asks Alice how her meeting with his own boss went. Alice says they swapped their favorite stories about him and laughed together. When he is surprised that his boss has stories about him, she reveals his boss assumed the tales were exaggerated urban legends.
punchline: The Boss's incompetence is so extreme that the stories about him sound too absurd to be true, and Alice confirms they are real.
summary: Alice and the boss's superior bond over tales of his ineptitude, which are so outlandish they were assumed to be myths.

file: 2000/2000-06-20_male brain_treat like dirt_good personalities_overated_getting hot.gif
title: Women Prefer Being Treated Badly

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Help me understand the male brain, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I treat you like dirt and you ask me out on a date?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good personalities are overrated.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're getting me all hot over here.

situation: Alice asks Dilbert to explain how the male brain works. She points out that she treats him like dirt, yet he asks her out on a date. Dilbert says good personalities are overrated, and Alice sarcastically replies that his remark is getting her all hot.
punchline: Dilbert's explanation that good personalities are overrated is a backhanded insult that makes Alice's mean behavior sound attractive, and her sarcastic reply shows she finds it anything but flattering.
summary: A woman puzzled by a coworker's romantic interest despite her rudeness gets an answer that reveals he values something other than character.

file: 2000/2000-06-18_work place violence_prevention training_violent emplyees_identify_beards_creepy_ineffective males_widely disprected.gif
title: Violence Training Describes Wally Perfectly

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Welcome to workplace violence prevention training.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: How can we identify potentially violent employees?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ooh! Ooh!

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Wally?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do they have beards?

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Um... no. That was a stupid answer.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Violent employees are usually creepy, ineffective males who are widely disrespected.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I change seats?

setting: Conference room during a training session
situation: A trainer leads a workplace violence prevention class and asks how to spot potentially violent employees. Wally eagerly raises his hand and offers a silly answer about beards, which she dismisses. She then describes the typical violent employee as creepy, ineffective and disrespected, and Dilbert asks to move away from Wally.
punchline: The trainer's profile of a dangerous employee matches Wally exactly, so Dilbert wants to sit somewhere else.
summary: A safety class lecturer lists the traits of dangerous coworkers, and everyone realizes the description fits the man sitting next to Dilbert.

file: 2000/2000-02-03_unvested stock_quit_lose stock_brain irrationality_small loss_huge opportunity_stupid.gif
title: Garbage Man Explains Loss Aversion

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I quit I'll lose some unvested stock. That's why I'm willing to suffer my job.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: A normal brain irrationally puts more weight on a small loss than a huge opportunity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But now that you explained it...

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Now you're just stupid.

situation: Dilbert is taking out the trash and tells a garbage man that he stays in his miserable job only because quitting would forfeit his unvested stock. The garbage man explains that a normal brain overvalues a small loss compared with a huge opportunity. When Dilbert says that now he understands, the garbage man replies that this makes him stupid.
punchline: Once Dilbert knows his reasoning is an irrational bias, continuing to stay in the job is no longer a normal brain quirk but plain stupidity.
summary: A garbage man points out that Dilbert's reluctance to leave a bad job over some stock is a known thinking error, then insults him for knowing it and staying anyway.

file: 2000/2000-07-18_staff cuts_target t shirt_special target.gif
title: Award T-Shirt Marks Layoff Target

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This special T-shirt is awarded to Ted for all of his achievements.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next on the agenda...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're planning some staff cuts.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss presents Ted with a special T-shirt as an award for his achievements, and Ted pulls it on. The shirt has a bullseye target printed on its front. The Boss then moves on to the next agenda item and announces planned staff cuts while Ted sits there wearing the target.
punchline: The 'award' shirt is really a bullseye marking Ted as the one who will be laid off, so the praise is a cruel setup for the staff cuts announcement.
summary: A manager hands out a prize shirt that turns out to be a bullseye, followed straight away by news of layoffs.

file: 2000/2000-04-30_dogcart consults_software has bugs_repackaging_rust inhibitor_error messages_people aren't stupid_they are_spit when type.gif
title: Marketing Bugs as Rust Inhibitor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your software product is riddled with bugs.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend repackaging it as a rust inhibitor for computers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The ads will say "You know it's working because of all the error messages."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People aren't stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to my research, they are.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I need that rust inhibitor; I spit when I type.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I think the rust turned my exclamation upside down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the letter "I".

setting: Conference room during a consulting session
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells a client his buggy software should be sold as a rust inhibitor for computers, with error messages passed off as proof it works. The Boss objects that people aren't stupid, but Dogbert's research chart says otherwise. The client then falls for the pitch, confusing a letter 'I' with a rusted exclamation point.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical marketing premise that customers are stupid is proven right when the client believes the bogus rust inhibitor and mistakes a letter "I" for a corroded exclamation mark.
summary: A consultant proposes disguising a faulty program as anti-corrosion treatment and then watches a gullible customer prove his low opinion of the public correct.

file: 2000/2000-05-26_firing ted_organize goodbye party_suprise_what happens.gif
title: Surprise Party for Fired Ted

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: At ten you'll be firing Ted.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll organize his goodbye party.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you know what would be more efficient?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happens after we yell "Surprise"?

setting: Boss's office and a party room at the office
situation: Carol, the boss's assistant, tells The Boss he will fire Ted at ten o'clock and that she'll organize Ted's goodbye party. The Boss suggests something more efficient, and the next panel shows employees in party hats waiting to yell "Surprise" to Ted, with Dilbert asking what happens next.
punchline: The Boss's idea of efficiency is to hold the goodbye party as a surprise before firing Ted, leaving the employees to wonder what happens when Ted learns the party is for his own termination.
summary: To save time, a boss has the farewell party thrown before the firing, so the staff must greet an unsuspecting Ted with a surprise that is secretly his own send-off.

file: 2000/2000-04-08_tiny dried peanut_what would dogbert do_what would dogbert do_god like_worship_dog worship_friends_ask yourself.gif
title: Ratbert Asks What Dogbert Would Do

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: At all times I ask myself, what would Dogbert do?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Then it doesn't matter that my brain is the size of a tiny dried peanut.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: That thought would make Dogbert hungry.

setting: Outdoor sidewalk beside a grassy hedge
situation: Ratbert walks along a sidewalk, thinking aloud about guiding his life by asking what Dogbert would do. He reasons that this makes his own tiny brain irrelevant. Then he stops and realizes that the size of his brain would make Dogbert hungry, meaning he might be eaten.
punchline: Ratbert's plan to emulate Dogbert unravels when he realizes that Dogbert would see his peanut-sized brain as a snack.
summary: A small lab rat tries to borrow his clever friend's wisdom as a life philosophy, only to realize that friend would treat him as lunch.

file: 2000/2000-06-21_insulted_same level_attractness_hot sexy car_electric car.gif
title: Attractive Car Required For Date

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Frankly, I'm insulted that you asked me out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It means you think we're about the same level of attractiveness.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You'd better have one heckuva sexy car.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's electric.

setting: Apartment entryway, near a coat rack and a vase of flowers
situation: Dilbert helps a woman put on her coat after asking her out, and she says she is insulted by the invitation. Dilbert points out that her being insulted implies she rates them equally in attractiveness. She then demands he at least own a very sexy car, and he answers that his car is electric.
punchline: Dilbert's electric car is a deflating answer to her demand for a sexy car, since in 2000 an electric car was seen as a dull, nerdy vehicle rather than a status symbol.
summary: A woman scoffs at a date invitation, then sets a high bar for car coolness that the awkward engineer's eco-friendly vehicle fails to meet.

file: 2000/2000-06-01_500 with tax_complains about tax_morale improvement award_morale display.gif
title: Morale Award Shrinks After Taxes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The five hundred dollar morale improvement award goes to Ed.

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: Gaa!! It's only $240 after taxes!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So that's what good morale looks like.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently we've had it the whole time.

situation: The Boss announces that a coworker named Ed has won a $500 morale improvement award. Ed looks at his check and angrily shouts that taxes have cut it to only $240. Two coworkers with coffee mugs then remark on Ed's furious reaction.
punchline: Ed's angry outburst is presented as what 'good morale' looks like, implying the office's morale was already this poor and the award did nothing to improve it, with a dig at how much taxes reduce the prize.
summary: A prize meant to lift spirits only makes the winner furious when taxes eat more than half of it, leaving his coworkers to wryly note the state of morale.

file: 2000/2000-07-04_adventures of lulu_no sense of proportion_assinment_work_declares war_anger_resentment.gif
title: Lulu Declares War Over Assignment

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Adventures of Lulu the woman who has no sense of proportion

transcript.speaker: Lulu
transcript.text: Gaaa! Does this mean you hate me?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called an assignment.

transcript.speaker: Lulu
transcript.text: This is war!

situation: A title panel introduces Lulu, a woman with no sense of proportion. The Boss hands her a sheet of paper and she reacts with panic, asking if he hates her. He calmly explains it is simply an assignment, and she responds by declaring war on him.
punchline: Lulu treats a routine work assignment as a personal attack and escalates to declaring war, illustrating her complete lack of proportion.
summary: A boss hands a coworker some routine paperwork and she responds as though he has launched a personal attack, vowing retaliation.

file: 2000/2000-03-30_bad assumptions_analysis_applied flawed logic_predetermined answer_disillusioning_pie chart_science.gif
title: Analysis Built on Boss's Assumptions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did the analysis using your bad assumptions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I applied your flawed logic and arrived at your predetermined answer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shall I begin disillusioning the team?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This needs a pie chart.

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss an analysis and explains that he used the Boss's own bad assumptions and flawed logic to reach the answer the Boss had already decided on. He offers to start disillusioning the team about the result. The Boss ignores the criticism and asks only for a pie chart.
punchline: The Boss is oblivious to the insult and cares only about how the results are presented, not whether the analysis is sound.
summary: An engineer delivers a study that merely echoes his manager's own faulty premises, and the manager responds by requesting a prettier graphic.

file: 2000/2000-07-21_no respect_work_send resume_located.gif
title: Résumé to a Place Nobody Wants

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm tired of getting no respect at work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to send my résumé to a company that's located in a place I'd never want to live.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wonder why they don't respect you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's what I want to know!

situation: Dilbert complains to Dogbert, who is reading a book on the couch, that he gets no respect at work. He announces a plan to send his résumé to a company in a place he would never want to live. Dogbert wonders aloud why people don't respect him, and Dilbert earnestly agrees that he wants to know too.
punchline: Dilbert's plan to apply only to companies in undesirable places shows exactly why he gets no respect, yet he is oblivious and thinks Dogbert is sympathizing rather than mocking.
summary: A man set on sending job applications only to places he'd hate to live fails to see why his own judgment earns him ridicule.

file: 2000/2000-07-17_marketing_respectfully decline_join hallucination_bah_business.gif
title: Declining the Boss's Hallucination Invitation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard that you won't give Marketing the information they need.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I respectfully decline the invitation to join your hallucination.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your system works.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Next time try shortening it to "bah".

situation: The Boss accuses Dilbert of withholding information that Marketing needs. Dilbert politely refuses to accept the premise, calling it the Boss's hallucination. Afterward Dilbert tells Dogbert that the polite-refusal system works, and Dogbert suggests a shorter version.
punchline: Dogbert points out that Dilbert's elaborate, formal way of refusing could be replaced by a simple, dismissive "bah" to the same effect.
summary: Dilbert deflects a boss's baseless accusation with a stiffly formal refusal, then gets advice from his dog that a grunt would do just as well.

file: 2000/2000-04-20_4 hour meeting_company sadist_donuts_invited_no agenda_suppose to hurt.gif
title: Four-Hour Meeting With Donuts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Company Sadist

transcript.speaker: Company Sadist
transcript.text: You're invited to my four-hour meeting.

transcript.speaker: Company Sadist
transcript.text: There's no agenda. It's just supposed to hurt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Any donuts?

transcript.speaker: Company Sadist
transcript.text: Yes, but I'll drop one on the floor and hide it with the others.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like those odds.

situation: The Company Sadist, a co-worker whose job is making others miserable, hands Dilbert an invitation to a four-hour meeting. He openly admits it has no agenda and exists only to cause pain. Dilbert asks about donuts and accepts the sadist's sabotage of the snacks as a fair gamble.
punchline: Dilbert is so resigned to miserable meetings that he will happily endure a pointless four-hour torture session for a decent chance at a donut, even a contaminated one.
summary: A workplace tormentor summons Dilbert to an agenda-free marathon meeting, and Dilbert's only concern is whether the free pastries are worth the pain.

file: 2000/2000-06-25_grossly underpaid_dilbert_work for money_valuable_money_challanges_work for challenges_exchange.gif
title: Challenges Instead of Money Raise Request

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm grossly underpaid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want a raise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, Dilbert, Dilbert, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People don't work here for the money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They work here for the challenge!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If challenges are more valuable than money...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't you give me your money and I'll give you my challenges?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I must kill him before he infects the others.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a raise, claiming he is grossly underpaid. The boss insists employees work for the challenge rather than money, so Dilbert proposes swapping the boss's money for his own challenges. The boss, in a thought bubble, decides he must eliminate Dilbert before his logic spreads.
punchline: Dilbert turns the boss's claim that challenge outweighs money back on him, and the boss's reaction shows he never believed it and fears employees catching on.
summary: A worker uses his manager's own pay-versus-challenge reasoning to propose a trade, and the manager privately plots to silence him.

file: 2000/2000-05-24_ceo spokeperson_leaning on chair_dressed like nun_director_bossy_blunt director.gif
title: Dogbert Directs the CEO's Commercial

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: CEO as spokesperson

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Shouldn't I hold up our product instead of leaning on a chair?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: NO!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That helped your hair but you're still dressed like a nun.

situation: A female CEO is filming a commercial as her company's spokesperson, with Dogbert acting as the director in a beret and holding a megaphone. She tentatively suggests holding up the product instead of leaning on a chair, and Dogbert shouts her down. After her hair is fixed, he bluntly criticizes her outfit.
punchline: The CEO's marketing suggestion is ignored while the director dismisses her appearance, pointing out that she dresses like a nun.
summary: A film director dog bellows at an executive through a megaphone, rejecting her idea and then insulting her wardrobe.

file: 2000/2000-03-17_discover shared vision_foster enrollment_compliance_modify conceptual map_organizational complexity.gif
title: Is Any Of That Work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Should I be trying to discover a shared vision that will foster enrollment rather than compliance?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or should I modify my conceptual map to focus on organizational complexity?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is any of that the same as work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It pays the same.

situation: Wally stands in front of the Boss's desk and rattles off two rounds of management-consultant jargon about shared visions, enrollment versus compliance, and conceptual maps. The Boss, seated in his chair, asks whether any of it counts as actual work. Wally replies that it pays the same.
punchline: Wally admits that spouting buzzwords earns him the same salary as doing real work, so he has no incentive to do the real thing.
summary: A lazy employee buries his boss in business-speak and then cheerfully concedes that the empty talk is just as well rewarded as genuine effort.

file: 2000/2000-05-21_behind schedule_created without knowledge_future_wild guesses_surrigates_knowledge_project dealines_trade_show dates_failure assured_apologize_budgets are created.gif
title: Schedules Are Wild Guesses, Budgets Doom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you explain why your project is behind schedule?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes. A schedule is an artificial device created without knowledge of the future.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wild guesses are used as surrogates for knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Project deadlines are tied to trade show dates instead of reality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then management cuts the budget until failure is assured.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I assume you called me here so you can apologize for your role in all this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like to hear how budgets are created?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to explain why his project is behind schedule. Dilbert calmly explains how schedules are guesses, deadlines are set by trade show dates, and management slashes budgets to guarantee failure. The Boss then sarcastically assumes Dilbert is there to apologize, and Dilbert offers to explain how budgets are created.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's blame back on him by showing that management's own practices cause the delays, and he threatens to explain the even more absurd budget process next.
summary: A manager demands an explanation for a late project and gets a deadpan lecture on how his own organization sets its projects up to fail.

file: 2000/2000-08-02_promotion in title_senior vice duke_imperial majesty_engineering_business cards_vice duke.gif
title: Grandiose Title, No Business Cards

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I'm giving you a promotion in title.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now you're the Senior Vice Duke and Imperial Majesty of all Engineering.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Can I have business cards now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, you're only a Vice Duke.

situation: The Boss tells Ted he is being promoted in title only and bestows an absurdly grand name, Senior Vice Duke and Imperial Majesty of all Engineering. Ted, pleased, asks whether he can now have business cards. The Boss refuses, saying he is only a Vice Duke, apparently ignoring the title he just gave him.
punchline: The Boss hands out an inflated, meaningless title as a substitute for real benefits, then contradicts himself to deny even the small perk of business cards.
summary: A manager showers an employee with a ridiculous royal-sounding job title but won't back it up with even the most basic perk.

file: 2000/2000-03-06_your cucbicle_connect network_stop by_every few minutes_the boss_emplyee.gif
title: Six Weeks Without a Network

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This will be your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In six weeks our I.T. people will connect you to the network so you can do your job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll stop by every few minutes to see what you're doing.

situation: The Boss shows a new employee to his cubicle and explains that the I.T. department won't connect him to the network for six weeks, so he can't do any real work until then. The Boss then cheerfully announces he will check in every few minutes to monitor what the employee is doing.
punchline: The Boss plans to constantly monitor an employee who has been given no tools to work with, which highlights the absurdity of demanding visible productivity while providing no means to be productive.
summary: A manager welcomes a new hire to a cubicle that is useless for weeks, then promises to hover over him constantly anyway.

file: 2000/2000-07-05_assignment_confronts lulu_dilbert confronts lulu_huge crisis_series of crisises_smite_static guard_god softening.gif
title: Lulu's Crises Invite Divine Smiting

transcript.speaker: Lulu
transcript.text: Come help me on this assignment. It's a huge crisis!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lulu, do you ever wonder why your life is a series of crises?

transcript.speaker: Lulu
transcript.text: I assume God is softening me up before smiting me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me while I put on my static guard.

situation: Lulu, a coworker, comes to Dilbert's desk asking for help with an assignment she calls a huge crisis. Dilbert asks if she ever wonders why her life is a constant string of crises. She calmly says she assumes God is softening her up before smiting her, so Dilbert says he needs to put on his static guard.
punchline: Dilbert protects himself from the lightning bolt he expects to strike Lulu, since being near someone about to be smitten is hazardous.
summary: A coworker who lurches from emergency to emergency blames divine wrath, and her colleague prepares to protect himself from the incoming bolt.

file: 2000/2000-04-21_company sadist_forwarded email_email insulted_interesting theory.gif
title: Forwarded Email Insults Half the Team

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Company Sadist

transcript.speaker: Company Sadist
transcript.text: I forwarded your e-mail to everyone.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa! That e-mail insulted half the people on our project!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's an interesting theory about why my hair is brown.

setting: Office cubicle and a conference room
situation: The Company Sadist gleefully tells Alice he has forwarded her private e-mail to everyone, and he laughs as she panics because it insulted half the project team. In the meeting that follows, Alice, sitting with Dilbert and another coworker, tries to brush off the fallout by making an absurd remark about her hair.
punchline: Alice's non-sequitur about her hair color is a desperate attempt to pass off her insulting e-mail as harmless, since the insult clearly had nothing to do with hair.
summary: A malicious coworker spreads a colleague's insulting message to the whole team, and she tries to deflect the blowback with a ridiculous excuse.

file: 2000/2000-03-13_idea_change department name_engineering_similar idea_marketing_done_business.gif
title: Adding E- To Department Names

transcript.speaker: Engineering Manager
transcript.text: My idea is to change our department name from Engineering to...

transcript.speaker: Engineering Manager
transcript.text: e-Engineering.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: I'm working on a similar idea for Marketing but it's not done yet.

situation: At a meeting table, a bald, bespectacled manager announces his big idea to rename the Engineering department, building suspense before revealing it is simply 'e-Engineering'. A manager from Marketing then says he is working on a similar idea for his own department but hasn't finished it.
punchline: The 'innovative' rebranding is just sticking an 'e-' prefix on the old name, and the Marketing manager's remark that his similar idea isn't done yet shows everyone is copying the same dot-com buzzword trend with no real thought.
summary: A manager proudly unveils a department rename that merely tacks a trendy prefix onto the old title, and a rival manager is already planning to copy the trick.

file: 2000/2000-04-04_wally disability_spy on him_need video evidence_vigorous activity_vigourously.gif
title: Spying on Wally's Vigorous Activity

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally is out on disability. I want you to spy on him.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We need video evidence of Wally doing a vigorous activity.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Can you think of anything that Wally does vigorously?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd rather not.

setting: Office, with a final panel in a coworker's cubicle
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, instructs a green-shirted employee holding a camcorder to spy on Wally, who is out on disability, and to catch him on video doing something vigorous. The employee then asks Alice whether she can think of anything Wally does vigorously. Alice, with her big hair and a grim expression, declines to answer.
punchline: Alice's reluctance to name any vigorous activity implies that the only thing Wally does vigorously is something unpleasant or embarrassing, which she would rather not describe.
summary: HR sends a coworker to film a sick-leave employee in action, and the only person who might know what he does energetically refuses to say.

file: 2000/2000-01-31_20% more money_hire someone_loyal_40% more_science_mime_wall blocks.gif
title: Boss Pays More for Loyalty

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Another company offered me twenty percent more.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will you match it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I prefer to hire someone who is loyal, even if I have to pay forty percent more.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Managing is supposed to be a science!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My mime wall blocks your sound.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that another company offered him a 20 percent raise and asks whether the boss will match it. The boss refuses, saying he would rather hire a loyal replacement even at a 40 percent higher salary. When Dilbert protests that management should be a science, the boss pretends to be trapped behind an invisible mime wall so he can't hear him.
punchline: The boss would rather pay twice as much to replace a loyal-seeming employee than keep a current one for less, and he dodges the obvious flaw in this logic by pretending to be a mime stuck behind an invisible wall.
summary: A manager turns down a modest counteroffer in favor of an even costlier new hire, then mimes his way out of the argument.

file: 2000/2000-07-27_upgraded three things_broke three things_terms_computer work.gif
title: IT Upgrade Breaks Three Things

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: Well, I upgraded three things and I accidentally broke three things.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Does my computer work?

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: In I.S. terms, I came out ahead.

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: No, but if it did, it would be much faster.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Snap

situation: An IT technician works at Alice's desk, upgrading her computer, and reports he upgraded three things but also accidentally broke three things. Alice asks whether her computer works, and he dodges the question with industry jargon before admitting it doesn't. Alice angrily snaps her pencil in frustration.
punchline: The IT worker spins breaking as many things as he fixed as a success, and admits the computer doesn't work but would be faster if it did.
summary: A technician proudly breaks even on a computer upgrade while the user just wants a working machine.

file: 2000/2000-06-12_employees_ignorant_intranet collaboration_sign it_their ignorance_tools_dogbert consults_business.gif
title: Selling Collaboration Tools for Ignorance

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: All of your employees are ignorant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can fix that by selling you intranet collaboration tools.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But if they're sharing their ignorance...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (thought)
transcript.text: Sign it. Sign it. Sign it.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that all of his employees are ignorant. He offers to fix this by selling the company intranet collaboration tools, then warns that the tools might just spread the ignorance around. The Boss starts signing a contract while Dogbert silently thinks 'sign it'.
punchline: Dogbert admits his own product could simply let employees share their ignorance, but the Boss is so eager to buy that he signs anyway, which is exactly what Dogbert wants.
summary: A canine consultant pitches software to a gullible manager, even conceding the product might backfire, while mentally urging him to sign the deal.

file: 2000/2000-01-13_didn't listen_good work_magazine_more assignments_new boss_boss_secretary.gif
title: Carol Mistaken for the New Boss

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When you finish this, I have more assignments for you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Carol, you're the Boss's secretary, not my boss. And this is a page from a magazine.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Keep up the good work.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You didn't listen. That can only mean you're my new boss.

situation: Alice walks up to Carol's desk and hands her a page, announcing she has more assignments for her. Carol points out that Alice isn't her boss and that the page is just a magazine page. Alice ignores her and tells her to keep up the good work, which Carol takes as proof that Alice has become her new boss.
punchline: Carol concludes that ignoring what people say and carrying on regardless is the defining trait of a boss, so Alice's refusal to listen proves she is now in charge.
summary: A coworker blithely ignores every objection from the secretary she is handing work to, which convinces the secretary that she must be management now.

file: 2000/2000-05-20_performance review_weaknesses need improvement_become invisible_blurry_multitasking_too often.gif
title: Too Fast to See Review

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any weaknesses that need improvement?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I work so fast that I become invisible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I seem blurry right now, it's because I'm multi-tasking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Once a year is way too often for this.

setting: The Boss's office during an annual performance review
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert in his performance review whether he has any weaknesses to improve. Dilbert answers with absurd boasts that he works so fast he becomes invisible and blurry from multitasking. In his private thought he admits that doing this review once a year is far too often.
punchline: Dilbert gives deliberately ridiculous self-praise as his 'weakness' while privately revealing he finds the annual review itself a tiresome, pointless exercise.
summary: Asked to name a flaw in his appraisal, Dilbert brags about supernatural speed while secretly dreading the whole ritual.

file: 2000/2000-03-25_return to future_majesty_retroactive_time travelers_boss around_dance.gif
title: Retroactive Majesty and Time Traveler Dancing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I must return to the future now, your Majesty.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They don't call me Majesty, yet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll make it retro-active...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...so you could boss around the time travelers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In that case, dance for me.

situation: Dilbert, who claims to be a time traveler, tells Dogbert he must return to the future and addresses him as 'your Majesty.' Dogbert points out he isn't called that yet, and Dilbert explains he will make the title retroactive so Dogbert can boss around time travelers. Dogbert immediately exploits the new authority by ordering Dilbert to dance.
punchline: As soon as Dogbert is granted retroactive power over time travelers, he uses it for petty personal amusement by making Dilbert dance.
summary: A time-traveling Dilbert flatters Dogbert with a retroactive royal title, and the new monarch promptly puts his first subject to work as his personal entertainer.

file: 2000/2000-06-23_chatter non stop_every woman_no male traits_galk.gif
title: Date Etiquette Role Reversal Questions

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Do you mind if I chatter nonstop about people you don't know?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Do you mind if I gawk at every woman who walks by?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: In fact, I would appreciate it if you displayed no male traits whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can do.

setting: A restaurant table during a date
situation: Dilbert sits across from a woman at a small table with a flower and wine glasses. She asks whether he minds her chattering nonstop about strangers, then whether he minds her gawking at every woman who passes, before demanding he show no male traits at all. He politely agrees to everything.
punchline: The date gleefully asks for behaviors that are stereotypically hers while banning stereotypically male ones, and Dilbert's meek compliance shows how thoroughly he is a pushover.
summary: A woman on a date lays out a one-sided set of conditions for the evening, and her compliant companion accepts them all.

file: 2000/2000-12-13_eternity_flaming worms_if i die_succession plan_tiptoes_what to do_dogbert consults.gif
title: Dogbert's Afterlife Succession Plan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been told to make a succession plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The plan should say what to do if I die.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can help.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And if Satan makes you stand in flaming worms up to your nose, try standing on your tiptoes for eternity.

situation: The Boss tells consultant Dogbert he has been told to create a succession plan, meaning a plan for what happens if he dies. Dogbert offers to help, then writes the plan, which consists of advice for surviving in hell rather than anything about who takes over the business.
punchline: Dogbert takes 'what to do if I die' literally and gives the Boss tips for coping with damnation, implying the Boss is headed to hell and that the consultant's advice is useless for the actual business need.
summary: A consultant answers his boss's request for a plan covering his own death by offering survival tips for the underworld.

file: 2000/2000-10-26_internet_personal rasons_whole world_knowledge_entertainmemt_finger tips_ice cream_so hungry_eating in cubicle_technology.gif
title: Catbert Tempts Dilbert With Ice Cream

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I... must... resist... using... the Internet for personal reasons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaa! There's a whole world of knowledge and entertainment at my fingertips... teasing me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ice cream! I'm so hungry!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No eating in your cubicle.

situation: Dilbert sweats at his computer, struggling to avoid using the Internet for personal reasons and nearly breaking under the temptation. Catbert, the evil HR director, appears over the cubicle wall with a fishing pole dangling an ice cream cone in front of Dilbert. When Dilbert reaches for it, Catbert reminds him that eating in a cubicle is forbidden.
punchline: Catbert baits Dilbert with ice cream, which Dilbert desperately wants, only to cite the no-eating policy and punish him, showing HR's sadistic enjoyment of tricking employees into rule violations.
summary: A tormented employee fights the urge to browse the web, only for a sinister HR cat to lure him into a different rule violation with a fishing-rod snack.

file: 2000/2000-11-15_genetic anamolies_genetic engineering_grow on_hand growing on head_new temp_temp agnecy_wear goggles.gif
title: Genetically Engineered Temp Workers Gone Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Temp Agency uses genetic engineering to grow our own workers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Isn't that dangerous?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wear safety goggles.

transcript.speaker: Temp
transcript.text: I'm the new temp.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Um... I'm Alice.

situation: Dogbert explains to the Boss that his temp agency grows its own workers through genetic engineering. The Boss asks whether that is dangerous, and Dogbert says he wears safety goggles. A new temp then arrives, who appears to be a normal man whose raised hand looks like it is growing out of the top of his head, and Alice stands beside him, confused.
punchline: Dogbert's only safety measure is goggles, and the resulting temp worker is a genetic mishap, apparently with a hand growing from his head, showing that the agency's risky cloning produces defective workers.
summary: A dog running a staffing agency brags about lab-grown employees, shrugs off the danger with eye protection, and delivers a hapless, deformed result.

file: 2000/2000-09-16_email monkey_cold turkey_little chatting_not addictive_hop on.gif
title: Email Monkey Meets Cold Turkey

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I used to have an e-mail monkey on my back, but I went cold turkey.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I still do a little chatting but that's not addictive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, just shut up and hop on.

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: I'm ROFL.

setting: Office, with Dilbert holding a coffee mug beside a coworker
situation: A coworker boasts that he quit his e-mail addiction (an actual monkey on his back) by going cold turkey (a literal turkey now clings to him). Dilbert skeptically questions whether his remaining chatting habit is really non-addictive. The coworker snaps at him to shut up, and a small monkey nearby is seen laughing.
punchline: The coworker claims to have kicked his online addiction but has only swapped it for another, and his irritable reaction when challenged proves Dilbert's point.
summary: A man who says he beat his e-mail habit gets defensive when told his chat habit is just as addictive, with literal animals illustrating each idiom.

file: 2000/2000-11-06_passport_cubicle tranquility_no one ever thought_undesirables.gif
title: Do Not Disturb Sign Backfires

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This sign is my passport to cubicle tranquillity.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I wonder why no one ever thought of it before.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nice sign. Does it keep away the undesirables?

situation: Alice proudly shows off a handwritten 'Do Not Disturb' sign she plans to use to get peace in her cubicle, while Dilbert stands nearby holding a coffee mug. Wally then wanders up, comments on the sign, and asks if it keeps away undesirables, which she answers with an angry glare.
punchline: Wally's casual remark about 'undesirables' means he is the very kind of unwelcome visitor the sign is meant to repel, and he is oblivious to it while Alice fumes.
summary: A woman's plan for undisturbed quiet is spoiled the moment a clueless colleague strolls up and comments on her new sign.

file: 2000/2000-10-15_old computer_give to school_hard drive_tax accounting_night mare_school playground_old refrigerator_better idea.gif
title: Dumping Old Computer On Playground

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do I get rid of my old computer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why don't you give it to a school?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, it would take me a week to find someone to take it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The hard drive is broken and it has no software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it would cause a tax accounting nightmare.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could leave it on the school playground at night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's what I did with my old refrigerator.

transcript.speaker: Hooded figure
transcript.text: What I hate most is that I didn't have a better idea.

setting: Dilbert's office and a school playground at night
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss how to dispose of his old computer, and the Boss suggests donating it to a school. Dilbert lists the obstacles: it takes a week to find a taker, the machine is broken and has no software, and it creates a tax accounting mess. The Boss then suggests secretly dumping it on a school playground at night, and a hooded figure is shown doing just that, annoyed that the idea came from someone else.
punchline: Dilbert shoots down the charitable option with bureaucratic objections, then admits that illegally dumping the junk at a school at night is exactly what he did with his old refrigerator, and he resents not coming up with the idea himself.
summary: A worker wanting to offload outdated hardware finds that donating it is too much hassle, so he falls back on sneaking it onto a schoolyard under cover of darkness.

file: 2000/2000-12-15_cross charge time_attended meeting_drunken moneky_refund_money back_unfair preactices.gif
title: Refund Demanded for Useless Meeting Attendee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did you cross-charge your time to my budget?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I attended your meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All you did was sit there like a drunken monkey. I want a refund.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Talk to my boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...so it doesn't seem fair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ka-ching!

situation: Dilbert confronts a coworker who billed his meeting attendance to Dilbert's project budget. When Dilbert complains the coworker contributed nothing and demands a refund, the coworker redirects him to his own boss. Dilbert then pleads his case to that boss, who gleefully celebrates the money.
punchline: The boss who profits from internal cross-charging has no interest in refunding anything, so the complaint is met with delighted cash-register glee.
summary: A man tries to claw back money after a worthless colleague bills his department for sitting in a meeting, only to find the colleague's manager happily pocketing the fee.

file: 2000/2000-10-18_dozen_dysfunctional families_dysfunctional recruitment_recruit emloyees_trunk.gif
title: Dogbert Recruits From Dysfunctional Families

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
