transcript.text: You need "Dogbert's Dysfunctional Employee Recruitment Services."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I only recruit employees who were raised in dysfunctional families. They don't mind being mistreated!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How soon can you get me some?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have a dozen in the trunk of my car.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, pitches his recruitment service to the Boss, explaining that he only supplies employees from dysfunctional families because they tolerate mistreatment. The Boss eagerly asks how soon he can get some, and Dogbert reveals he already has a dozen in his car trunk.
punchline: Dogbert implies he has literally kidnapped a dozen people and stashed them in his trunk, while the Boss happily wants to hire workers who will accept abuse.
summary: A scheming dog consultant sells his boss a supply of workers conditioned to accept abuse, and has a batch conveniently stashed in his car.

file: 2000/2000-12-11_enough engineers_all requests_sales support_online data base_contempt_disbelief_mixture.gif
title: Dilbert Meditates Instead of Glaring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't have enough engineers to handle all the requests for sales support.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Build an online database to log all the requests.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It might look as if I'm staring at you with a mixture of contempt and disbelief, but I'm actually meditating.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that engineering is understaffed for all the sales support requests. The Boss responds by telling him to build an online database to log the requests, which does nothing to address the shortage. Dilbert stares at him and claims he is merely meditating.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically disguises his contempt and disbelief at the Boss's useless non-solution as meditation, since logging requests does not add any engineers.
summary: Asked for more staff, a boss offers a tracking system instead, and his employee's incredulous stare gets passed off as a moment of zen.

file: 2000/2000-12-24_birthday_mothers birthday_warp up present_an hour later_throwing towel_element of suprise_no waste paper_cookies.gif
title: Dilbert Skips Wrapping, Borrows Mom's Towel

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been thinking about your birthday, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: How sweet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It seems so inefficient to wrap up your present.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll just rip up the wrapping paper an hour later.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I was thinking of throwing a towel over it instead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'd get all of the element of surprise without wasting paper.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I can use one of your towels so I don't have to lug one from my house.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Of course, dear. I wouldn't want you to lug a big heavy towel just for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good. It's settled.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Those aren't for you.

situation: Dilbert tells his mother he has been thinking about her birthday and proposes covering her present with a towel instead of wrapping it, to save paper. He then suggests using one of her own towels so he doesn't have to carry one over. She sarcastically agrees, and when he reaches for her plate of cookies, she tells him they aren't for him.
punchline: After Dilbert cheaply gets out of buying wrapping paper and a towel by using his mom's own, she gets back at him by refusing to let him have any cookies.
summary: A son tries to cut corners on his mother's birthday gift by recycling her own towel as wrapping, and she responds with pointed politeness and a guarded plate of cookies.

file: 2000/2000-11-24_staying real_keeping to core_good_duuude_say thing_no meaning.gif
title: Meaningless Slang Compliment From Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Dilbert, my man, you're stayin' real and keepin' to the core.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that good?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't even know what it means.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do you say things that have no meaning?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Du-u-u-de!

setting: Conference room table in an office meeting
situation: At a meeting table, a coworker in a blue sweater compliments Dilbert with trendy-sounding slang about staying real and keeping to the core. Dilbert asks if that is good, and the coworker admits he has no idea what it means. When Dilbert asks why he says meaningless things, the coworker just answers with a drawn-out 'Dude!'
punchline: The coworker uses empty buzzword-style slang with no understanding of it, and when challenged he has no real answer, only more slang.
summary: A colleague showers Dilbert with hollow jargon he admits he doesn't understand, then deflects the criticism with a stretched-out exclamation.

file: 2000/2000-10-09_misaligned_position code_module_problem_anonymous note_disappearing link.gif
title: Catbert Withholds Pay Over Misaligned Code

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We can't pay you this week because your position code is misaligned with your module.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Worse yet, no one knows what that means or whose responsibility it is to fix it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who told you about the problem?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It was an anonymous note with disappearing ink.

setting: Dilbert's office, with Catbert sitting on a desk
situation: Catbert, acting as human resources, informs Dilbert that he won't be paid this week because of a vague payroll problem involving a misaligned position code. He adds that nobody knows what the problem means or who is supposed to fix it. When Dilbert asks how Catbert found out about it, Catbert says an anonymous note written in disappearing ink told him.
punchline: The unexplained payroll error has no owner and no way to be traced, since the only evidence of it came from an anonymous note in vanishing ink, leaving Dilbert with no recourse.
summary: An HR cat denies a worker his paycheck over an incomprehensible coding error that nobody is responsible for and whose source has literally vanished.

file: 2000/2000-11-26_pet project_isn't feasible_working numebrs_underlying reality_massaged the numbers_working_numbers_impossiblepossible_new numbers_other ideas_fiddle with numbers.gif
title: Fiddling With Numbers To Save Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My analysis shows that your pet project isn't feasible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try working the numbers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That wouldn't change the underlying reality.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if we massaged the numbers?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Massaging the numbers means the same thing as working the numbers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't make the impossible possible by hallucinating new numbers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any other ideas?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That depends on what the phrase "fiddle with the numbers" means.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his analysis shows the Boss's pet project is not feasible. The Boss repeatedly asks him to work, massage, or otherwise alter the numbers, while Dilbert objects that this can't change reality. In the last panel Dilbert gives in, asking what 'fiddle with the numbers' would mean.
punchline: After insisting that manipulating numbers is pointless and dishonest, Dilbert caves and effectively offers to fudge the data when asked for other ideas, showing how pressure from management erodes integrity.
summary: A manager keeps pressing an analyst to doctor his figures so a doomed favorite project looks viable, and the analyst's resistance finally crumbles.

file: 2000/2000-09-14_email_addiction_monkey on back_resist_key board with foot.gif
title: E-mail Monkey Addiction Excuse

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have an e-mail monkey on my back, but I can quit whenever I want.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't need to check it every minute. I can resist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But look! The stupid monkey hit my keyboard with his foot!

situation: Dilbert, with a literal monkey clinging to his back, thinks to himself that he is not addicted to e-mail and can quit at any time. He then sits at his computer and checks it anyway, blaming the monkey for hitting the keyboard with its foot.
punchline: Dilbert makes a flimsy excuse to cover his compulsive e-mail checking, just like an addict denying his dependence while blaming the 'monkey on his back' for the relapse.
summary: A man insists he can give up checking his inbox whenever he likes, then promptly blames the primate perched on him when he gives in.

file: 2000/2000-11-25_not care_subordinates_all changed_not caring funtion.gif
title: Delegating the Not-Caring Function

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I used to not care about my subordinates.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But that's all changed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I delegate the not-caring function to what's-her-face over here.

situation: The Boss tells Wally that he used to not care about his subordinates, but that has changed. In the last panel he gestures toward a woman at her desk, whose name he doesn't know, and says he now delegates the not-caring to her.
punchline: The Boss's apparent change of heart is just more indifference: he doesn't care enough even to learn his employee's name, and he hands off the job of not caring to someone else.
summary: A manager claims he has changed his attitude toward his staff, then reveals he has simply outsourced his indifference to a coworker whose name he can't remember.

file: 2000/2000-10-11_planning weddings_temporary zombie division_raising babies_divorcing_took dog_good places booked.gif
title: Transferred to the Temporary Zombie Division

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Helen, I'm transferring you to the temporary zombie division.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You will be with other people who are planning weddings, raising babies and divorcing.

transcript.speaker: Zombie employee
transcript.text: She took my dog.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: All the good places are booked.

situation: The Boss tells an employee named Helen she is being moved to a 'temporary zombie division' for people whose personal lives are consuming them, such as weddings, babies and divorces. In the last panel, Helen stands among co-workers walking with arms outstretched like zombies, complaining about a divorce and about booking wedding venues.
punchline: Employees distracted by major life events are treated by management as brain-dead zombies, shuffled into a holding division until their personal lives settle down.
summary: A manager sidelines a distracted worker into a holding pen for staff too wrapped up in life events to be productive.

file: 2000/2000-12-01_know first aid_marketing_picked intern_engineering dead pool_team building pot luck_lunch_business.gif
title: Engineering Dead Pool Betting on Intern

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll see if the guys in marketing know first aid.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Really? I picked that intern in our engineering dead pool!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently our team-building potluck lunch didn't take.

situation: After a medical emergency involving an intern, Dilbert offers to go and find someone in marketing who knows first aid. A coworker responds that he had picked the intern in the engineering department's dead pool, treating the emergency as a betting win. Dilbert remarks that the team-building potluck lunch clearly failed to create any bonds.
punchline: The engineers are so callous that they are running a betting pool on which intern will die, showing that the team-building lunch had no effect on their sense of camaraderie.
summary: While someone seeks help for a collapsed intern, a coworker celebrates winning a macabre office betting pool on the intern's demise.

file: 2000/2000-12-19_casual dress day_hurting productivity_need to cancel_real problems_irrational management_comfortable plants.gif
title: Blaming Comfortable Pants for Productivity

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Casual dress day is hurting our productivity. We need to cancel it.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Is it possible that our real problems are caused by irrational management?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I think comfortable pants are the problem.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Sounds right.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss announces that casual dress day is hurting productivity and should be cancelled. Catbert, the HR director, suggests that irrational management might be the real cause of the company's problems. The Boss dismisses this and blames comfortable pants, and Catbert agrees.
punchline: Management refuses to consider that its own irrationality is the problem and scapegoats casual clothing instead, while Catbert sarcastically or cynically goes along with it.
summary: A manager would rather blame relaxed clothing than examine his own bad decision-making, and the HR cat plays along.

file: 2000/2000-10-05_bad performance review_tape measure_measure twice.gif
title: Boss Botches Measure Twice Proverb

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My philosophy is: Measure twice...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then cut twice, then uh...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give the tape measure a bad performance review?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Ooh.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss begins to state his philosophy with the proverb 'measure twice.' Dilbert starts to finish it but trails off, and the Boss completes it with a nonsensical idea: giving the tape measure a bad performance review. A coworker giggles and another reacts with an impressed 'ooh' as if it were wisdom.
punchline: The Boss twists the carpenter's maxim into a management cliché, treating a tape measure like an employee that deserves a performance review, while subordinates sycophantically react to his nonsense.
summary: A manager mangles a woodworking proverb into an absurd plan to discipline a measuring tool, and his audience reacts as though he's said something clever.

file: 2000/2000-10-28_fired me yesterday_leaving previous job_non buisness_use of internet_crime dont pay.gif
title: Fired Yesterday, Rehired Today, Demands Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And what's your reason for leaving your previous job?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You fired me yesterday for non-business use of the Internet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Crime doesn't pay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait until you hear my minimum acceptable salary.

situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and asks why he left his previous job, not realizing the candidate is Dilbert, whom he fired the day before for personal Internet use. Dilbert points this out, and the Boss smugly says crime doesn't pay, prompting Dilbert to threaten an exorbitant salary demand.
punchline: The Boss's moralizing about crime not paying is undercut by Dilbert's salary demand, implying that firing him and then rehiring him will cost the company dearly.
summary: A manager quizzes a job applicant about his last position, only to be reminded that he himself dismissed the man the previous day, and the applicant promptly names a price for his return.

file: 2000/2000-10-23_questioned by boss_work here_take a bite.gif
title: Boss Doubts Dilbert Still Works Here

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What the...?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You still work here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's gonna take a bite out of my productivity.

situation: The Boss walks past Dilbert's cubicle, notices him sitting at his desk and is surprised, asking if he still works there. Dilbert, silent in the first two panels, thinks to himself that the encounter will cost him productivity.
punchline: Dilbert's private thought treats the Boss's insulting question as a time-wasting interruption, implying the Boss is the real drain on productivity and that the Boss barely knows who his own employees are.
summary: A manager who doesn't recognize his own employee wanders by and questions his presence, leaving the worker to grumble inwardly about the lost time.

file: 2000/2000-10-17_halluciantaing_dilbert_punish_ambiguous_untraceable_die dilbert.gif
title: Boss Punishes Dilbert Through Password

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did Dilbert do something terrible or am I hallucinating?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd better play it safe and punish him in ways that are ambiguous and untraceable.

transcript.speaker: Network Administrator
transcript.text: I had to change your network password to "die-dilbert-die"

transcript.speaker: Network Administrator
transcript.text: and I can't say why.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss sits at his desk thinking he may have hallucinated Dilbert doing something terrible. Unsure, he decides to punish Dilbert in vague, deniable ways. A network administrator then tells Dilbert that his password has been changed to 'die-dilbert-die' and she can't explain why.
punchline: The Boss's cowardly plan for untraceable punishment is immediately carried out through an absurdly hostile network password, implying he orchestrated it without any justification.
summary: Unsure whether Dilbert actually wronged him, the boss opts for deniable retaliation, which promptly arrives as a menacing new login credential.

file: 2000/2000-10-12_believe loser_implied_picking stock_stock tip.gif
title: Stock Tip From a Loser

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Do you want a stock tip?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you asking me to believe you're a loser at every aspect of life except picking stock?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: That's not what I'm asking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's implied.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker offers Alice a stock tip, and she sarcastically challenges him to claim he is a failure at everything except picking stocks. Later the coworker eats lunch with Dilbert and insists that isn't what he was asking, and Dilbert points out that it's implied.
punchline: Offering a stock tip implies the offerer is a pathetic loser in all other areas of life, so his financial expertise is itself an insult to his credibility.
summary: A coworker's investment advice is met with a withering reminder that his only apparent success is in the stock market.

file: 2000/2000-11-20_internet music_free_digital tops_here with engineers_ideas_applied to others.gif
title: Free Music, Unpaid Engineers Idea

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: All music on the Internet should be free. Artists could make money from digital tips.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Great idea. We'll do the same thing here with the engineers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever noticed that my ideas are only brilliant when applied to other people?

situation: During a meeting, a coworker argues that music on the Internet should be free and artists could earn money from digital tips. The Boss, who is seated at the table, enthusiastically decides to apply the same idea to the engineers, meaning they would work for free and rely on tips. Dilbert then comments dryly that the Boss only finds ideas brilliant when they affect other people.
punchline: The Boss loves the idea of working for tips only because he intends to make the engineers, not himself, the ones who work for free.
summary: A casual remark about free online music inspires the boss to propose that his engineers work without a salary and live off tips.

file: 2000/2000-10-03_architectural materpiece_experience_no storage espace_new office building_architectectural masterpiece.gif
title: Voices Warn About Storage Space

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new office building will be an architectural masterpiece!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The voices in my head are shouting "No storage space! No storage space!"

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What is happening to me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's called experience.

setting: Conference room during a presentation about a new office building
situation: The Boss proudly presents a drawing of the company's new office building, calling it an architectural masterpiece. A coworker at the table clutches his head, hearing voices complaining about a lack of storage space, and panics about what is happening to him. Dilbert calmly tells him it is simply experience.
punchline: Dilbert recasts the coworker's apparent madness as hard-won experience: he has seen enough badly planned buildings to know that flashy architecture usually means no storage space.
summary: A manager brags about a stunning new building while a veteran employee is tormented by a mental alarm about missing storage, which a colleague identifies as the product of experience.

file: 2000/2000-12-29_managers brain_like pump_prime it_learns first_form foundation_future perceptions_talking smack.gif
title: Priming the Manager's Brain Pump

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: A manager's brain is like a pump. If it becomes empty you must prime it.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Whatever he learns first will form the foundation for all of his future perceptions.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This guy has been talking smack about you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Unh...

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, explains to Dilbert that a manager's mind is like a pump that must be primed, because whatever it learns first shapes all later perceptions. He then turns to the slumped, empty-headed Boss and plants the idea that Dilbert has been talking smack about him.
punchline: Catbert demonstrates his theory by cynically priming the Boss's blank brain with a false accusation against Dilbert, so the Boss will permanently view Dilbert negatively.
summary: An HR villain shows how easily a vacant-minded manager can be manipulated by feeding him the first impression he'll ever have of someone.

file: 2000/2000-10-19_dysfunctional family_worthless_seventy hours_weekly_more like you_screams at worker.gif
title: Dysfunctional Upbringing Makes Ideal Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I understand that you were raised in a dysfunctional family.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're gonna work seventy hours a week or you're worthless!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You love me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are there any more like you at home?

situation: The Boss interviews an employee and learns he grew up in a dysfunctional family. He then screams that the employee must work seventy hours a week or be considered worthless. The employee, tearful, interprets the abuse as affection, and the Boss asks whether there are more people like him at home.
punchline: The employee's abusive upbringing has conditioned him to mistake verbal abuse for love, making him the perfect exploitable worker, and the Boss wants to recruit more of his family.
summary: A boss discovers that a worker's troubled childhood makes him gladly accept abuse and overwork, and eagerly seeks more such recruits.

file: 2000/2000-10-16_hurt birds_served chicken sandwhiches_bird society_audobon.gif
title: Pretending Chicken Sandwich Needs CPR

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just met with the Birdabon Society. I had to promise we won't hurt any birds.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our caterer served chicken sandwiches for lunch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I pretended to give mine CPR but I was really eating it.

situation: The Boss stands beside Dilbert's desk and explains that he promised a bird protection society the company would not hurt any birds. He then mentions that the caterer served chicken sandwiches for lunch. He admits he got around the awkwardness by pretending to resuscitate his sandwich while actually eating it.
punchline: The Boss's absurd workaround to avoid hypocrisy, faking CPR on a chicken sandwich while eating it, shows how management satisfies the letter of a promise while ignoring its spirit.
summary: Having vowed to a bird-lovers group that the company won't harm birds, the boss deals with a lunch of chicken sandwiches by feigning to revive his meal while devouring it.

file: 2000/2000-10-07_beatings_coworkers_improve moral_performance review_team player_beatings deserved.gif
title: Alice's Violent Team Player Review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Lastly, what have you done to improve the morale of your co-workers?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I didn't give them the beatings they so richly deserved.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll shorten that to "team player"?

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: During her performance review, the Boss asks Alice what she has done to boost her co-workers' morale. Alice, arms crossed, says she improved morale by refraining from beating them up. The Boss cheerfully decides to record this as 'team player' on her review.
punchline: Alice claims credit for morale simply by not assaulting her colleagues, and the Boss's willingness to spin that into 'team player' shows how low the bar is and how review language sanitizes anything.
summary: Asked how she lifts her colleagues' spirits, a hostile employee credits her restraint from violence, and her manager happily rewrites that as praise.

file: 2000/2000-12-26_rifle though pockets_meditate_mixed with management.gif
title: Meditation Empties The Boss's Mind

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think he tried to meditate.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: That's the problem.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You shouldn't mix meditation with management. The mind gets too empty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What can we do?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I plan to rifle through his pockets.

situation: The Boss lies unconscious on an exam table while a doctor examines him and Dilbert looks on. Dilbert explains that the Boss tried to meditate, and the doctor says meditation and management don't mix because the mind gets too empty. When Dilbert asks what can be done, the doctor says he plans to rifle through the Boss's pockets.
punchline: The doctor treats the Boss's empty mind as a medical emergency but his only remedy is to steal from the incapacitated patient, mocking both management's mental vacancy and unscrupulous professionals.
summary: A physician diagnoses the incapacitated boss with a dangerously blank mind and then announces he'll help himself to the patient's belongings.

file: 2000/2000-09-28_show plan_budget_resources_weakness.gif
title: Asking Boss for Resources Is Weakness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sure your boss will increase the budget if you show him my plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just asked him for something else. I can't keep asking him for resources!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you think that doing your job is a sign of weakness?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Look what it did to you.

situation: Dilbert suggests that the Boss show Dilbert's plan to his own superior to get a bigger budget. The Boss refuses, saying he has already asked for something else and can't keep requesting resources. When Dilbert points out that requesting resources is part of the Boss's job, the Boss replies by pointing at Dilbert as proof of what doing the job does to a person.
punchline: The Boss treats doing one's job as a sign of weakness and uses Dilbert's own overworked, struggling state as evidence that diligently asking for resources only leads to misery.
summary: A manager dodges requesting more funding for his team by insisting that Dilbert's own state shows what actually working leads to.

file: 2000/2000-09-15_ankle_connection_cure is deactivate_email monkey_on back_palm strapped.gif
title: Catbert Cures Asok's Email Monkey

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Asok, you have a bad case of e-mail monkey-on-the-back.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The only cure is to deactivate your internet connection.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No problem. Heh, heh.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I know you have a Palm VII strapped to your ankle.

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: Heh heh

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells Asok he suffers from an e-mail addiction, depicted as a monkey clinging to his back. He prescribes cutting off his internet connection as the only cure. Asok calmly agrees, but Catbert reveals he knows Asok has a wireless Palm VII hidden on his ankle, so the cure won't work.
punchline: Asok pretends to accept the cure, but Catbert knows he has a hidden wireless device, showing his e-mail addiction can't be shaken and that Catbert is always one step ahead.
summary: An evil H.R. cat diagnoses an employee's e-mail addiction and prescribes disconnection, then calls out the concealed wireless gadget the man was relying on.

file: 2000/2000-11-30_one vote_cpr_heimlich maneuver_two votes_yelling boo_drill hole_below.gif
title: Committee Votes on Rescuing Choking Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, we have one vote for using CPR, one vote for the Heimlich maneuver...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And two votes for sneaking up behind him and yelling "Boo."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't see how we can get behind him.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What if we drill a hole from below?

setting: Office, among a group of coworkers
situation: During an emergency, Dilbert tallies a group vote on how to help a colleague who appears to be choking or in distress. The options include proper first aid, but two people vote to scare him by yelling "Boo." When Dilbert notes they can't get behind the man, a coworker suggests drilling a hole from below.
punchline: The group treats a medical emergency like a committee decision, choosing absurd, useless options and dismissing the correct ones.
summary: A team puts a life-or-death rescue to a vote and ends up favoring ridiculous, impractical ideas over real first aid.

file: 2000/2000-12-23_exceeding expectations_padding objectives_whistle blower_award.gif
title: Whistle-Blower Award for Sandbagging Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As you know, I'm the only employee who is not exceeding expectations.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You should punish the others for unscrupulously padding their objectives!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Those lying weasels!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I get a whistle-blower award for this?

situation: Wally sits in front of the Boss's desk and points out that he is the only employee not exceeding expectations. He urges the Boss to punish his coworkers for inflating their performance objectives, calling them lying weasels. He then asks whether he can receive a whistle-blower award for reporting them.
punchline: Wally admits his own poor performance is the baseline, then tries to turn his coworkers' goal-padding into a reward for himself by posing as a heroic whistle-blower.
summary: A slacker employee tries to turn his coworkers' inflated targets into a prize for himself by reporting them to the boss.

file: 2000/2000-12-27_avoid work_faking coma_punch repeatedly_get alice_right or left handed.gif
title: Punching Boss to Test Coma

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He might be faking a coma to avoid work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The only way to find out is to punch him repeatedly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should get Alice.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you remember if I'm right- or left-handed?

situation: The Boss lies motionless on a conference table or couch while Dilbert and Wally stand over him. Wally suspects he is faking a coma to dodge work and proposes punching him repeatedly to find out. Dilbert suggests fetching Alice instead, while Wally eagerly asks which of his hands is dominant, preparing to start punching.
punchline: Wally is so keen to hit the unconscious boss that he treats the diagnosis as an excuse for violence, and he can't even remember which hand he punches with.
summary: Two coworkers hover over their unresponsive manager, and one of them cheerfully plans a fist-based test to expose a suspected fake coma.

file: 2000/2000-11-01_new job_starts with l_window shuts_company_business.gif
title: Catbert Spelling Out Layoffs

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need a new job within the company before the window shuts.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Catbert is already up to "O." Next week he gets an "S."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's he spelling?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He wouldn't say, but it starts with an "L."

situation: A coworker in a yellow-patterned tie tells Dilbert he needs to transfer to a new job within the company before a deadline passes. He explains that Catbert, the evil HR director, is revealing one letter at a time, already at "O" with an "S" coming next week. The coworker deduces the word starts with "L" and, though he never says it, it is obviously "LOSE" or "LOSS" and means layoffs are coming.
punchline: Catbert is gradually spelling out an ominous word starting with "L-O-S", signaling impending layoffs, and the coworker is too anxious or in denial to say it aloud.
summary: A nervous employee races to find another position before the HR director's slow letter-by-letter reveal announces job cuts.

file: 2000/2000-12-10_doing it wrong_response time_sub second_two seconds_always right_never wrong_screaming.gif
title: Dilbert Concedes Absurd Math to Win

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And we'll have sub-second response time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, it's already two seconds, and your change will add two more.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why do you always have to be right?!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Just once can't you admit I'm right?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I admit that two plus two equals less than one.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't mean now, jerk. I mean in general.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. In general I admit that the rules of physics are optional.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're doing it wrong!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're right. My fault again.

situation: Alice promises sub-second response time, but Dilbert points out that the system is already at two seconds and her change will make it slower. Furious that he is always right, Alice demands he admit she is right, so Dilbert sarcastically agrees to absurd claims about math and physics. She then screams that he is doing it wrong, and he gives in.
punchline: Dilbert shows that the only way to 'admit Alice is right' is to agree to nonsense, and when she still berates him, he concedes everything sarcastically because arguing with her is futile.
summary: A colleague who cannot stand being corrected demands agreement, so a sarcastic engineer endorses impossible claims until she finds fault with that too.

file: 2000/2000-12-14_the succession plan_leader_multi viatmin_safe now_mixed blessing.gif
title: Succession Plan: Save the Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The succession plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If anything happens to me, Wally will be your leader.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have a multi-vitamin! Quick, take it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're safe for now.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This turned out to be a mixed blessing.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that if anything happens to him, Wally will become the team's leader. Alarmed at the prospect of Wally in charge, Alice and Dilbert hurriedly force a multi-vitamin on the Boss to keep him healthy. Wally, who has just lost his shot at power, remarks that it was a mixed blessing.
punchline: The team is so horrified by the idea of Wally as leader that they go out of their way to protect their incompetent boss, while Wally ruefully notes that the outcome is mixed for him.
summary: Learning the lazy Wally would inherit command, coworkers rush to keep their clueless manager alive and well.

file: 2000/2000-12-21_incomprehensible accent_won't ask questions_coffee pot.gif
title: Incomprehensible Accent Avoids Coffee Questions

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm thinking of adopting an incomprehensible accent so people won't ask me questions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...are you leaving that coffee pot empty right in front of me?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Meeyerna derna furna algonkin buhjoorna.

setting: Office break room with a coffee maker
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker pours the last of the coffee into his mug and announces that he wants to adopt an incomprehensible accent so people will stop asking him questions. Dilbert then points out that he has left the coffee pot empty right in front of him. The coworker immediately responds in gibberish, putting his new plan into action.
punchline: The coworker uses his fake incomprehensible accent at the first opportunity to dodge Dilbert's question about emptying the coffee pot without refilling it.
summary: A man who drains the coffee pot answers the resulting complaint with nonsense syllables to prove his new question-avoidance strategy works.

file: 2000/2000-12-25_clear mind_thoughts_forward basis_market space_done practicing.gif
title: Clearing Mind Yields Buzzword Nonsense

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I must clear my mind of all thoughts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At the end of the day we'll be in a market space on a going forward basis.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Om... Om... Page...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll come back when you're done practicing being useless.

situation: The Boss stands with his eyes closed trying to meditate and clear his mind while Dilbert knocks at his door. Instead of silence, the Boss starts spouting empty corporate buzzwords, then chants 'Om... Om... Page...' as if his meditation is also paging him. Dilbert decides to leave until the Boss has finished.
punchline: When the Boss empties his mind of all thoughts, what comes out is the same meaningless buzzword jargon he always speaks, so Dilbert notes that he is just practicing being useless.
summary: A manager attempts meditation but his blank mind only produces corporate jargon, prompting an employee to walk away unimpressed.

file: 2000/2000-11-09_learning golf_male dominated golf events_golf events.gif
title: Alice Takes Up Golf

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm learning to golf.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now I won't be excluded from all the male-dominated golf events.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you been dominating golf events?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes I can make them miss putts on TV.

situation: Alice announces she is learning to golf so she won't be excluded from male-dominated golf events. Dilbert asks, using her phrasing, whether she has been dominating golf events. The Boss, apparently off to the side, chimes in that he sometimes makes golfers miss putts on TV, misreading the question entirely.
punchline: Dilbert's question gets answered by the Boss, who absurdly claims he can make pro golfers miss putts on television, as if he were somehow 'dominating' golf events from his desk.
summary: A coworker takes up golf to join the networking scene, and a clueless executive mistakes a question about dominating events for a boast about jinxing televised putts.

file: 2000/2000-10-02_evil director_union work_employees moving company computer_old evil_pdas_laptops_cut of giblets_union steward stuart.gif
title: Union Steward Proposes Old Evil

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: What new evil do you bring me, Union Steward Stuart?

transcript.speaker: Stuart
transcript.text: Employees should not be allowed to move company computers. That's union work.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's old evil.

transcript.speaker: Stuart
transcript.text: It's new if we include PDAs and laptops.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I like the cut of your giblets.

situation: Catbert, the Evil H.R. Director, asks union steward Stuart what new evil he has brought. Stuart proposes that employees be forbidden from moving company computers because that is union work, and Catbert dismisses it as old evil. Stuart expands the rule to cover PDAs and laptops, which wins Catbert's approval.
punchline: Union rules that silly are not new, but extending them to portable devices counts as fresh evil, and Catbert admires the pettiness in his odd, cat-like way.
summary: A union representative pitches a petty equipment-moving rule to a malevolent HR cat, who only approves once it is stretched to handheld gadgets.

file: 2000/2000-11-28_beef eating_just stress_mandatory cpr_middle aged men_training for emplyees_pear shaped.gif
title: Mandatory CPR Training Heart Attack Fears

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company will be holding mandatory CPR training for all employees.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Gaa!!

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: I am surrounded by pear-shaped, beef-eating, middle-aged men who I prefer not to touch.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Uh-oh... I hope that's just stress.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces at a meeting that the company will hold mandatory CPR training for all employees. A coworker in a green shirt panics, realizing he is surrounded by out-of-shape middle-aged men he would have to perform mouth-to-mouth on. He then notices chest discomfort and worries he might be the one needing CPR.
punchline: The man's dread of having to give CPR to his unhealthy colleagues turns into fear that he himself is having a heart attack, implying he is exactly the sort of person nobody wants to resuscitate.
summary: A new compulsory resuscitation course makes one worried employee realize his out-of-shape coworkers, and perhaps his own aching chest, are the real hazard.

file: 2000/2000-12-07_excused_god judge you_honor_judge_jury selction_legal.gif
title: Changing Religion to Escape Jury Duty

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Jury selection

transcript.speaker: Juror in turban
transcript.text: Your honor, it is against my religion to judge others. Only God may judge.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: You're excused.

transcript.speaker: Bald juror
transcript.text: Ooh ooh! I just changed my religion!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Jerk.

situation: During jury selection, a juror in a turban tells the judge that his religion forbids judging others, and the judge promptly excuses him. A bald juror sitting nearby, who also wants out, eagerly raises his hand and announces he has just changed his religion. Dilbert silently thinks the man is a jerk.
punchline: Seeing that a religious objection gets someone out of jury duty, another juror instantly and shamelessly invents a conversion to qualify for the same exemption.
summary: A juror's faith-based excuse works so well that his neighbor opportunistically adopts a new belief on the spot to dodge duty too.

file: 2000/2000-12-18_casula dress_encourage flirtatious_ladies concentrate_seater_turtleneck_warning cones.gif
title: Warning Cones Around Adorable Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: I worry that casual dress days encourage flirtatious behavior.

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: I mean, look how adorable I am in my turtleneck sweater. How are the ladies supposed to concentrate?

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: Do you think I should put warning cones around my cubicle?

situation: A bald employee in a red turtleneck sweater stands in front of The Boss's desk and voices concern that casual dress days encourage flirting. He then reveals the real worry is that his own adorable appearance will distract the women in the office, and suggests putting warning cones around his cubicle. The Boss sits silently behind his desk, looking unimpressed.
punchline: The employee's pretense of worrying about workplace flirting is really self-flattery, as he assumes his turtleneck sweater is so irresistible that coworkers need to be warned away from his cubicle.
summary: A vain co-worker pitches a dress code concern to the boss that turns out to be a boast about his own irresistible charm.

file: 2000/2000-12-12_perfromance review_say its good_rub in face_expectations.gif
title: Boss Won't Praise Work Before Review

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that what you wanted?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not saying.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I tell you it's good, you'll rub it in my face at your performance review.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: See how you are?

situation: Dilbert hands in a piece of work and asks the Boss whether it is what he wanted. The Boss refuses to say whether it is good, claiming Dilbert would use any praise against him at the performance review. When Dilbert apologizes, the Boss treats the apology as proof of Dilbert's bad character.
punchline: The Boss withholds all feedback out of paranoia that praise will be used against him, then blames Dilbert for being the kind of person who would do that, even though Dilbert did nothing.
summary: A manager declines to evaluate an employee's work out of fear that approval will be quoted back at him come review time, and then accuses the employee of being difficult.

file: 2000/2000-10-04_customer type_feeble minded people_reorganize_second guess_dogbert consults.gif
title: Reorganize By Feeble-Minded Customers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need to reorganize by customer type.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One division would focus on selling to feeble-minded people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you gesturing at me because I would work in that division?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's your second guess?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the company to reorganize its divisions by customer type. He suggests one division should sell to feeble-minded people and gestures toward the Boss. The Boss asks if he is being pointed at because he would work in that division.
punchline: Dogbert's sarcastic reply, asking for the Boss's second guess, confirms that the Boss is indeed the kind of person who belongs in the feeble-minded division.
summary: A consultant dog proposes sorting a company by customer type and slyly implies his client belongs in the division for the dim-witted.

file: 2000/2000-11-16_alice_hand_head_new temp_new temp likes_shakes hand on head.gif
title: Alice's Crushing Handshake

transcript.speaker: New Temp
transcript.text: It's a pleasure to meet you, Alice.

transcript.speaker: New Temp
transcript.text: Ooowee! That was a good hand shake.

situation: A new temp greets Alice and offers a handshake. In the second panel Alice grips his hand so violently that his whole body is thrown into convulsions and his head bobs, and afterwards he admiringly calls it a good handshake.
punchline: Alice's famously fierce temper makes even a simple handshake a painful, body-wrenching ordeal, yet the temp cheerfully takes it as a compliment.
summary: A newcomer's greeting to Alice turns into a violent handshake that leaves him shaking but oddly impressed.

file: 2000/2000-11-08_talking to much_compensate_society expectation_think up ideas_sit quiet_nothing good.gif
title: Dogbert Advises Boss: Talk More

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can compensate for your lack of knowledge by talking too much.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And don't be limited by society's expectation that you be interesting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes I like to sit quietly and think up ideas.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nothing good can come from that.

situation: Dogbert, standing on the Boss's desk, coaches him on how to hide his ignorance by talking constantly and not worrying about being interesting. The Boss responds that he sometimes likes to sit quietly and think up ideas. Dogbert dismisses that approach as never producing anything good.
punchline: Dogbert insults the Boss by implying that his thinking is worthless, so the only way he can seem competent is to keep talking.
summary: A consultant dog teaches his clueless manager to bluff through conversation, then waves off the idea of quiet reflection as pointless.

file: 2000/2000-09-22_doomed projects_fake mergencies_more efficient_unnecessary meetings_to do list.gif
title: Dilbert's To-Do List Reveals Dogbert's Wisdom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This to-do list will make me more efficient.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have three fake emergencies, two doomed projects, four unnecessary meetings...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I figured out why you never ask me how my day went.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Off you go.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and then his home
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer thinking that a to-do list will make him more efficient, but the list he mentally compiles is full of fake emergencies, doomed projects and pointless meetings. He then goes home and tells Dogbert he has realised why Dogbert never asks about his day. Dogbert curtly sends him away.
punchline: Dilbert's workday is so full of pointless nonsense that even his own dog doesn't want to hear about it, so Dogbert dismisses him.
summary: After tallying up a workday made of bogus crises and useless meetings, Dilbert understands why nobody at home wants to hear about it.

file: 2000/2000-10-21_satisfied with job_afraid of change_purr_best work.gif
title: Catbert Convinces Employee She's Afraid

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You think you're satisfied with your job.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: In reality you're just afraid of change!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purrr purrr

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That was some of my best work.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells a seated female employee that she only thinks she is satisfied with her job. He declares that she is really just afraid of change, leaving her looking worried. He then walks away purring, proud of the psychological manipulation.
punchline: Catbert gleefully congratulates himself for talking a contented employee into doubting her own happiness, showing H.R. as a source of manufactured dissatisfaction.
summary: An H.R. cat plants unease in a content worker by reinterpreting her satisfaction as fear, then struts off pleased with his cruelty.

file: 2000/2000-11-29_cpr_take kidney_leave in ice_strip him_save him.gif
title: Boss Confuses CPR With Kidney Theft

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Asok is down. Does anyone know CPR?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is CPR the one where we take his kidney and leave him in a tub of ice?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'd better strip him and shave him just in case.

situation: Asok has collapsed and only his upturned legs are visible, while Dilbert asks if anyone knows CPR. The Boss offers a bizarre guess that CPR means harvesting the victim's kidney and leaving him in a tub of ice. Dilbert doubts this, so the Boss suggests stripping and shaving Asok anyway, just in case.
punchline: The clueless Boss confuses emergency first aid with a black-market organ theft and still insists on doing the worst parts of it to be safe.
summary: When a coworker collapses, the oblivious boss misremembers first aid as a kidney heist and proposes undressing and shaving the victim anyway.

file: 2000/2000-11-04_incurable romantic_shoe_foot fungus_cured_table leg.gif
title: Romantic Cured By Dilbert's Foot Fungus

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I've always been an incurable romantic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I take off my shoe? I've got some sort of fungus that needs air.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm cured!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to scratch it on the table leg. Oops. Is that you?

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a date with a woman who declares she is an incurable romantic. Dilbert asks to remove his shoe to air out a foot fungus, then mentions scratching it on the table leg and fumbles when he touches her leg by mistake. She is instantly repulsed.
punchline: Dilbert's gross foot-fungus confession instantly cures the woman of her romanticism, literally making her 'cured' as she recoils.
summary: A date's romantic declaration is destroyed when her companion airs out his fungal foot and rubs it on what he thinks is the table.

file: 2000/2000-11-10_feminist freak out_hin_hiney_tall the hun_behind back_harsh_slave driver_ruthless_alice.gif
title: Boss Calls Alice 'Hun'

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks, hun.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hon?!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You sexist %!*%! I will burn your village and make slaves of your children!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's short for Attila the Hun. Everyone calls you that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That seems harsh.

situation: The Boss hands Alice a paper and thanks her, calling her 'hun'. Alice assumes it's a sexist pet name and explodes with threats to burn his village and enslave his children. The Boss calmly explains it is short for Attila the Hun, the nickname everyone uses for her behind her back.
punchline: Alice's furious threats of pillaging and enslavement prove that her nickname 'Attila the Hun' fits her perfectly, even as she finds the nickname harsh.
summary: A manager's casual endearment turns out to be a nickname for a ferocious employee, who reacts exactly as the name predicts.

file: 2000/2000-12-17_attending meetings_busy_funding_get funding_need a budget_past year_top priority_one task.gif
title: Boss Forgot Funding, Attended Meetings

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everything is ready. We just need the budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You did get the funding... didn't you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been very busy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This project has been your top priority for over a year!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You only had one task: get funding.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What have you been doing for the past year?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I remember attending meetings...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aay-iii-yiii-yiii!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you need anything, just holler.

situation: Dilbert reports that his project is ready and only needs its budget, then discovers the Boss never secured the funding. The Boss claims he has been busy, and when Dilbert demands to know what he did all year, the Boss can only recall attending meetings. Dilbert screams in frustration while the Boss cheerfully offers help.
punchline: The Boss failed at his single task for a whole year, can only remember sitting in meetings, and responds to Dilbert's breakdown with an oblivious offer of help.
summary: A manager who spent a year doing nothing but sitting in meetings never got the money his employee's project needed, and shrugs off the screaming fallout.

file: 2000/2000-11-07_boring_director of information_e-diot_easy way_title.gif
title: The Boss Becomes the E-diot

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You should put an "E-" in front of your title.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's too boring just being the Director of Information, Operations and Technology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, call me the E-diot.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If only there were an easy way to remember that.

characters: Director of Information, Operations and Technology
setting: Office, in the boss's office and at a cubicle
situation: A bald, bespectacled executive holding a coffee mug tells the boss to add an "E-" in front of his title because his current one is boring. The boss enthusiastically announces he wants to be called the "E-diot." Alice, sitting at her desk, sarcastically remarks on how easy that would be to remember.
punchline: Adding "E-" to the boss's title produces "E-diot," which Alice sarcastically notes is already a perfect description of him, so it will be easy to remember.
summary: A trendy dot-com title upgrade turns the clueless boss into an unwitting self-described idiot, and Alice is happy to point it out.

file: 2000/2000-09-13_email_email monkey_feeling of self worth_quit whenever.gif
title: Email Monkey on His Back

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Send

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ooh!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I get a tiny feeling of self-worth when I send e-mail to my boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Looks like someone has an e-mail monkey on his back.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I can quit whenever I want!

setting: Office cubicles and a break area
situation: A cubicle worker thinks about hitting send on an email and gets a thrill from it. He admits he feels a tiny bit of self-worth whenever he emails his boss. Two coworkers holding coffee mugs note he has an 'e-mail monkey on his back', while he sits with an actual monkey clinging to him and insists he can quit anytime.
punchline: The employee's dependence on sending emails for validation is treated like a drug addiction, complete with the addict's denial that he can stop whenever he wants.
summary: A man hooked on the little ego boost of emailing his boss is diagnosed by coworkers as having a literal monkey on his back.

file: 2000/2000-09-26_bought cisco_cardboard box_dogcart consults_entrepreneurial_misdialed bookie_revive spirt.gif
title: Founders Were Bums Who Bought Cisco

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can revive the entrepreneurial spirit here by reminding people of the early years.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your founders were two bums who began in a cardboard box.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One bum misdialed his bookie and accidentally bought Cisco stock at the IPO.

setting: Conference room during a consulting presentation
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises a company to revive its entrepreneurial spirit by recalling its early years. He presents a picture of the company's founders as two bums living in a cardboard box. He explains that their success came from one bum accidentally buying Cisco stock at its IPO after misdialing his bookie.
punchline: The company's celebrated founding story is really just dumb luck, so there is no real entrepreneurial spirit to revive.
summary: A consultant dog tells executives their company's heroic origin was nothing more than a homeless man's wrong-number stock purchase.

file: 2000/2000-10-31_30 day dance of death_new job within_spray paint.gif
title: Catbert Spray-Paints Ted's Termination Notice

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ted, your thirty-day dance of death begins today.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You must find a new job within the company during that time.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Is the spray-paint absolutely necessary?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's an "L."

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells Ted that he has thirty days to find another job inside the company or be let go. While explaining the rules, Catbert sprays paint on Ted, and when Ted objects, Catbert explains he is marking him with an 'L'.
punchline: Catbert is branding Ted with a spray-painted 'L' for 'loser', adding public humiliation to an already dire layoff process.
summary: An HR cat gives an employee a month to find a new internal position while cruelly tagging him with graffiti.

file: 2000/2000-09-19_house on fire_servant_killing spiders_wounded flies_work at home person says_what family hears.gif
title: Work-at-Home Warning Gets Mistranslated

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: What the work-at-home person says

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't disturb me unless the house is on fire.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: What the rest of the family hears

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am your servant. My specialty is killing spiders.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: What the spiders hear

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The house is full of wounded flies.

setting: Dilbert's home, in front of a blue couch where two pets sit
situation: In three identical panels, Dilbert, working from home, makes a statement while a yellow pet and a white pet sit on the couch behind him. Captions show how the same sentence is understood by himself, by his family, and by the spiders in the house. Each audience hears something entirely different from what he meant.
punchline: What the home-working person intends as a demand for uninterrupted peace is heard by the family as an offer of household servitude, and by the spiders as an invitation to feast.
summary: A telecommuter's request for quiet turns into a chore offer for his family and a free buffet announcement for the arachnids.

file: 2000/2000-10-27_fired everyone_used the internet_personal stuff_wrinkle_policy_web.gif
title: Catbert Fired Everyone, Including Internet Users

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I fired everyone who used the Internet for personal stuff.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The only wrinkle in that policy is that you and I are the only employees left.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And frankly, I use the web for personal stuff too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you teach me how?

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells the Boss he has fired every employee who used the Internet for personal reasons. He then admits that this leaves only the two of them in the company, and that he uses the web for personal stuff as well. The clueless Boss responds by asking Catbert to teach him how.
punchline: The strict policy wiped out the whole company, and the Boss, instead of being alarmed, only wants to learn how to do the forbidden personal web browsing himself.
summary: A ruthless HR cat enforces a web-usage rule so thoroughly that only he and his oblivious boss remain, and the boss just wants browsing lessons.

file: 2000/2000-11-12_south pole_sending away_control freak_manipulating_sending dilbert_cold.gif
title: Sent to the South Pole

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I signed you up for a trip to the South Pole.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... why?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You'll love it. You leave tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am not going to the South Pole!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh, I get it; you're a control freak.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa! Can't you see that it's you who is trying to control me?!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: All I see is you trying to manipulate me into not sending you to the South Pole.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It seemed easier.

situation: Alice announces she has signed Dilbert up for a trip to the South Pole leaving tomorrow. When Dilbert refuses, she accuses him of being a control freak, then claims his protests are manipulation to avoid being sent. In the last panel Dilbert, already dressed in a parka with luggage, concedes that going was easier than arguing.
punchline: Alice's circular logic makes any objection look like manipulation, so Dilbert gives up and goes to the South Pole because it's less effort than fighting her.
summary: A coworker forces an unwanted polar trip on Dilbert and turns his every objection into proof that he is the one being controlling, so he just surrenders.

file: 2000/2000-09-23_key to success_really fast_speed_ok to fail.gif
title: Doing Wrong Things Really Fast

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Speed is the key to success.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it okay to do things wrong if we're really, really fast?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Um... no.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I'm all confused, thank you very much.

situation: The Boss presents a slide with a running stick figure and declares that speed is the key to success. Dilbert raises his hand and asks whether doing things wrong is acceptable if done very quickly. Alice answers no, and the Boss complains that the question has confused him.
punchline: The Boss's speed-obsessed slogan collapses under a simple logical question, and he responds with irritation at being confused rather than rethinking his message.
summary: A manager's rush-everything motto is undermined when an employee asks the obvious follow-up about quality versus speed.

file: 2000/2000-12-28_tape pencil_hand_raise_would be unethical_ten percent_hiccup damage_moral compass.gif
title: Hiccup Damages Moral Compass Fraud

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll tape a pencil to his hand and use it to sign off on a raise for me.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That would be so unethical...

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Hiccup

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: May I have ten percent?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That hiccup damaged my moral compass.

situation: Wally tells a coworker he plans to tape a pencil to the unconscious Boss's hand and use it to sign off on a raise for himself. The coworker calls it unethical, then hiccups and immediately asks for ten percent of the take. Wally gets the paperwork signed while the coworker blames the hiccup for his lost conscience.
punchline: The coworker's ethics vanish at the first opportunity for profit, and he absurdly blames a hiccup for his moral lapse.
summary: A scheme to forge the sleeping Boss's signature on a raise gains a quick accomplice whose conscience conveniently gives way.

file: 2000/2000-11-23_tips today_how much_three breath mints_death threat_scrawled napkin_napkin guy.gif
title: Waiter's Tips: Mints and Death Threat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much did you make in tips today?

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: Three breath mints and one death threat scrawled on a napkin.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: I hope I don't forget which breath mint came from the napkin guy.

setting: A restaurant or workplace break area with a light blue background
situation: Dilbert, holding a handful of cash, asks a bald, bespectacled waiter how much he made in tips. The waiter replies that he received only breath mints and a death threat written on a napkin. He then worries about confusing the mint from the threatening customer with the others.
punchline: The waiter's tips are worthless junk, and his real concern is that one of the breath mints came from a man who threatened to kill him and might be tainted or dangerous to eat.
summary: A waiter reports his meagre haul of mints and a threatening note, then frets about accidentally eating the mint from the person who menaced him.

file: 2000/2000-09-10_mapped genome_hr dept_had resources_pencil_technology_predictions from genes_genome_dna_work perfromance_traits_violation of rights.gif
title: Catbert Predicts Wally's Boring Genome

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I mapped your genome, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't know the Human Resources department had that technology.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I used a pencil.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your genes predict that you will be a bitter, lazy, Caucasian guy with six hairs and poor vision.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You'll hate cubicles, measurable objectives, and cats who map your genome.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is a violation of my right to privacy! I'll fight it all the way to the Supreme Court!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No, according to my map, you'll lose interest and fall asleep.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I wonder if this technology will ever fall into the wrong hands.

situation: Catbert, the HR cat, announces he has mapped Wally's genome, then reveals he did it with a pencil. He reads off 'predictions' that are just a description of Wally as he already is, and Wally threatens a privacy lawsuit. Catbert predicts Wally will lose interest and fall asleep, which he promptly does.
punchline: The 'genetic predictions' are simply obvious observations about Wally's existing laziness, and Wally proves the prediction right by dozing off, while Catbert ironically muses about the technology falling into the wrong hands even though he is the one misusing it.
summary: The HR cat claims to have decoded his coworker's DNA with a pencil and confidently forecasts a future that matches the man's present slackness exactly.

file: 2000/2000-11-19_business book_change happens_forward_meds filler_parable_picnic_served as hamburgers_two bulls.gif
title: Dogbert Writes Padded Change Book

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm writing a business book called "Change Happens. Get Over It."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The title says it all.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah, it needs filler.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about a parable?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good idea.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Two bulls were talking.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One bull says, "I'm afraid of change."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The other bull says, "Get over it."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Later that day they were both ground into hamburgers and served at a picnic.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The hard part will be finding someone to write the foreword.

situation: Dogbert announces he is writing a business book titled "Change Happens. Get Over It." and admits it needs filler. Dilbert suggests a parable, and Dogbert types out a story about two bulls, one afraid of change and one dismissive, who both end up as picnic hamburgers.
punchline: The parable's grim ending mocks the glib 'get over it' advice of business books, and the final line implies the book is so thin that even finding someone to endorse it will be harder than writing it.
summary: A dog author pads a flimsy self-help title with a dark farm fable and worries only about who will praise it.

file: 2000/2000-10-30_flunking all classes_son_computer job_fill in blanks_people don't like.gif
title: Filling In The Blanks

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My son is flunking all his classes. I'm hoping he can get a job involving computers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carrying them?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People don't like it when you fill in the blanks in their stories.

situation: A female coworker tells Dilbert that her son is failing all his classes and she hopes he can find a computer job. Dilbert completes her thought by asking if she means the computers would carry him. Afterward he remarks to Dogbert that people dislike having the blanks in their stories filled in.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic guess implies that computers are so easy or forgiving that a failing student could get by on them, and he sums up the lesson that people resent hearing the unspoken part of their own story said out loud.
summary: After a coworker voices a hopeful plan for her struggling son, Dilbert bluntly finishes her sentence and then muses on why that goes over badly.

file: 2000/2000-11-21_wally_engineer_snide of attitude_incomprehensible_technical review_sarcasm_engineering.gif
title: Wally Waits Tables as Engineer

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My name is Wally and I'll be your engineer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our special today is incomprehensible mumbling in an acronym sauce with a snide of attitude.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll just have a technical review.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you want sarcasm with that?

setting: Office cubicle, staged like a restaurant table
situation: Wally stands over Dilbert's desk with a notepad and pencil, introducing himself like a waiter and reciting the day's 'special' as a description of his engineering style. Dilbert plays along and orders a technical review, and Wally asks if he wants sarcasm on the side.
punchline: Wally's engineering help is framed as a restaurant menu where the only offerings are jargon-filled mumbling and a snide attitude, with sarcasm as a default add-on.
summary: An engineer takes a coworker's request like a waiter, offering a menu of obscure jargon and a bad attitude.

file: 2000/2000-12-05_jruy duty_what excuse_happy to serve_civic responsibility_insanity_good one.gif
title: Dilbert's Civic Duty Mistaken for Insanity

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Jury duty

transcript.speaker: Mustached Juror
transcript.text: What excuse are you planning to use?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm happy to serve. It's my civic responsibility.

transcript.speaker: Mustached Juror
transcript.text: Insanity; good one.

situation: Dilbert sits in the jury box reading a red book while a mustached fellow juror asks what excuse he plans to use to get out of jury duty. Dilbert sincerely says he is happy to serve out of civic responsibility. The other juror assumes this is a clever lie, claiming insanity to avoid serving.
punchline: Dilbert's sincere willingness to serve is so unthinkable to the other juror that he assumes Dilbert is feigning insanity as an excuse.
summary: A cheerful volunteer for jury duty is assumed by his skeptical neighbor to be pretending to be crazy.

file: 2000/2000-12-03_flex time_5 hours in morning_break for then hrs_5 hours later_filthy cubicle_downside_plan_staff meeting_cherish_clever schemes_sarcasm.gif
title: Wally's Flex Time Scheme

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd like to work flex time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll work for five hours before anyone else gets to the office...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I'll take a break for ten hours...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I'll work five more hours after the witnesses... er... co-workers go home.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll know I'm working hard because my cubicle will be filthy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But I have to be perfectly honest; there's a down side to this plan.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I would miss your staff meetings that I cherish so much.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm having trouble keeping my clever schemes separate from my sarcasm.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway near the cubicles
situation: Wally asks the Boss for a flex time arrangement, describing a schedule in which he works at hours when no one is around to see him. He claims his filthy cubicle will prove he is working hard, then sarcastically says he would miss the staff meetings. In the last panel he confides to Dilbert that he can't tell his schemes from his sarcasm.
punchline: Wally's flex time plan is really a scheme to avoid being seen working at all, and the closing line admits that even he can't tell whether he is being sincere or sarcastic.
summary: Wally pitches a bizarre work schedule that ensures nobody ever sees him on the job, then wonders aloud whether he is scheming or just being sarcastic.

file: 2000/2000-12-09_crime_finding guilty_jury finding_proram_witness protection.gif
title: Jury Foreman Seeks Witness Protection

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The jury verdict

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We find the defendant guilty...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...of this crime and maybe a few others that didn't come up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lastly, do you have any brochures for the witness protection program?

setting: A courtroom, with the jury box and judge's bench
situation: Dilbert, serving as jury foreman, reads out the verdict to the judge. He finds the defendant guilty of the charged crime and of a few other crimes that were never raised in court. He then asks the judge for witness protection brochures, afraid of what the convicted defendant will do.
punchline: The jury foreman is so frightened of the criminal he just convicted, who is apparently guilty of many other crimes too, that he asks for witness protection information as part of his verdict.
summary: A juror reading out a guilty verdict suddenly worries about his own safety and asks the judge how to go into hiding.

file: 2000/2000-10-08_the inspirational ceo_poor results_engineers_cause & effcet_generate results_pathetic losers_losers_energy_squirming_health.gif
