title: Inspirational CEO Calls Everyone Losers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The inspirational CEO

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Our company is too good to have results this poor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: %#!* engineers.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying the laws of cause and effect do not apply?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Logically, if we were good, we would generate good results.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it not more likely that we are pathetic losers who get exactly what we deserve?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Yes, individually you're all losers. But together we're a great company.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Thanks to my leadership.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I feel like squirming but I don't have the energy.

setting: Company meeting or all-hands presentation with a CEO at a podium
situation: A CEO tells the staff their company is too good to be getting such poor results. Dilbert asks whether the laws of cause and effect apply and suggests the employees might simply be pathetic losers getting what they deserve. The CEO agrees they are individually losers but claims the company is great because of his leadership.
punchline: The CEO sees no contradiction in calling every employee a loser while crediting himself for the company's greatness, and the demoralized staff are too drained even to squirm.
summary: A boastful executive blames poor results on everyone but himself, and an engineer's logical challenge only earns an insulting, self-congratulating reply.

file: 2000/2000-11-22_working for tips_rfp_spec binder.gif
title: Waiter Insults Customer Over RFP

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate working for tips.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: No, I ordered the R.F.P.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you were thinking R.F.P. But you said spec binder, you arrogant cow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With any luck, she'll say, "You had me at cow."

setting: Restaurant, with Dilbert working as a waiter
situation: Dilbert, moonlighting as a waiter in an apron, delivers a red binder to a woman who says she actually ordered the R.F.P. Dilbert snaps at her, blaming her for misspeaking and calling her an arrogant cow. Then he hopes in a thought bubble that she will find it charming, while she glares at the binder.
punchline: Dilbert insults a customer and then naively hopes she'll respond with a romantic movie-style line, when she is plainly furious.
summary: A waiter who resents tip-based pay gets an order wrong, loses his temper at the diner, and then fantasizes that she'll find his rudeness irresistible.

file: 2000/2000-10-29_flirting_cashier_phoney_customer service smile_required_looks like flirting_wally.gif
title: Mistaking Customer Service Smile for Flirting

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Thank you. Have a nice day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's flirting with me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...would you like to go out on Saturday?

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: I wasn't flirting. This is my phony customer service smile.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Employees are required to smile.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, but NOW you're flirting, aren't you?

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: No, still phony.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally has to see this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, it looks like she's flirting with me!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is this great or what?

situation: Dilbert is checking out and takes the cashier's friendly smile as flirtation, so he asks her out. She explains the smile is a required, fake customer service expression, and she keeps insisting it is phony even when he presses her. Dilbert then brings Wally over to watch, pretending she's flirting with him.
punchline: Dilbert, rejected and still in denial, uses the cashier's obviously fake smile to stage a show for Wally, hoping to enjoy the awkwardness he's causing.
summary: A hopeful man asks out a store clerk whose cheerful grin turns out to be nothing more than a job requirement.

file: 2000/2000-09-20_escalate_escalator_marketing guys_misunderstands_need to escalate_goes to store.gif
title: Boss Takes Escalate Literally, Rides Escalator

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The marketing guys are stalling. You need to escalate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Must escalate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll never understand how this helps.

setting: The Boss's office, then a department store
situation: Carol tells the Boss that the marketing department is stalling and that he needs to escalate the issue. The Boss mutters that he must escalate and walks off, and in the last panel he is riding an escalator in a department store, puzzled about how this will help.
punchline: The clueless Boss misunderstands the management term 'escalate' (raise an issue up the chain of command) and literally goes to ride an escalator.
summary: A manager told to push a stalled project up the chain mistakes the jargon for a mode of transport and heads to a shopping mall.

file: 2000/2000-09-30_bags of crud_highly valued_stock options_worth a fortune_worthless_shut up.gif
title: Stock Options Insult Reversed Quickly

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My stock options are worth a fortune now, you miserable bag of crud!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, look, they're back down to worthless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try telling him that bags of crud are highly valued in some societies.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Shut up.

setting: The Boss's office and a conference room
situation: Wally gloats at the seated Boss that his stock options are now worth a fortune and insults him. The Boss, reading a newspaper, calmly checks the market and says the options have already dropped back to worthless. Later in a meeting, Dilbert suggests telling the Boss that bags of crud are prized in some cultures, and Wally tells him to shut up.
punchline: Wally's smug boasting about his stock options is deflated within one panel when the market crashes, leaving him embarrassed and snapping at Dilbert's teasing.
summary: A gloating employee's brief stock-option windfall evaporates just as he finishes insulting his manager, leaving him sour.

file: 2000/2000-09-18_fun organization_rubber chicken_hurt so much.gif
title: Boss Announces Fun Organization, Gets Hurt

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, this is going to be a fun organization.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When are you leaving?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had no idea that a rubber chicken could hurt so much.

situation: The Boss sits at the head of a conference table and announces that the company will now be a fun organization. Wally responds by asking when he is leaving. In the last panel the Boss is bruised and ruffled, and Dilbert stands beside him holding a rubber chicken, implying he was just beaten with it.
punchline: The Boss's forced-fun initiative is so unwelcome that his employees respond with open hostility and physically attack him with a rubber chicken, the symbol of tacky corporate fun.
summary: A manager's attempt to mandate workplace fun ends with him battered by the very novelty prop he thought would cheer everyone up.

file: 2000/2000-12-02_asok alive_cpr_angles_ratbert_rat is blue_lifesavers.gif
title: Who Gave Asok CPR?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm alive!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which one of you angels administered the life-saving CPR?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Speaking of "lifesavers," I could sure use one right now.

situation: Asok wakes up on the floor and announces he is alive while coworkers stand over him. The Boss asks which of the assembled coworkers gave him life-saving CPR. Ratbert, a small blue creature, steps forward and makes a joke about needing a lifesaver, implying he is the one who performed the CPR and now has a bad taste in his mouth.
punchline: Ratbert is the one who gave Asok mouth-to-mouth CPR and wants a breath mint (a Life Savers candy) to get rid of the aftertaste.
summary: After a collapsed coworker revives, the small blue rat who rescued him reveals his heroism with a candy-flavored quip.

file: 2000/2000-10-24_catbert_personal use_stealing from company_human resources_form a gang_business.gif
title: HR Employee Admits Stealing Too

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your personal use of the Internet is like stealing from the company!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You work in Human Resources; that's like stealing from the company, too.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Maybe we should form a gang.

setting: Office desk in Catbert's Human Resources office
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, accuses a bald, bespectacled employee of stealing from the company through personal Internet use. The employee fires back that Catbert's own HR job is a form of theft too. He then suggests the two of them team up as a gang of thieves.
punchline: The employee implies that HR contributes nothing of value and is itself a drain on the company, so the two 'thieves' might as well join forces.
summary: Accused of wasting company resources online, a worker turns the tables by calling the accuser's entire department a form of theft.

file: 2000/2000-11-27_cpr dummy_lie on back_mouth open_your help.gif
title: Wally Becomes the CPR Dummy

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, we can't find our CPR dummy. I need your help.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Finding it?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yes, assuming you can do that while lying on your back with your mouth open.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Wally that the company's CPR training dummy has gone missing and that he needs Wally's help. Wally assumes he is being asked to help search for it. Catbert clarifies that he wants Wally to stand in for the dummy.
punchline: Catbert is not asking Wally to find the dummy but to replace it, insultingly implying that Wally is as lifeless and useless as a training mannequin.
summary: A request for help locating a missing training mannequin turns into an insult when the HR cat wants the lazy employee to fill in for it.

file: 2000/2000-10-13_new guy_rude or shy_rudy_shilo_don't know name_boss introductions_no one knows_name him.gif
title: Naming the Rude or Shy Newcomer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the new guy. I don't know his name.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's either rude or shy. No one knows for sure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you figure it out, name him either Shilo or Rudy.

situation: The Boss introduces a silent new employee to Dilbert but admits he doesn't know the man's name. He explains that nobody can tell whether the newcomer is rude or shy, and tells Dilbert to name him accordingly once he figures it out.
punchline: The Boss thinks a person's name should be chosen based on a guess about his personality (Shilo for shy, Rudy for rude), rather than simply asking him what he's called.
summary: A manager presents an unnamed, unresponsive new hire and suggests a coworker pick a nickname based on whether the fellow is bashful or impolite.

file: 2000/2000-09-11_good look at file_murder confession_the file_sign papers.gif
title: Boss Signs Murder Confession Unread

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Now sign this and this and this.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is a murder confession.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's for the file.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someday I'm going to take a good look at that file.

situation: Carol, the Boss's secretary, hands her boss a stack of papers and tells him to sign them. He notices one is a murder confession, but she says it's just for the file. He signs anyway, musing that he will eventually look through that file.
punchline: The Boss knowingly signs a confession to murder without objection, assuming the file is never read, while vaguely promising himself he'll review it someday, showing his habit of signing things without scrutiny.
summary: A secretary has her boss sign a pile of documents, including a confession to murder, and he shrugs it off as filing paperwork he'll never actually review.

file: 2000/2000-12-31_advice_collect crcystals_ctcystals can heal_scientific evidence_point of view_ignorant_dinner date_spoiled.gif
title: Dilbert Fails At Being Less Himself

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Any advice?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try to be less like you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That might work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Less like me...less like me.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I collect crystals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know of any scientific evidence that they can heal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whew.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: But it's my point of view that they do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When did ignorance become a point of view?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too much like me.

setting: Dilbert's home, a hallway, and a restaurant
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for dating advice and is told to be less like himself. He hands flowers to his date and tries to follow the advice, but when she says she collects healing crystals he cannot stop himself from challenging the lack of scientific evidence. He then ruins the dinner by asking when ignorance became a point of view.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to be less like himself collapses the moment his rationalist instincts kick in, and he realises at dinner that he behaved exactly like himself.
summary: A date goes sour when a man told to act unlike himself can't resist debunking his companion's belief in crystal healing.

file: 2000/2000-12-22_free for lunch_remind myself_lucky_laziness_personality_looks_renaissance loser_psychology.gif
title: Lunch Invitation Becomes Backhanded Insult

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, are you free for lunch?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to remind myself how lucky I am that I don't have your laziness or personality or looks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Would you say I'm kind of a Renaissance loser?

situation: Dilbert pokes his head over the cubicle wall and asks Wally to lunch. He explains that he wants to be around Wally to remind himself how fortunate he is not to share Wally's laziness, personality or looks. Wally, unfazed, asks whether that makes him a 'Renaissance loser'.
punchline: Wally treats Dilbert's insulting invitation as a compliment, proudly noting that he is a loser in many different areas, like a Renaissance man is skilled in many.
summary: A colleague invites a slacker to lunch purely to feel superior, and the slacker responds by proudly claiming a well-rounded failure.

file: 2000/2000-09-17_business manager_for celebrities_have locks_life story_sign here_film on thursday_someone steal your fortune_the biography channel.gif
title: Dogbert Manages Celebrity Fortunes, Then Profits

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I decided to become a business manager for celebrities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because banks have locks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Everything you own has been put in my name..for...um..tax purposes.

transcript.speaker: Celebrity
transcript.text: You're such a good friend.

transcript.speaker: Celebrity
transcript.text: How can I ever repay you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can sign this.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It gives me the rights to your life story.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In the unlikely event that someone steals your fortune and you become a pathetic drug addict...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...I can sell your story to the "Biography" channel.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They start filming on Thursday.

situation: Dogbert explains to Dilbert that he became a celebrity business manager because it gives him access to money. He tells a celebrity client that all his assets are now in Dogbert's name, and the celebrity gratefully signs a document giving Dogbert the rights to his life story. Dogbert then reveals he can sell the story of the client's downfall, with filming starting almost immediately.
punchline: Dogbert has already stolen the celebrity's fortune and arranged to profit again from the ruin he caused, as the biography filming starts in just days.
summary: A scheming dog fleeces a famous client of everything he owns and then cashes in on the tragic tale of his ruin.

file: 2000/2000-10-06_executive offices_office too far_forgetting you name_move office_secretary_forgets boss.gif
title: Office Too Far From Executives

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your office is too far from the executive offices.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It is?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They are actively forgetting your name even as we speak. It's going...going...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Gone!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, we have to move my office!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Have we met?

setting: Office, the Boss's office and Carol's desk outside it
situation: A bald coworker holding a coffee mug warns the Boss that his office is too far from the executive offices, so the executives are literally forgetting who he is. Alarmed, the Boss rushes to his secretary Carol and demands they move his office. Carol replies as if she has never met him.
punchline: Carol's 'Have we met?' shows that even the Boss's own secretary has forgotten him, proving the coworker's warning about being out of sight and out of mind.
summary: A colleague convinces the Boss that distance from the executives is erasing him from their memory, only for his own secretary to prove how forgettable he is.
themes: out of sight out of mind

file: 2000/2000-11-14_catbert_evil director_most evil way_database_customer information_sell mailing list_spam_balckmail_data bse_clumping.gif
title: Catbert Weighs Evil Database Uses

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the most evil way to use our database of customer information?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should we sell our mailing lists, spam without mercy, or just blackmail customers?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Um... Do you have me in that database?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We know all about your clumping problems.

situation: The Boss asks Catbert, the evil H.R. director, to pick the most evil way to exploit the company's customer database: selling mailing lists, spamming, or blackmail. Catbert nervously asks whether he himself is in the database. The Boss replies with a creepy, personal remark about his clumping problems.
punchline: The Boss's reply shows the database already contains embarrassing personal details, so blackmail is clearly already underway, with Catbert as a target.
summary: A cat in charge of human resources frets about being included in a customer database that his boss is ready to abuse in sinister ways.

file: 2000/2000-10-22_deliver bad news_meet goals_fire an engineer_sales people_immoral_punish engineers_hole puncher.gif
title: Firing Ted, Borrowing His Hole Puncher

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes a manager must deliver bad news.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Luckily I enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our sales force failed to meet their goals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I have to fire an engineer to reduce expenses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should fire the incompetent sales people!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's immoral to punish innocent engineers for the sins of sales people! I will fight this all the way!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm firing Ted, not you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you wait until I borrow his hole puncher?

situation: The Boss announces that because the sales force missed its goals, he must fire an engineer to cut expenses, and he admits he enjoys delivering bad news. Dilbert objects on moral grounds and vows to fight it, until the Boss clarifies he is firing Ted, not Dilbert. Dilbert immediately drops his principled stance.
punchline: Dilbert's fierce moral outrage evaporates the moment he learns someone else is the target, and he only cares about grabbing Ted's hole puncher before Ted is let go.
summary: A boss's plan to sacrifice an engineer for sales failures sparks righteous indignation that vanishes once the victim turns out to be a coworker.

file: 2000/2000-09-24_angle_central cubicle commitee_floaty device_guidelines!_shift_stapled_wally pool.gif
title: Cubicle Committee Polices Computer Angle

transcript.speaker: Cubicle Committee Member
transcript.text: Halt!

transcript.speaker: Cubicle Committee Member
transcript.text: You moved your computer without approval from the Central Cubicle Committee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was simply adjusting the angle.

transcript.speaker: Cubicle Committee Member
transcript.text: Gasp

transcript.speaker: Cubicle Committee Member
transcript.text: Fool! It will cost $200 for a team of technicians to move it back!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's better this way so my plant won't fall off.

transcript.speaker: Cubicle Committee Member
transcript.text: We have guidelines!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know. I stapled them to my wall.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'd be surprised at what isn't allowed.

situation: A tall-haired official from the Central Cubicle Committee confronts Dilbert for moving his computer without approval, claiming it will cost $200 to have technicians move it back. Dilbert calmly explains he only adjusted it for his plant and mentions he stapled the guidelines to his wall. In the last panel, Wally lounges in a pool in his cubicle on a pink floaty and remarks on the surprising range of things not allowed.
punchline: The committee obsesses over a trivial computer adjustment while Wally sits in an inflatable pool in his cubicle, implying that the rules are enforced arbitrarily and absurdly.
summary: A bureaucratic cubicle inspector scolds Dilbert over a slightly turned monitor while a coworker floats in a private pool nearby.

file: 2000/2000-12-16_questions_ever alone_with people.gif
title: Dilbert Presents, Feels Alone Among Colleagues

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are there any questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever feel alone when you're with people?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I try to.

situation: Dilbert finishes a presentation next to an org-chart slide and asks if anyone has questions. His audience is unresponsive: one coworker sits with arms crossed, another stares blankly, and a third drools beside a bottle. Dilbert then asks Dogbert, who is reading a paper, whether he ever feels alone in a group, and Dogbert replies that he tries to.
punchline: Dogbert says he deliberately tries to feel alone around people, a misanthropic reply that also underlines how disengaged and lifeless Dilbert's audience is.
summary: After a presentation to a checked-out audience, a lonely engineer wonders aloud about isolation in a crowd, and his dog says he actively seeks it.

file: 2000/2000-11-17_agency_get it_hand_joke_play on words_dogbert temp.gif
title: Temp Agency Hand Pun

transcript.speaker: Temp Worker
transcript.text: I'm from the Dogbert Temp Agency. Do you need a hand?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I get it. Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Temp Worker
transcript.text: Get what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I said, "Don't get mad; try counting to fifteen."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ouch.

situation: A temp worker from the Dogbert Temp Agency, who has one hand raised on top of his head, offers Dilbert a hand at his computer. Dilbert laughs at the pun, and the temp doesn't understand what's funny. Later Dilbert retells the story to a coworker, delivering the line that counting to fifteen is the advice he gave the one-handed temp.
punchline: The temp's offer of 'a hand' turns into a cruel joke when Dilbert tells him to count to fifteen, which is impossible for someone with only one hand showing, since he can only count to five, so the insult is lost on him but not on the coworker who winces.
summary: A temp offers a helping hand, and Dilbert later boasts to a colleague about the sneaky insult he slipped past the oblivious temp.

file: 2000/2000-10-10_payroll problem_wrong person_speak with supervisor_forward call.gif
title: Call Forwarded to the Wrong Person

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to find someone who can help me with a payroll problem.

transcript.speaker: Call Center Employee
transcript.text: You're close. I'm the guy who forwards your call to the wrong person.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to speak with your supervisor.

transcript.speaker: Call Center Employee
transcript.text: I'll forward your call.

setting: Office cubicles, on a phone call
situation: Dilbert phones the company looking for help with a payroll problem. The man who answers cheerfully explains that his job is forwarding calls to the wrong person. When Dilbert asks for a supervisor, the man just forwards the call again.
punchline: The employee's only function is to misroute callers, so asking for his supervisor simply sends Dilbert to yet another wrong person.
summary: A frustrated caller discovers that the person answering the phone exists solely to bounce calls to people who cannot help.

file: 2000/2000-12-20_can't lift arms_employees work harder_motivated_uncomfortable clothes_casual dress days.gif
title: No Casual Days: Uncomfortable Clothes Policy

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There will be no more casual dress days.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We believe that employees work harder when they are wearing uncomfortable clothes.

transcript.speaker: Employee in armor
transcript.text: I feel all motivated but I can't lift my arms.

setting: Office, at a desk during an HR announcement
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces to an employee that casual dress days are cancelled because uncomfortable clothing supposedly makes people work harder. In the final panel the employee sits at his desk wearing a suit of armor while Dilbert stands beside him in a bulky spacesuit.
punchline: Taking the 'uncomfortable clothes boost productivity' logic to absurd extremes, the employees wear armor and a spacesuit and are too encumbered to actually do any work.
summary: An HR policy demanding miserable attire backfires when staff show up in clunky costumes that leave them motivated yet physically unable to function.

file: 2000/2000-11-02_begging for job_boss_callous_mean_office.gif
title: No Jobs In Your Heart

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Catbert says I have to get a new job within the company.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Could you find it within your heart...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll check.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nope. No jobs in there.

situation: An employee tells his boss that Catbert, the HR head, requires him to find a new position inside the company. He asks the boss to find one in his heart. The boss reaches over, pretends to check his own heart, and reports back that there are no jobs in there.
punchline: The boss literally interprets 'finding it in your heart' as a heartless joke, callously dismissing the employee's plea for help.
summary: A worker pleads for a transfer from his boss, who mockingly checks his own heart and coldly declares it empty of openings.

file: 2000/2000-11-13_gigantic database_customer behavior_information_non linear math_data mining technology_optimize retail channels_spam_meeting here.gif
title: Data Mining Equals Spam Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have a gigantic database full of customer behavior information.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excellent. We can use non-linear math and data mining technology to optimize our retail channels!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If that's the same thing as spam, we're having a good meeting here.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert the company has a huge database of customer behavior information. Dilbert enthusiastically proposes using non-linear math and data mining to optimize retail channels. The Boss, misunderstanding the technical jargon, asks whether that is the same as spam.
punchline: The Boss reduces a sophisticated analytics proposal to spam, showing he only follows buzzwords and measures the meeting's success by whether it matches something he vaguely understands.
summary: A manager mistakes a data analyst's talk of advanced mining techniques for junk email marketing and declares the meeting a success if they match.

file: 2000/2000-09-25_dogbert consults_obvious generalities_fees_recommending.gif
title: Consultant's Free Advice Costs $90,000

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my report full of obvious generalities.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My fee is $90,000.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What are you recommending?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend telling everyone it was free.

setting: The Boss's office, across his desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, hands the Boss a thick red report that he admits is full of obvious generalities. He then announces a $90,000 fee. When the Boss reads the report and asks what it recommends, Dogbert advises him to tell everyone the consulting was free.
punchline: The consultant's only real advice is to hide how much the worthless report cost, since the client would be embarrassed to admit paying $90,000 for platitudes.
summary: A consultant delivers an expensive, empty report and suggests the client conceal what it cost.

file: 2000/2000-12-06_hole in head_jurors_jury box_jury selction_medical condition_questioning_serving_judge_legal.gif
title: Juror Needs Jury Duty Confusion

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Jury selection

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Juror eight, do you have any medical problems that would prevent you from serving?

transcript.speaker: Juror Eight
transcript.text: No, I need jury duty.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Would it be fair to say you don't know what you need?

transcript.speaker: Juror Eight
transcript.text: Why does everyone ask me that?

situation: A judge questions prospective jurors about medical problems that might keep them from serving. Juror eight, a man with an odd hole or opening in his head, says he needs jury duty. The judge points out he apparently doesn't know what he needs, and the juror complains that everyone says that to him.
punchline: The judge politely implies the juror is clueless or brain-damaged, and the juror's puzzled reply shows he is routinely told this and still doesn't understand why.
summary: A confused prospective juror insists he needs jury duty, prompting the judge to gently suggest he lacks self-awareness.

file: 2000/2000-12-08_cleint_lawyer_juror_sleeping juror_snoring_fell asleep_legal.gif
title: Jury Sleeps Through Closing Argument

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: My client's life now rests in your capable hands.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Zzzz zzzzz zzz

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Jury deliberations

transcript.speaker: Juror
transcript.text: Did anything happen after "please rise"?

situation: A defense lawyer delivers his closing argument, telling the jury that his client's life is in their hands. The jurors, including Dilbert, are all fast asleep. In the deliberation room, a juror admits he has missed everything since the start of the trial.
punchline: The jurors who will decide a man's fate slept through the entire trial, having noticed nothing since the bailiff said "please rise."
summary: A whole jury dozes through the case, then tries to decide a verdict without having witnessed any of it.

file: 2000/2000-10-25_you're fired_used internet_personal reasons_groceries_more time working_evil but true.gif
title: Catbert Fires Employee Over Groceries

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our records show that you used the Internet for personal reasons.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're fired.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Please, I merely ordered groceries online so that I might have more time for working.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: My motto is, you can't spell "who cares?" without H.R.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's evil, but it's true.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells an employee that company records show he used the Internet for personal reasons and fires him on the spot. The employee pleads that he only ordered groceries online to free up more time for work. Catbert answers with his motto about H.R. and the employee grudgingly concedes the point.
punchline: Catbert's motto points out that the letters "H.R." are hidden inside "who cares?", mocking the department's total indifference to employees, and the employee admits it is accurate.
summary: An HR cat sacks a worker for shopping online and brushes off his reasonable excuse with a wordplay motto about indifference.

file: 2000/2000-11-18_blank copies_copied wrong sides_intern_new temp_talk to  hand_tells off.gif
title: Blank Copies Blamed on Blank Originals

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: These copies you made for me are blank.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's because all the originals were blank.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe you could have checked the other sides.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Talk to the hand.

situation: A coworker holding a stack of paper complains to Wally that the copies Wally made for him are all blank. Wally calmly says the originals were blank too. When the coworker points out Wally could have checked the other sides of the pages, Wally raises his hand and tells him to talk to the hand.
punchline: Wally wasted effort copying blank pages without bothering to check them, and when his laziness is pointed out he dismisses the criticism with a 'talk to the hand' brush-off.
summary: A worker gets a pile of empty photocopies and discovers the person who made them never looked at the pages and refuses to accept any blame.

file: 2000/2000-09-21_current version_making changes_slap forehead_test software_major changes.gif
title: Testing Software Before Tuesday's Changes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you test the software today?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I'm making major changes Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could test the current version.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wish people wouldn't slap their foreheads and say "Aye-yi-yi-yi" every time I talk.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to test the software today, but Dilbert says he can't because he plans major changes on Tuesday. The Boss suggests testing the current version instead, and Dilbert responds by slapping his forehead in exasperation. The Boss, in a thought bubble, wonders why people react that way whenever he speaks.
punchline: The Boss makes an obvious suggestion that exposes his own ignorance of how testing works, and is baffled that his reasonable-sounding input leaves people groaning in despair.
summary: A manager's naive suggestion to test the existing code leaves his engineer clutching his head, while the manager puzzles over why everyone reacts that way to him.

file: 2000/2000-10-01_vital records protection plan_extensive interviews_key stakeholders_digitized_records_encryotion_natural magnets_project team status report_liars.gif
title: Wally Improvises a Records Protection Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, what's the status of our vital records protection plan?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Think fast.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I...uh...did extensive interviews with key stakeholders.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I...uh...formed a plan...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now all the records are digitized and stored with 512 bit encryption...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: ...at the center of the earth...on natural magnets.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I meant you should read the project team's status report.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They claim to have a plan.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Liars.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss asks Wally for the status of the vital records protection plan. Wally, caught unprepared, invents an absurd plan on the spot involving digitized, encrypted records stored on magnets at the center of the earth. The Boss reveals he only wanted Wally to read the project team's report, so Wally pivots to calling the real team liars.
punchline: Wally, having improvised a ridiculous fake plan, instantly accuses the actual project team of lying when their real plan contradicts his invention.
summary: Put on the spot in a meeting, a slacker fabricates an outlandish data-protection scheme and then brands the real team dishonest when his story is exposed.

file: 2000/2000-10-20_kiss daughter goodnight_working too hard.gif
title: Boss Mocks Employee's Unattractive Daughter

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: You're working me too hard! I want to get home in time to kiss my daughter goodnight!

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: And I'm not the only one who feels this way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've seen your daughter and I'm fairly certain you're the only one.

situation: An employee stands in the boss's office and complains that he is being overworked because he wants to get home to kiss his daughter goodnight. He adds that others feel the same way. The boss, seated at his desk, replies that having seen the daughter, the employee is probably the only one who wants to kiss her.
punchline: The boss dismisses the complaint with a cruel insult, implying the employee's daughter is so unattractive that no one else would want to kiss her goodnight.
summary: A worker pleads for shorter hours to see his child, and his boss shuts him down with a brutal jab about her looks.

file: 2000/2000-11-11_hawaiian shirt day_dishing punishment_perks_fake smile.gif
title: Hawaiian Shirt Day Disguised Punishment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I declare next Friday to be "Hawaiian Shirt Day."

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Hey, you're disguising punishments as perks!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're on to us.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Did you try the fake smile?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces a Hawaiian Shirt Day, and an employee points out that he is dressing up a punishment as a perk. The Boss grins, then privately tells Catbert that the staff has caught on. Catbert, the evil human resources director, asks whether he tried the fake smile.
punchline: Management knowingly passes off unpleasant measures as employee benefits, and when caught, the only fallback is to feign sincerity with a fake smile.
summary: A manager's cheerful casual-dress announcement gets called out as a disguised penalty, and his HR adviser suggests faking a grin to cover it.

file: 2000/2000-09-29_huge demand_laugh at yourself_employes.gif
title: Demand for Employees, Except You

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, there's a huge demand for employees like you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But not you specifically.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...Which is funny if you think about it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, if you can't laugh at yourself, who can you laugh at?

situation: The Boss approaches Ted, who is holding a coffee mug, and appears to compliment him by saying employees like him are in high demand. He then clarifies that nobody actually wants Ted himself, and tells him to find it funny. Ted's expression grows increasingly blank and uneasy as the Boss laughs it off.
punchline: The Boss turns a backhanded insult into a lesson about self-deprecating humor, telling Ted to laugh at the fact that he is personally worthless to the job market.
summary: A manager dangles a flattering remark about job demand, then yanks it away by insisting the worker himself is unwanted, and expects a laugh.
keywords: funny if you think about it

file: 2000/2000-12-04_away from job_blah blah_cell phones_jurors_jury duty_jury room_read book_talking.gif
title: Jury Duty Book Reading Ruined

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aahh, one sweet week away from my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have hours of quiet time to read my new book.

transcript.speaker: Woman on phone
transcript.text: There's a guy here with a book.

transcript.speaker: Jurors
transcript.text: Yadda yadda blah blah. Blah yadda. Blah blah. Yack yack.

setting: A courthouse jury room, with Dilbert's office shown in a flashback panel
situation: Dilbert walks toward the jury room, happily imagining a week away from work with plenty of quiet time to read his new book. In the jury room, every other juror is chattering on a cell phone. A woman beside him tells her caller that there's a guy here with a book, treating his reading as a bizarre oddity.
punchline: Dilbert's hope for peaceful reading time is crushed by a room full of constant cell phone talkers, who regard a man reading a book as a strange curiosity.
summary: A man looking forward to reading during jury duty finds himself surrounded by noisy phone chatterers who find his book fascinating.

file: 2000/2000-11-05_an olympic gold medal_apply own job_emailed jokes_fired_posthumous medal_reclassification of job_requires phd_synchronized swimming 1992_top ten signs.gif
title: Reclassified Job Requires Impossible Qualifications

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Am I fired?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Of course not, Ted. I enjoy e-mailed jokes as much as anyone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm still laughing about your "Top Ten Signs That Your Boss Is A Hairless Rodent".

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I asked you here to discuss the reclassification of your job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Starting today, the job requires a Ph.D.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Feel free to apply for your own job.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Whew! Luckily, I have a Ph.D.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, the job also requires an Olympic gold medal.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Synchronized swimming, 1992.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: And a posthumous Congressional Medal of Honor.

situation: Ted nervously asks the Boss whether he is fired after sending a mocking e-mailed joke about the boss. The Boss says he is only reclassifying Ted's job, adding requirements like a Ph.D. and an Olympic gold medal so Ted must reapply for his own position. Ted turns out to meet every requirement, even absurd ones.
punchline: The Boss invents increasingly impossible job requirements to push Ted out, but Ted already has every one of them, including a posthumous medal he could not possibly have received.
summary: A boss tries to engineer his employee out of a job with absurd new qualifications, only to discover the employee somehow already has them all.

file: 2000/2000-11-03_last day_farewells_working_row_stay in touch_stranger.gif
title: Farewell Tour Reaches Total Stranger

transcript.speaker: Departing Employee
transcript.text: Today is my last day. I'm saying my farewells.

transcript.speaker: Departing Employee
transcript.text: We've never talked, but I was working my way down the row and here you are.

transcript.speaker: Departing Employee
transcript.text: So... let's stay in touch.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Don't be a stranger.

situation: An employee on his last day goes down the row of cubicles saying goodbye to everyone. He reaches a coworker he has never spoken to and awkwardly admits it, then suggests they stay in touch. The silent coworker replies with the stock phrase 'don't be a stranger'.
punchline: The two are literally strangers who have never talked, so the polite farewell cliché 'don't be a stranger' is absurdly ironic.
summary: A leaving worker bids an obligatory goodbye to someone he has never met, and the hollow pleasantries of parting become unintentionally ironic.

file: 2000/2000-09-12_emergency flashlight_plays flashilights_jedi_starwars_immature.gif
title: Hiding Flashlights From Lightsaber Play

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hid the emergency flashlights so no one can play with them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Who plays with flashlights? That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) The short Jedi will die first.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces he has hidden the emergency flashlights so employees can't play with them. Wally scoffs that nobody would play with flashlights. In the last panel the Boss, secretly holding a flashlight like a lightsaber, imagines a Star Wars-style duel in which the short Jedi dies first, apparently eyeing the shorter Wally.
punchline: The Boss's claim that others would play with the flashlights is projection, since he is the one who pretends they are lightsabers and is already planning a Jedi duel in his head.
summary: A manager confiscates flashlights to stop staff from playing with them, then gets caught up in his own private Star Wars fantasy.

file: 2000/2000-10-14_300 times_coffee_funny_jokes_not funny_sugar.gif
title: Coffee With Your Sugar Joke

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Why don't you have a little coffee with your sugar, Alice?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Heh, heh. It's funny because it's usually the other way around.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: I don't see how something can be funny 300 times but not 301 times.

situation: Alice is stirring a mug of coffee at the break room counter, loaded with sugar packets, when a bald coworker in glasses teases her to have some coffee with her sugar. He laughs at his own joke and explains why it's funny. In the last panel he stands alone, puzzled that his joke no longer gets a reaction.
punchline: The coworker has made the same tired joke 300 times and is baffled that Alice doesn't find it funny the 301st time, missing that repetition is what killed the humor.
summary: A man who keeps repeating the same sugar-and-coffee quip to a coworker can't understand why it has stopped being amusing.

file: 2000/2000-12-30_more email_storage space_all files_complain_ignore requests_your only choices_please veryone.gif
title: Deleting Files Instead of Adding Storage

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I asked for more e-mail storage space and you deleted all of my files!

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: You complain when I ignore your requests and you complain when I delete your files.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Those aren't your only choices!!

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: I can't please everyone.

setting: Office cubicle, IT support worker's desk
situation: Dilbert confronts an IT support guy at his desk because he asked for more e-mail storage and instead had all his files deleted. The IT guy argues that he gets complaints whether he ignores requests or deletes files. Dilbert points out those are not the only two options, and the IT guy shrugs it off.
punchline: The IT guy frames his choices as only ignoring users or destroying their data, and then claims he can't please everyone, using a false dilemma to excuse his poor service.
summary: A tech support worker justifies wiping an employee's files by pretending his only alternative was to disregard the request.
